Earlier today, the attacker behind the recent @binance  exploit, apparently in error, sent approximately 8.0M NEWT directly to the NEWT token contract address (0xd0ec028a3d21533fdd200838f39c85b03679285d), along with 17 other tokens: $ANIME, ethereum:0x8290333cef9e6d528dd5618fb97a76f268f3edd4, $ARPA, $BARD, $CELR, ethereum:0x3597bfd533a99c9aa083587b074434e61eb0a258, ethereum:0x0f81001ef0a83ecce5ccebf63eb302c70a39a654, $FTT, $GLM, $HIGH, $HOT, $KNC, $LQTY, $RARE, ethereum:0x259338656198ec7a76c729514d3cb45dfbf768a1, $SIGN and $WOO. These tokens are worth roughly $3.5 million at current prices.

To be clear, the NEWT token contract itself was not compromised.

We have reviewed the contract carefully, and unfortunately these tokens cannot be recovered. The NEWT token contract was built to be immutable: it has no owner or admin, all admin rights were renounced onchain in 2025, and upgrades are permanently disabled. That design exists to protect holders, so that no one, including the Foundation, can ever move or alter their tokens. These safeguards mean there is no way for anyone to retrieve tokens sent to the contract itself.

These tokens are now permanently locked. They are out of the attacker’s control and can never be sold into the market.

We have shared our findings with Binance and we will keep helping however we can.

The Binance hack is yet another $6.3B reminder that in crypto, the technical details almost never decide the narrative. To the outside world, the headline is simply: crypto got hacked again, this time at the biggest exchange, and the infrastructure can't be trusted.

That reputation still costs the industry more than the financial loss. Every headline like this slows institutional adoption and gives skeptics another easy talking point.

However, markets read events differently. A loss of this size that gets absorbed, with withdrawals paused, about $3B frozen, and users made whole, looks a lot more like capitulation than collapse. Moments like this tend to mark bottoms, not tops.

With this hack, it looks like attackers are scaling with AI and going after people and pipelines, not cryptography. In the age of AI and crypto, cybersecurity is about to change profoundly in both scope and profitability, and the companies that become that new layer will be enormous. That's an area I’m looking into at @coinfund.

你不是跟其他用戶對賭，而是全部跟 OLP（他們自己的做市商）對賭。OLP 會拿自己的資金去外部交易所（包含 Binance）對沖風險。如果對沖虧損導致 OLP 破產：

你原本的抵押品還是可以提
但未實現/已實現損益會變成壞帳，可能拿不到

所以「資金在鏈上」是事實，但讓人感覺「完全安全」其實不是。Variational 應該更透明，直接公開 OLP 目前的外部曝險、資本緩衝、甚至對沖地址，而不是只說「資金都在鏈上」。
author: UST_mean
quoted_text:
is Variational telling half-truths about fund safety?

interesting take from Degen Guy
Variational’s statement on the Binance hack sounds reassuring - “user money is on-chain, doesn’t go to external hedge exchanges, 100% withdrawable anytime”

technically true, collateral sits in isolated on-chain settlement pools and isn’t sent to CEXs

but there’s a nuance they didn’t mention

on Omni you don’t trade against other users - you trade against a single counterparty, OLP (their internal market maker). All trades go through RFQ, and OLP is the one that has to pay you your profit

OLP hedges its exposure with its own capital on external exchanges (including Binance and others). If OLP loses money on hedges and becomes insolvent:

- your original collateral can still be withdrawn
- but unrealized and realized PnL turns into bad debt and doesn’t get paid

so the platform really doesn’t touch your deposits, but your profit depends on OLP’s solvency, which is directly tied to the risks of the same external exchanges they hedge on

the statement is technically correct, but it creates a feeling of full safety that doesn’t actually exist

to really reassure users they should show OLP’s current external exposure and capital buffer, not just say “collateral is on-chain”
until then it looks like a careful half-truth

I recommend subscribing to his TG channel - justdegenguy

10/29 币安被盗事件又给全行业敲了一次警钟。被攻破的不一定是代码。所有的创始人、开发团队，甚至是运营、HR等等看似离代码很远的岗位，每个人都可能是黑客的突破口。

2024年11月，我们面试过一个前端开发人员。我们收到的是中文简历，中文名字。履历里面记录了他在Bybit, 阿里巴巴等工作经历。在面试的时候，我们发现他的口音是韩式英文，并且不会说中文。我们要求他打开摄像头，摄像头那端，他的像素模糊，画面质感像15年前的摄像头。他带着头戴式耳机，有刘海，和下面截图的这个人非常相似。

我问他会不会说中文，他说不会。我问他是哪里人，他说是日本人。然后我问他在中国和新加坡的工作经历，他含糊其辞。几轮交流下来，我们怀疑他是不是朝鲜黑客，于是结束了面试。从他的简历和背景来看，造假的概率很高。

事情过去了接近两年，今天看到这张照片恍然大悟。

也在此给所有的项目方提醒：面试一定要求开摄像头，PDF不要轻易下载。一定要让全公司的同事都有安全防范意识，不要留下弱点让黑客攻击。

最后，希望加密社区团结一致。我们都在这里支持币安 @cz_binance  @heyibinance @zachxbt

就在两周前，字节跳动创始人张一鸣与 Seed 负责人吴永辉共同召开了一场 Seed 全员会（All Hands）。
久未露面的张一鸣也表达了自己对 seed 的支持。我们（晚点）独家了解到：

➡️ 训大模型本就是一件很难的事，团队不必过度焦虑。他明确一段时间内可接受模型落后于行业，希望大家以追求智能上限为目标，期待 Seed 模型能力能跻身世界第一梯队。

➡️ 认可编程（Coding）是当前的关键方向，所以要把火山引擎、飞书和豆包的资源整合到一起，只有这样才能构筑在算力和数据上的优势。但他也提醒，编程只是眼下的热点之一，不应该完全被它牵着走，编程之外还有更多更大的机会。

➡️ 表扬了 Seedance，认为这个模型在市场上很特别，也有领先的技术优势。相比追随其它领先模型的既有路线，他更鼓励 Seed 做出有自己特色的模型。

➡️ 反对蒸馏，认为蒸馏能在短期内改善模型表现，但本质上仍是在复制 Claude 已有的能力。沿着这条路走，最多只能不断逼近对方，很难真正实现超越。

➡️ 希望 Seed 可以从更底层的维度去构建自己在 AGI 上的壁垒。

➡️ 过去几年，字节已经在 AI 方向投入了很多；未来，还会投入更多。

SITUATION EXPLAINED: Google DeepMind researchers say AI has barely changed the economy because AI agents still can't work together like human teams.

• Google DeepMind's AGI economics director Alex Imas, researcher Andrew Koh and co-founder Shane Legg published the essay
• Better individual skills like coding or writing shift wages and jobs gradually, but better teamwork between AI agents could change them suddenly
• Today's models are weak in the same places, so running more copies adds capacity but doesn't cover each other's blind spots
• In a quiz of 100 people, the researchers found that pairs matched to cover each other's weak spots beat random pairs by 32%
• For now, the essay predicts falling pay for workers whose skills AI already matches, and rising pay for specialists and the managers who coordinate teams
• The paper maps 4 stages of AI, and at the "super cooperative" stage, whole industries could consolidate into a few AI-only firms and wages could drop sharply
• Legg told the Financial Times he's "comfortable" with a 50% chance of what he calls "minimal" AGI by 2028

@theojaffee: "The fully automated firm is when I think we get things that look really crazy, like really wild sci-fi, real superintelligence, real x-risk if we do it wrong."

text:
In memory of Sir Patrick Stewart -

Despite our difference on Faith, like so many I find so much more in common with such people, and will miss him and his style of wit and wisdom, which can be understood best by the way Charles Dickens moved him so much so by 'The Christmas Carol'

Patrick Steward first read a Christmas Carol as a middle-aged man on a rainy day in a country hotel, picking up a paperback copy he had never read. By the end he was in tears—not from sentimentality, but from the force of a story about isolation, greed, and the last-minute possibility of change. That theme stayed with him. 

Over decades he returned to Scrooge, insisting the tale was serious, adult work about passion, cruelty, happiness, and the hard work of becoming someone better.

What he valued in it was never abstract. It was the conviction that a person can open a closed heart, that we have some responsibility for one another, and that cruelty need not be the final word. Those are virtues Christians have long held dear: compassion, charity, the hope of redemption, and the call to care for those who have less. 

In so many ways Patrick Stewart out-performed so many who call themselves Christians who would not be so moved to tears over such a salvation as Ebenezer Scrooge, ...such a change of heart.   If we cannot agree on Who to worship. May we at least agree on those qualities that brought this man to tears.

text:
$AMZN 
why I see $323 within 12 months (+42%)

Amazon just posted the highest operating margin in its history, and the stock fell more than 10% from Wednesday's close to ~$227 after hours.

Why:a slight miss on EPS and revenue, softer ads, a Q4 profit guide below expectations, and a capex bill that keeps growing. The capex is the real debate. 

My view: the market is underpricing how fast the earnings base is growing underneath it 👇

1) AWS is the core of the thesis
Revenue $46B, +39.3% YoY, the 6th straight quarter of acceleration

Operating profit $17.8B, a 38.7% operating margin

Backlog $578B, up $82B in one quarter

Management expects 40%+ growth in both 2027 and 2028, on a $184B run rate

Backlog isn't profit, but it is contracted demand. Few companies get that kind of visibility.

My 2027: AWS revenue ~$250B (+42%). 
I will use a 36.5% operating margin (vs 38.7% in Q3) to allow for higher depreciation, infrastructure costs and lower-margin AI services → ~$91B of AWS operating profit.

2) Retail is quietly getting more profitable
• Ads: ~$19.6B a quarter. Growth slowed, mostly because Prime Day moved into Q2. Management expects high-teens growth again in Q4, the first thing I'll check.
• Delivery: shipping costs +11% vs units +12%. Excluding fuel and transport inflation, costs rose only ~8%.

3) Earnings power
Q3 operating profit was $28.1B. Reported growth was +61%, but Q3 2025 carried ~$4.3B of settlement and severance costs. Underlying growth: ~29%.

My 2027 estimates:
• Revenue: $974B
• AWS revenue: $250B
• AWS operating profit: $91B
• Total operating profit: $143B (vs ~$110B in 2026, +30%)
• Normalized EPS: $9.70

Normalized = excluding gains on stakes like Anthropic, which have inflated 2026 GAAP EPS. My figure is below some pre-earnings estimates because I load in depreciation, financing costs and the investment program.

4) Valuation
$9.70 × 31 = $300.70, plus ~$16/share for the strategic stakes (Anthropic, OpenAI) after discounts = $316.70 base case. The stakes sit outside my EPS, so nothing is counted twice.

• Bear (20%): $193.50 (−15%). Spending outruns returns, earnings disappoint, the multiple compresses.
• Base (50%): $316.70 (+40%). AWS delivers, retail margins improve, confidence returns.
• Bull (30%): $421.50 (+86%). AWS and retail beat, the market pays up.

Probability-weighted: $323.50, +42.5%.

🚩🚩To be clear on what drives this: at $227 the market pays ~23× my 2027 EPS. If Amazon delivers the earnings but the multiple stays there, the target is ~$239 (+5%). So this is as much a call on confidence returning as on earnings.

⚠️ 5) The risk: capex
• 2026 capex: ~$220B. Management says 2027 will be meaningfully higher; I assume $300B.
• Trailing 12-month FCF is already −$42B. On ~$245B of operating cash flow, $300B of capex means ~−$55B of FCF in 2027.
• Amazon is borrowing more to fund it.

The question isn't whether AWS grows. It's whether this spend earns its return. I'd turn cautious if 2027 capex lands well above $320B without stronger revenue and cash-flow guidance, or if AWS margins slip materially.

Bottom line
I'm not assuming perfection: AWS margin below today's, investment costs inside EPS, negative FCF. But writing off every AI dollar before the returns show up isn't reasonable either. At ~$227, I think the reward justifies the risk.

Next tests: Q4 ad growth, AWS holding 40%+, and the 2027 capex plan.

Oct 2027 targets: Bear $193.50 | Base $316.70 | Bull $421.50
Weighted: $323.50 (+42.5%)

Not financial Advise just my take on Amazon recent move

today we are announcing openrouter for commerce: https://t.co/qLbYqziMtG

a single endpoint that integrates 5k stores, including Doordash, Amazon and most shopify stores, with payments using Agentcard (Stripe Link and Shop coming soon).

we built opencommerce to solve 3 problems:
* coverage: one endpoint to integrate 5k stores. agentic purchasing is a core feature for most personal assistants, but not their main business. searching for products and buying on behalf of users shouldn’t be as painful as it is today (e.g. it shouldn’t involve browser automations or dealing with PSPs). opencommerce solves that: 1 tool, every online store.

* reliability: 100% uptime. the challenge with browser automations is that they fail (e.g. captchas, bot-detection, etc). we run thousands of tests every couple of hours on every one of the stores to guarantee that the integration works when your user tries to buy something.

* speed: responses in under 10s. consumers are used to Amazon speed, and agentic purchases have so far felt like a downgrade. most agents spend minutes finding products before they come back with results. we monitor speed and improve it constantly.

今天英特尔这份三季报公布，服务器确实兑现了增长，而且比我原先想的更强。但PC客户削减采购的速度，把四季度利润往下拉得很重。但低估了这一轮PC调整，同时高估了数据中心增长对集团盈利的支撑。

看下面之前前瞻与实际公布的数据对比，核心是四季度指引远低于预期。如果只看三季度总收入，我此前的166亿美元与实际只差0.87亿美元。但把分部拆开，这个“接近”就没有那么值得高兴了。我之前前瞻模型是CCPG收入88亿美元、DCAI收入68亿美元。实际分别为80.97亿美元和73.18亿美元。客户端少了7.03亿美元，数据中心多了5.18亿美元，两个方向的偏差相互抵消了大半。

总收入估得接近，掩盖了对业务结构变化的低估。此前预计服务器的增量可以覆盖PC的温和下行。现在看到，PC采购调整已经明显加深，四季度还会继续传导，这个假设还得改

盘后股价跌幅超过20%。我的理解是市场开始重新估算未来几个季度的利润，三季度多赚的那部分，已经不足以抵消后续预期的下修。

业务上的亮点：
1）服务器比预想更强，三季度DCAI收入73.18亿美元，同比增长78%，环比增长约17%；营业利润约30.39亿美元，营业利润率约41.5%，高于二季度的39.5%。收入和利润一起改善，前瞻里期待的服务器增量确实落到了报表上。

2）代工亏损收窄 + 制程进展是进步

但这些亮点还不足以抵消PC调整带来的冲击、以及CFO说27年大概率无法实现正自由现金流带来的担忧。

前瞻里最大的失误，是把PC的调整估得太轻，也把集团盈利修复想得太顺，虽然服务器超预期。

现在看英特尔面临了跟昨天谷歌同样的问题，就是面向AI这一块业务都很强劲（英特尔是服务器、谷歌是云业务），但是传统的主业都面临了困境。

the time for mourning coding is long over

Saw a few discussions about size of hack, why impact to bitcoin price is small, etc. 👇 

$6.3 billion is the biggest in USD terms, but not in BTC terms. MtGox was 650,000 BTC!

Other important numbers to consider:

% of bitcoin (in relation to BTC total supply), ie, market impact. MtGox is big there again at 5%+.

Number of users impacted, and % of user assets impacted. MtGox (the largest CEX at the time) and FTX (not small) were all near 100% of users and their asseets.

Most important: Who is impacted? Does the platform cover it all? (only one victim), as in recent two CEX cases and Binance.

Obviously, still a major disaster for the industry, Binance (and me). It hurts, but we survive. 

Most importantly, we protect our users.

作为一个前 $INTC 英特尔工程师，我在 2024 年 12 月写下了我对这家公司的看法。
我劝告投资者远离英特尔。

我的观点变了吗？

我从未持有过英特尔股票。不是在股价上涨的时候。我曾在那里工作。我知道那些失败从来不是需求问题。它们是管理与执行的问题。
最近我买了一小部分 2028 年看涨期权。我和前同事聊过。在谭立武（Lip-Bu Tan）的领导下，公司专注于利润。老旧、低效的旧势力正在被清除。晶圆厂表现更好。18A 工艺的良率在改善。
我一直对良率持怀疑态度。不只是英特尔，而是任何美国晶圆厂，鉴于我们多年来流失了多少人才。这种怀疑正在开始消退。

昨天的电话会议很艰难。供应是天花板。基板短缺。一场悲剧性事故关闭了 Fab 28。股价下跌了 21%。
经过很多焦虑，我决定持有。这是原因。
英特尔是两家截然不同的业务。一家是为服务器和 PC 设计 CPU。另一家是吞噬资本支出的晶圆厂。对两者来说，需求都不是问题。执行才是。
英特尔仍然显露出疲态。但它现在有十年来最好的 CEO，而且美国政府持有股份。它比我观察过的任何时候都更有能力修正错误。需求很强劲。

所以我会给它一个机会。叫我愚蠢吧。
author: IamRamenPanda
quoted_text:
An a former $INTC Intel engineer I wrote my thoughts on the company back in December, 2024.
I advocated investors against Intel. 

Have my views changed? 

I never owned Intel. Not when the stock ran. I worked there. I knew the failures were never about demand. They were about management and execution.
Lately I bought a small number of 2028 calls. I talked to former colleagues. Under Lip-Bu Tan, the company was focused on profits. The old, inefficient guard was being cleared out. The fab was doing better. 18A yields were improving.
I've always been skeptical about yields. Not just at Intel, but at any US fab, given how much talent we've lost over the years. That skepticism is starting to ease.

Yesterday's call was rough. Supply is the ceiling. Substrates are short. A tragic accident shut Fab 28. The stock fell 21%.
After a lot of angst, I'm holding. Here's why.
Intel is two very different businesses. One designs CPUs for servers and PCs. The other is a fab that drains capex. Demand isn't the problem for either one. Execution is.
Intel still shows wear and tear. But it has a better CEO than it has had in a decade, and the US government owns a stake. It's more able to fix its mistakes today than at any point I've watched.Demand is robust.
And there's the bigger picture. Intel is the only leading-edge US fab, and the only one showing real signs of change. 
China is ahead in many ways. Depending on Taiwan is not a long-term plan. Trillions of dollars of US tech run on chips made on an island Beijing claims as part of One China.

Intel can't fail.

So I'll give it a chance. Call me foolish.

text:
I have been debating for months with fellow security people who say AI hacking will not be a big deal. 

My argument has consistently been that so much of the fruit is not just low-hanging, but sitting on the ground. That the internet is powered by fragile software, managed by regular people who make mistakes. And that extraordinary harm can come from exposing our flawed systems to more scrutiny. 

This is a case in point. Billions in losses from one guys laptop. 

How many similar situations do you think there are in the world? Across all our systems globally. That have trillions of dollars and in fact the entire economy running through them? 

And that’s just misconfigurations! That’s not even counting AI finding new stuff. 

The only reason things were stable before is because there were a tiny number of attackers and far too much surface area to cover. AI just changed all the math. 

This has only just begun.

Very few podcasts will actually make you smarter AND make you laugh.

No politics, no egos, just tech.

The biggest news this week:

- Anthropic Files S1 Ahead of $2TRN IPO
- Instinct's Rumoured $30BN Fundraise
- Microsoft Lays off 27,000 While Meta Taps Equity Markets for $95BN Capex Spending Spree

My notes with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. Analysis of Anthropic S1

Anthropic's S1 beat expectations on margins and operating income, even after stock-based compensation, leaving the burden of proof on the naysayers. It also looked strong on customer concentration, compute efficiency and cash. Some questions remain, including the undisclosed Q3 revenue number.

2. Is the Value Extraction Requirement From the Latest Models a Benefit or a Curse of Anthropic?

Eighty percent of Anthropic's revenue comes from models less than six months old, and 70 to 80% of compute costs go to training. Models are expensive to build and highly profitable to serve, but only for six to twelve months. Few companies can write a $10 to 12BN compute check, so this short shelf life can favour Anthropic if it stays aggressive.

3. Brutal Reality Is Microsoft Have Just Admitted They Don't Want 27% of Their Workforce

Whatever gets said on LinkedIn, Microsoft's move says it does not want 27% of its people. That is a worse scarlet letter than a pure layoff, because the company has told these employees they do not meet its minimum bar.

4. Chinese Open-Source Models Have Peaked and Will Decline From Here

Chinese open-weight models are close to finished in the US, and this is the beginning of the end for them. Despite DeepSeek's latest raise, it is starting to be banned across all federal agencies.

5. Why No CIO Will Take a Chance on a Chinese Model

Even if confidential data reaches Alibaba servers in Asia only one time in 100,000, without consent, no CIO or CISO will approve the model. If it keeps happening and Alibaba stays silent, anyone using these models will lose their job.

6. Why OpenAI Is an Underappreciated Asset to Invest in Today

OpenAI is mispriced at the $1.25 TN round. Brief market panic has created a dislocation like Anthropic's round at around $183BN, even though OpenAI has closed all its competitive gaps.

7. What Is the Upside of OpenAI at $1.25 Trillion?

OpenAI and Anthropic are both expected to become $10 to 20TN companies. Anthropic takes only 0.1% of Fortune 500 budgets today, and even conservative estimates put that at 2 to 3%. Because OpenAI is not priced to perfection, the worst case is doubling the money.

I’ve been reluctant to speak publicly about this, but using @ryskfinance without dark mode has started to affect my personal life.

At first, it was small adjustments. Lowering my brightness. Sitting further from the screen. Only checking positions during daylight hours. You tell yourself these are reasonable compromises for sustainable yield paid upfront.

Over time, your world gets smaller.

My wife and I now have an agreement that I won’t open Rysk in the bedroom. I respect that boundary. But it means that when I need to manage a position at night, I have to leave our bed and sit alone in the kitchen, illuminated by bone.

The team has been very clear that the colour is bone. I’ve passed this information on to my family.

My sleep has deteriorated. I’m less present at dinner. Sometimes my wife is talking and I’m still looking at the bone-coloured page. I’ve started taking walks without my phone, but certain shades of pavement remind me of Rysk. I just can’t stop thinking about it…

There are financial consequences too. I’ve begun selecting longer expiries simply to reduce how often I need to look at the website. But I keep coming back every Friday to see if my friends got exercised.

I still believe in the product. I love the product. That’s what makes this so difficult.

The team has indicated that dark mode could take approximately three years. I appreciate having a timeline. It gives us something to plan around. And it gives us hope.

My wife asked me last night whether I thought things would get better.

I told her 2029, subject to engineering capacity.

quoted_text:
Energy first, then compute.

@ChaseLochmiller, co-founder and CEO of @CrusoeAI is building a lot of the data centers that power the age of intelligence. They just closed a round at a $31B valuation, about 8 years into a company that started as two guys burning flared gas in the Bakken oil field to mine Bitcoin.

That wasn’t a pivot, btw. Chase was AI-pilled early.

The bet was: if data and compute are the bottleneck, compute becomes an energy problem. So instead of bringing stranded energy to a market, bring the market to the energy. Bitcoin was the easiest way to turn electrons into money while he waited for AI demand to show up. It showed up on November 30th, 2022.

He’s a learning machine. On track to be a professor, then a quant, then Everest, now running a 2,000+ person vertically integrated business with welders and AI researchers in the same company.

A few things we get into:

•Why Crusoe is an AI supermajor: upstream (power), midstream (data centers), downstream (AI cloud). Exxon famously doesn’t hedge oil because the stack hedges itself. Margins move around the stack; own the whole thing.  
•“Most startups die from suicide, not homicide.” We said the exact same thing at HubSpot. If someone else is chasing your opportunity, that’s a compliment.  
•Coopetition. He’ll partner with companies he competes with elsewhere.  Useful when you’re building infrastructure the entire industry needs.  
•The CEO journey isn’t linear. “As soon as I’m sick of hearing myself say something, we’re just scratching the surface.”  
•How he scales himself: a domain expert owns each vertical. Energy, data centers, manufacturing, AI cloud. He goes deep enough to get aligned on direction and understand how it connects to the rest of the business. Then he holds them accountable to execute. Alignment first, then trust with accountability.  
•Should every CEO hire a coach? Yes. His coach was as much therapist as coach, and it was critical for him and the company. We get into that more.
•People scale linearly, companies scale exponentially (h/t First Round). When you start thinking about letting someone go, that was probably the right time.  
•Actively hunt bad news. Good news is nice, but the CEO’s job is to “run into the burning buildings,” find what’s broken, and fix it.  
•Selling the Bitcoin business to NYDIG while it was making money. One word: focus.

•The data center backlash. “The industry has a marketing problem. The truth is on our side.”

text:
You thought this was a bad week in crypto? You might have missed the bigger news.

Two results just landed on elliptic-curve cryptography. Both are worrying. Neither one breaks a key anyone uses today.

1️⃣ The problem under ECC is less hard than we thought.

ECC is secure because the elliptic-curve discrete log is hard. The best general algorithm we had was Pollard's rho, and it is exponential: add bits to the key, and breaking it gets exponentially harder.

That assumption is now false, with one caveat. A paper from Bochum and MPI-SP gives a subexponential algorithm. It assumes an OpenAI claim that is still under review. If the claim holds, the new algorithm is faster asymptotically. In practice it changes nothing. On secp256k1, P-256, or Ed25519, rho is still the best algorithm, and it still takes the age of the universe. The new one only pulls ahead on hypothetical curves of enormous size, and there the cost is even more absurd.

https://t.co/k6ZpfloNvX

2️⃣ The quantum circuit is getting cheaper. The computer is not here.

We still have no quantum computer. The circuit that would run on one to break ECDSA keeps getting cheaper. https://t.co/bYawK8RPU3 is a public auto-research loop aimed at exactly that. Its current best is about 70% cheaper than the circuit Google reported, on logical qubits times Toffolis (0.91 billion against 2.99 billion). Google's circuit was already two to three times cheaper than the previous published one.

Alice & Bob @Alice__Bob , a French Quantum Computing company, just estimated that breaking secp256k1, the Bitcoin curve, takes at most about 30,000 cat qubits and one hour. That figure assumes a machine nobody has built. We are still far from it. The machine being asked for keeps getting smaller.

https://t.co/CXodOGwMes

What a crazy time to be alive.

How does it work under the hood?

It uses two Gemma models running on Google’s LiteRT runtime:

1️⃣ Conversation & Tool Calling:
When you speak to Reachy Mini by voice. Gemma 4 E4B runs locally to hold natural conversations and issues a tool call to start or stop the car.

2️⃣ Real-Time Vision & Driving:
Once in motion, a small Gemma-based decision model (EmbeddingGemma 2) runs directly on an @arduino  VentunoQ embedded board to steer the robot using real-time camera input.

Because both models run on LiteRT, the whole loop stays completely private, offline, and with low-latency.

author: cz_binance
quoted_text:
From a teachers perspective, the past 12 hours were an excellent teaching moment for why crypto is special.

And FWIW, my ultimate conclusion to my students was that everything worked as it was supposed to, and blockchain actually demonstrated why it is useful.

The credibly neutral networks did nothing despite the scale of the theft and the bearer assets remain stolen. The parts of the ecosystem that are more centralized played their part and intervened. And of course, everything was shockingly transparent in real time.

Having a hierarchy of neutrality and censorship-resistance, where base layers and assets are cypherpunk, but higher level networks and assets are not, is optimal.

Those who seek maximum protection can have it, at the risk of nobody coming to their rescue when something goes wrong. Those who want greater safety and convenience can have it too, at the risk of being abused by those meant to protect them down the line.

Importantly, individual choice and market forces decide which part of the hierarchy anyone lives on - not regulations or monopolists.

text:
Saw a few discussions about size of hack, why impact to bitcoin price is small, etc. 👇 

$6.3 billion is the biggest in USD terms, but not in BTC terms. MtGox was 650,000 BTC!

Other important numbers to consider:

% of bitcoin (in relation to BTC total supply), ie, market impact. MtGox is big there again at 5%+.

Number of users impacted, and % of user assets impacted. MtGox (the largest CEX at the time) and FTX (not small) were all near 100% of users and their asseets.

Most important: Who is impacted? Does the platform cover it all? (only one victim), as in recent two CEX cases and Binance.

Obviously, still a major disaster for the industry, Binance (and me). It hurts, but we survive. 

Most importantly, we protect our users.

(image from @MatthewRoszak)

I recently moved from Google DeepMind to OpenAI. As such, I got an accelerated version of what the public will experience, from witnessing OpenAI’s Oct 6 drop as a bystander to experimenting with the model. My work has not been that impacted by prior AI models (including Astra), but this one is on another level. The results seen thus far do not represent the limits of its capabilities.

OpenAI announced one or more results with the releases of GPT 5.5 (Erdos-1014), GPT 5.6 (Cycle Double Cover), and GPT 6 (non-sofic groups, …). I think it’s fair to say that, within a couple months of each release, people on laptops went on to elicit more than 10x the number of comparable results from the models. I expect the same to happen again relative to the Oct 6 release. When that happens it will be exciting, empowering, … and disruptive. The world needs to prepare carefully and thoughtfully.

Mathematics has been a cornerstone of human intellectual flourishing, and I certainly want that to continue. I hope there will be spaces for exploring mathematics in new ways, but also spaces for preserving the old artisanal ways. That will require strong leadership and significant change from academia.

author: EleanorTerrett
quoted_text:
I want to speak to you directly about what happened.

Bottom line - your money is safe, and we're covering every loss.

Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions.

To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single "one-click" action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual.

So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak.

We'll share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and every fact is verified - and publish an updated Proof of Reserves once remediation is complete.

What you need to know:
• Your funds are safe
• Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and company funds
• Estimated total impact: ~$6.3B, with ~$3B frozen on-chain so far, in coordination with our blockchain partners
• No evidence of any wallet private key leak
• Deposits are unaffected and operating as normal

What we've done:
• Temporarily suspended withdrawals while we complete a security revamp of the withdrawal service and its related addresses
• Revoked the affected address authorizations
• Engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds

Our team hasn't stopped. We're working closely with law enforcement to ensure the matter is handled appropriately - and I'll share what I can, as soon as I can.

10 月 28 日，知名开源开发者黄峰达（Phodal）宣布离开阿里 Qoder 团队。他在告别帖中感慨：「在阿里要做好一个产品，可太难了。技术只是其中一部分，更多挑战往往在技术之外。」

黄峰达此前在 Thoughtworks 工作十多年，曾任中国区开源负责人，开发过 AutoDev、ArchGuard 等开源项目。今年 5 月前后加入 Qoder 后，黄峰达参与了 Canvas 交互体系和 Agent 插件生态建设，还开发了开源工具 Better Harness，用于分析 AI 编程 Agent 的工作流程，找出容易出错的环节。9 月，他又参与推出 Mobile Use 插件，让 AI 修改手机应用代码后，还能在安卓、鸿蒙和 iOS 运行环境中检查实际效果。

他的离职正值 Qoder 持续调整产品线。8 月，曾牵头通义灵码项目的产品技术负责人陈鑫（神秀）也已离职。9 月，Qoder 披露年化经常性收入（ARR）达到 1 亿美元，但阿里云同时宣布逐步关停 QoderWork，将开发与办公用户分别引导至 Qoder 桌面版和千问办公。迁往后者的用户还需重新注册，原有积分权益不能直接互通。

New data means new relationships, and new ways to trade them.

AML Crypto and @officer_secret continues to track where stolen assets go. “We can see a lot of activity on TRON with our analysis of transactions, with hundreds of addresses.

Major findings:
▪️ 2,831 outgoing transactions from 284 addresses associated with exploiter between October 29, 20:44 and October 30, 12:44.

▪️ The average time between transactions was 20.35 seconds, with a median of just 3 seconds. 1,099 consecutive transaction pairs had identical timestamps to the second.

▪️ Peak activity was observed on October 30, between 06:00 and 06:59 UTC: 865 transactions in one hour, or roughly one transaction every 4.2 seconds.

▪️ The volume and frequency of transfers indicate that attackers may be using automated tools to generate new addresses and move funds. Some addresses are recycled across transaction routes, making tracing even more difficult.

Bitget Wallet, LayerZero, Symbiosis Finance, @near_intents, Meson, Allbridge, and ChangeHero (@Changehero_io)

We also found un-attributed addresses that may relate to other service providers.

We call on @Changehero_io, @near_intents and @binance to take action.

We call on both sides to review the identified addresses and to block transactions associated with the exploiter to the extent technically feasible.

AML Crypto is ready to provide actionable intelligence on exploiter controlled addresses at no cost, including newly identified wallets as the investigation progresses.

text:
Outside ETH, the attacker’s 684M TRX ($228M) is the only large stash it is moving. Its 18,270 BTC ($1.41B) and 233M XRP ($288M) have not moved since the hack.

Since midnight it has moved about $3M off Tron, almost entirely through DeFi. At 6:15 AM ET it split its TRX into five new accounts, then started selling small batches for USDT on SunSwap.

From there it used three routes. Tether’s own USDT0 bridge carried about $909K to Ethereum from 3:01 AM. Chainflip took about $1.19M, and its broker rejected five deposits, but each was resent and went through. 

JustLend (Compound Finance fork) served as a pass-through with 980K USDT deposited at 10:59 AM, with the claim handed between new wallets and withdrawn in pieces. About $480K is still there. It also parked some USDT in USDD, which has no freeze function, using USDD’s zero-fee swap module. (USDD is a DAI fork using old MakerDAO code)

About 857 ETH ($1.9M) now sits in eight new Ethereum wallets. Tether froze one receiving wallet at 9:36 AM, before a 206K USDT transfer arrived, and that is the only freeze of the Tron proceeds since last night.

However, it appears other Tron routes are still open. the TRX could mint about $190M of USDD or borrow about $99M on JustLend. cc @justinsuntron

text:
On Variational you can't withdraw your own funds permissionlessly

Read their contracts. As far as I can tell:

- Collateral sits in per-user usdc pools on arbitrum, ~$224m across ~208k pools
- You can deposit into your pool but you can't withdraw from it yourself. Every withdrawal goes through their oracle contract and only addresses with PROVIDER_ROLE can trigger it
- 17 addresses have that role, 16 of them plain wallets (EOAs). as far as i can read the code, any one of them can move usdc out of any pool on its own, and the contracts don't cap the amount
- The admin that hands out these roles and can pause the oracle is a single EOA: 0x8e4d1ad423e4f37600cda314fd3d99629ceaeabf. role changes take effect immediately
- Docs describe the olp vault as "a smart contract where the capital that powers OLP (USDC) is secured". the address they list for it, 0x74bbbb0e7f0bad6938509dd4b556a39a4db1f2cd, has no code. It's an EOA 
- the protocol treasury, 0x5e91b40467fb8902c46a7b6cb90482363188d645 (~$12m usdc), is one of the 17 provider keys

Docs say the keys live on fireblocks. If there are policies on them (limits, quorum) that answers most of this, but none of it is visible onchain

@variational_io how is the admin key secured, do provider keys have limits, and how does a user get funds out if your backend is down?

Correct me if I'm wrong

text:
怎么现在了还有人在 thread 里不停的推荐 Orca 呀？Orca 手机端是 TUI 呀（虽然Orca 手机端已经有 ChatUI 了，但是兼容性有各种问题，不光是交互很别扭很不跟手，而且很多界面压根没渲染好，比如 pi 都压根不支持）

我这个 Alma 中的 Herdr 在手机端是纯纯的 Native GUI 呀。在手机端用 TUI 是我这辈子永远都不可能想明白的诡异的需求。另外如视频所示，因为 Alma iOS 是纯正的 GUI，所以你可以在里面查看图片、上传图片，甚至可以标注图片做精细化修改，可以做各种各样 GUI 中丰富多元的交互，Orca 中怎么做呢？

其实 Alma 的桌面端也有 Herdr 的 GUI，你可能问，那这跟其他的 ADE 的区别是啥呢？其实最大的区别就是 Alma 中的 Herdr GUI 用 Claude Code 的时候是用的原生的Claude Code TUI，但是其他的 ADE 基本上都是用 ACP，ACP 是用的 Claude SDK，或者是 claude -p，咱先不说封不封号的问题，这两个在某些情况下会导致额外消耗两倍的Token。

quoted_text:
I suspect IBIT is already on North Korea’s shortlist.

In February 2025, the attackers behind the Bybit hack compromised a Safe{Wallet} developer’s Mac through a malicious project disguised as legitimate Docker-related tooling. They had access for 17 days before the theft, giving them enough time to manipulate the transaction interface used by Bybit’s signers. The signers believed they were approving a legitimate transaction. Instead, they unknowingly authorized the theft of $1.5 billion from a cold wallet.

The keys could stay offline while the signers approved a theft through a compromised interface.

TRM Labs attributes the recent Binance incident with high confidence to TraderTraitor, the North Korean group also linked to Bybit and the theft of 4,502.9 BTC from DMM Bitcoin. Binance’s preliminary investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop as the entry point. Binance says there’s no evidence that private keys were leaked, while TRM’s analysis suggests the attackers may have gained control of the signing infrastructure. If confirmed, the attackers could have moved funds through a compromised approval process without extracting the keys.

Now imagine the same thing happening to IBIT.

BlackRock’s IBIT is the world’s largest Bitcoin ETF, holding roughly 815,000 BTC worth around $63 billion. Coinbase remains its active Bitcoin custodian. Although Anchorage Digital has been appointed as an additional custodian, the fund’s latest quarterly filing says there are currently no plans to transfer any Bitcoin there.

That’s an extraordinary concentration of Bitcoin under one custodian. Regardless of how large or well-funded that provider is, a critical failure in its security infrastructure could put the entire fund at risk.

A $6 billion theft would wipe out roughly 9.5% of IBIT’s assets, equivalent to around $4 per share at current valuations.

Binance managed to freeze some stolen stablecoins. Bitcoin has no such mechanism, making stolen BTC far harder to recover.

BlackRock doesn’t separately insure the Bitcoin held by the fund. Coinbase has disclosed $320 million in commercial crime insurance coverage, shared across its customers. Its custody agreement also limits liability to $100 million per cold storage address, with any recovery subject to contractual terms, liability determinations, and other conditions.

If a major theft occurred and the fund couldn’t recover the Bitcoin or obtain sufficient compensation, the remaining losses would ultimately be borne by IBIT shareholders.

Bitcoin ETFs have made owning Bitcoin much more accessible, and there’s real value in that convenience. But as more capital flows into these products, enormous amounts of Bitcoin are also being concentrated among a handful of custodians and the infrastructure they depend on.

The larger these pools become, the more attractive they are to attackers. A compromise at any critical point could have consequences far beyond a single institution.

And that’s why security has no finish line.

Even the most sophisticated cold storage setup still depends on hardware, software, supply chains, signing workflows, and the people operating them. Keeping private keys offline is essential, but it doesn’t eliminate the risks surrounding the transaction approval process.

Spread your assets across independent custody setups. Keep your private keys offline. Verify transaction details on a trusted device screen, independently of the computer initiating the transaction. Continuously review your security architecture, and build it around the assumption that some part of your infrastructure will eventually be compromised.

There are no silver bullets in security, and no permanent guarantees. Stay vigilant, keep verifying, and never mistake a clean track record for proof that you’re safe.

Bunker mode.

author: taodotcom
quoted_text:
NOVA: Emission Split Update for Data Generation Fund
Owner 26% / Miners 33% / Validators 41%

With the launch of eTAO, subnet owners can now adjust how emissions are distributed. NOVA will be updating its split to allocate more resources toward what we believe is the highest-impact investment we can make in the subnet's future: experimental data generation.

Wet lab data is the best investment we can make both to prove out what the subnet produces and to increase the value of what gets built on top of it.

Data is the bottleneck
AI-driven drug discovery faces a fundamental constraint: the quality of our predictions is ultimately limited by the experimental data available to train and validate them.

Much of today's publicly available drug discovery data is fragmented across studies, generated using different experimental protocols, and inconsistent in quality and coverage.

Generating high-quality experimental data allows us to address that limitation directly. It gives miners better ground truth for model development, provides independent validation of their predictions, and helps us identify which approaches actually translate into experimental success.

The industry is making the same bet.

Some of the largest investments in AI-driven biology are now directed toward generating the experimental data necessary to train and validate better models.

Biohub committed $400M of a $500M, five-year initiative to data generation, infrastructure and measurement technology, and later expanded into a $1.8B effort backed by Meta, Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs, who collectively committed $300M.

The OpenAI Foundation gave $15M to OpenADMET to generate public ADME datasets, which will be used in prospective blind challenges against newly measured experimental data. Octant continues the high-throughput data generation behind it. 

Leash Bio used a $9.3M seed round to scale data collection for a foundational medicinal chemistry model, producing a dataset that screened 133 million molecules against each protein. 

Anthropic has set up a physical biology lab in the Bay Area.

What the additional funds will support
The additional owner allocation will go into a dedicated R&D fund for wet lab data generation.

1. ADME model training competition. The first use of the fund is generating the experimental data behind our ADME competition, currently in design and development. High-quality, standardized ADME data is what turns a competition from a benchmark into something that produces models with real predictive value.

2. Advancing assets under development. Where it makes sense, the fund can also support experimental work that moves our in-development assets forward.

Why this benefits the entire NOVA ecosystem
We believe generating experimental data is one of the most effective ways to increase the long-term value of the subnet.

For miners, better datasets and scientifically grounded evaluations create opportunities to develop more capable models, compete on meaningful performance improvements, and contribute work with greater real-world utility.

For validators, stronger experimental benchmarks improve the ability to assess model quality and reward useful contributions.

For tokenholders, better models, experimentally validated discoveries, and progress toward valuable therapeutic assets can strengthen NOVA's competitive position and long-term commercial potential.

The economic opportunity extends beyond any individual competition. We are building an increasingly capable scientific discovery platform, and the data generated through our R&D efforts can become a compounding asset for the entire ecosystem.

Miner incentives remain strong
Miners will still receive a meaningfully larger share than the owner (33% vs. 26%), and we believe the rewards will preserve healthy, competitive incentives for participation. Better data and better-validated competitions also make the work miners do more valuable over time.

Protecting token health
Funds from the R&D allocation will be converted to cover lab costs gradually, distributed over time rather than sold in size, to limit market impact and preserve token health.

The bottom line
We think this is the single best thing we can do to accelerate our progress, increase our chance of success, and create value for everyone with a stake in NOVA, including miners, validators, and tokenholders. It is time for us to scale real-world validation.

text:
Attended a fun session at a16z with @illscience and @joshelman yesterday. As usual they were dropping knowledge bombs:

1. There are three economic miracles. The old one is zero marginal cost software distribution. But recently there have been two more: 1) Coding going from the most precious asset in the world to one of the cheapest and 2) zero marginal cost digital labor with agents.

2. It's hard to appreciate what it feels like to be on the exponential. Just 10 to 20 million people account for $150 to 200 billion of token spend. "Some of the best companies that we work with have higher token spend than payroll." We are still early.

3. The AI workspace, like ChatGPT and the Claude desktop app, is going to be the container for all kinds of AI interactions and it's going to subsume the browser. Personally, these apps are already the browser for me. Chrome is just the middle layer.

4. The way to tell if you're an AI-native company is to ask: If the model gets twice as good, do your customers get twice as much value? Are you happy or sad that the model got better? If you're sad, you're probably on the wrong side of the exponential.

5. "I would much rather have AI be the boss of me than vice versa." For example, Anish's agent is responsible for a 30 minute block in his calendar every week to pick someone he should reconnect with.

6. Improving individual productivity does not always improve a team's productivity. Coding has taught us the wrong lesson on this. For many functions, having individuals be 10x more productive doesn't mean the team will be 10x. e.g., If everyone goes in a different direction.

7. It's actually easier to start a hard company than an easy company... because they're all hard. At least the hard companies are interesting to work on and people want to work with you on them.

Excited to do a podcast recording with Josh next week to go deeper on some of this.

author: soubhikdeb
quoted_text:
New challenge on Yukon: Circuit Breaker https://t.co/vpuIh2CnbR

It took 38 years to raise the best proven circuit lower bound from 3n to 3.1n. Days before this launch, an AI model pushed it to 3.5n.

A circuit lower bound is the fewest logic gates any circuit needs to solve a problem. Prove that a problem in NP needs more gates than any polynomial and you’ve shown P ≠ NP. That would settle whether every problem that’s easy to check is also easy to solve, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems.

We’re still far from that bound. Circuit Breaker, built with UCLA Math+AI, is where the push continues.

“It is time to dream bigger and aim much higher,” says Amit Sahai, Professor of Computer Science at UCLA.

text:
i have arrived at the sweet spot of product design. i finally made it.

feels like a big milestone tbh. 

it's the end of the chokehold that tactical design and technical implementation have had on me for most of the year.

now on the otherside, i can zoom out and think about behavioral design. 

and i feel like i'm 20 again, when i first came across the IDEO shopping cart case study and decided i wanted to be a designer when i grow up.

i've compressed almost every step of logging food into a few taps. and i thought that was the ultimate solution.

but that was naive. that's only half the problem.

i didn't realize how dark food tracking could be for many people. tracking is a slippery slope into eating disorders.

especially for women. the beauty standard is very high and most women are smaller and have lower energy expenditure. 

that combo creates a very narrow window of balance, and forces the choice between being hot and being healthy.

i'm 6'3". my calorie deficit is around 2,400 calories per day. a moderately active woman who's 5'5" needs to stay under 1,400 calories a day to be in a deficit.

one of my "low calorie" meals can be up to half their budgeted intake for the entire day. but we eat at the same restaurants that serve the same portions. 

the amount of will power and effort it takes to lose weight is exponentially higher.

when i was researching what types of calorie tracking content was going viral, it's almost exclusively women sharing their experience "recovering."

the problems to solve now are not speed, cost or UX, it's behavioral:

1. the app rewards restriction: the ring counts down to zero and the dopamine hit is seeing that you ate less at the end of the day.

2. "what the hell" effect: a study found that when one meal breaks a strict rule, people decide the day is ruined. which leads to shame, which leads to bingeing and then more shame.

3. compulsive logging: logging stops helping you eat well and starts being something you *have* to do to feel okay.

the irony is easier a tracker is to use, the easier it is to spiral into these problems.

idk what the solution to these problems are yet, but this is a much more exciting /goal prompt than streamlining the CI/CD pipeline.

text:
If you keep your Bitcoin on an exchange there are two doors that need to be guarded to keep your funds safe: your account login and the exchange custody system.

Multi-factor authentication, device verification, withdrawal restrictions like ForceField, etc. are great features to prevent an attacker from compromising your account.

However, none of these protections help you if the custody system backing the exchange is compromised, which is what just happened at Binance.

Here is how River manages securing your coins internally:

Hot wallet:

Coins in a hot wallet are the most at risk. These coins are on systems connected to the public internet to process demand withdrawals for clients. The strategy is to keep enough coins in here to allow everyone to withdraw on-demand, but never too much that a hack could be financially devastating. River maintains a very low hot wallet balance, and on top of this we have strict internal manual approval policies if withdrawals exceed certain rate limits. Even if an attacker got through every single line of network defense and completely compromised our systems, they wouldn't be able to walk away with much BTC before being shut out.

In order to ensure we always have sufficient coins hot, we have a staging "warm" wallet that is not accessible to process demand withdrawals, but can send funds to top up the hot wallet with sufficient internal approvals.

However, the ultimate layer of defense is cold storage:

Cold storage is a custody system where the signing keys are held offline, such that a full compromise of all computer systems could still not lead to a theft of funds.

At River, we prove every month that we have more coins cold than we have in client BTC liabilities. You can verify this yourself at https://t.co/wzII0qEb6k. Our multi-sig cold storage system is designed for Bitcoin and Bitcoin alone. We are not exposed to any of the smart contract complexity that was exploited in the Binance hack. We will be sharing more in depth about our cold storage in the coming months.

Some exchanges outsource custody, which effectively removes their ability to make any direct claim to you about the integrity and security of their systems. Choose your exchanges carefully. Ask yourself: “are the people running my exchange the most qualified to build a highly secure custody system?”

text:
It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now. 

The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.

But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.

I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.

With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.

author: jack__sanford
quoted_text:
A $6.3B hack at the world’s largest crypto exchange is a wake-up call for every organization responsible for protecting funds onchain.

Early findings suggest a compromised engineer’s laptop gave an attacker access to systems used to submit withdrawals. Funds were taken across ten blockchains. The full root cause remains under investigation.

An exchange holding this much customer capital needs controls that contain an intrusion before it becomes billions in unauthorized transfers. Replacing losses afterward cannot substitute for preventing them.

Most of the $6.3B was stolen in roughly 20 minutes.

As more assets move onchain, these failures put more capital at risk. More integrations, providers and privileged accounts create more routes to secure. Attackers already target employees and wallet providers; larger potential payouts give them more incentive.

Teams need to know who can reach their signing infrastructure, what they can authorize, which controls remain independent during a compromise, and how quickly they can detect and stop an intrusion.

We’re putting more of Sherlock’s work into opsec: tracing how access to an organization can become access to its funds, and helping teams close those paths.

In order for the world’s financial system to run onchain, protecting its assets has to mean securing everything with the authority to move them.

text:
New challenge on Yukon: Circuit Breaker https://t.co/vpuIh2CnbR

It took 38 years to raise the best proven circuit lower bound from 3n to 3.1n. Days before this launch, an AI model pushed it to 3.5n.

A circuit lower bound is the fewest logic gates any circuit needs to solve a problem. Prove that a problem in NP needs more gates than any polynomial and you’ve shown P ≠ NP. That would settle whether every problem that’s easy to check is also easy to solve, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems.

We’re still far from that bound. Circuit Breaker, built with UCLA Math+AI, is where the push continues.

“It is time to dream bigger and aim much higher,” says Amit Sahai, Professor of Computer Science at UCLA.

Jeff 再次提醒 Hyperliquid 的量化和做市团队：下单、撤单、改单尽量批量发送，尤其在网络拥堵时，同样的操作可以少占用限流额度。

🔷 效率差多少？看一个具体例子

79笔订单逐笔提交，消耗79个IP限流权重；打包提交只消耗2个，减少约97.5%。目前每个IP的REST请求共享每分钟1200个权重。

🔷 拥堵时，批量操作同样更省额度

官方文档明确：拥堵时的计权，同时考虑批次内的操作数量和每次提交的固定开销。把多笔下单或撤单合并发送，可以减少额度占用。

🔷 账户限制依然有效

批量提交79笔订单，地址端仍按79次计算。

也就是说，IP限流、地址额度、拥堵时的计权各有规则，不能把“79笔只占2个权重”理解成所有限制都打了折。

🔷 机器人可以怎么优化？

官方建议，可每0.1秒汇总一批订单或撤单；只挂单的ALO订单，与IOC/GTC订单分开打包；已经收到处理结果的撤单，避免重复发送。

这类优化有助于做市商在行情剧烈波动时，更有效地更新报价、撤掉过时订单，让有限的处理额度发挥更大作用。

text:
I think a new system of record is forming where agent memory, BI and business ontologies overlap.

Most people are building it as a knowledge graph or a Postgres DB with RAG. That's a filing cabinet, and it's already commoditised. A human still has to connect the dots.

Memory covers what happened and when. It also has to cover why.

And there's a big difference between an agent receiving the why and an agent reasoning with it. A reason saved as text is one more fact in the store. The agent might retrieve it. It can't do anything with it.

When I studied cognitive development they called this Formal Logic: if X then Y, if Y then Z.

When the WHY is stored as logical relationships, the system can walk the chain. If X turns out false, Y loses confidence and Z is now in question. You get the list of what else is affected, without anyone having to go looking for it.

That's what enables agents to:
- weight tradeoffs across the whole org's logic
- work through cascades of goals on their own
- plan, act, learn and adjust under uncertainty

Companies won't want the labs owning this layer. It holds their most critical knowledge, and many want it local. The labs also get paid per token, and this layer cuts token usage.

This is what I'm building with Tortoise: goals, decisions, assumptions and evidence in a network of quantified logical relationships, with confidence computed so new evidence propagates. A "cognitive layer" for agents: complex reasoning, memory, learning

quoted_text:
I suspect IBIT is already on North Korea’s shortlist.

In February 2025, the attackers behind the Bybit hack compromised a Safe{Wallet} developer’s Mac through a malicious project disguised as legitimate Docker-related tooling. They had access for 17 days before the theft, giving them enough time to manipulate the transaction interface used by Bybit’s signers. The signers believed they were approving a legitimate transaction. Instead, they unknowingly authorized the theft of $1.5 billion from a cold wallet.

The keys could stay offline while the signers approved a theft through a compromised interface.

TRM Labs attributes the recent Binance incident with high confidence to TraderTraitor, the North Korean group also linked to Bybit and the theft of 4,502.9 BTC from DMM Bitcoin. Binance’s preliminary investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop as the entry point. Binance says there’s no evidence that private keys were leaked, while TRM’s analysis suggests the attackers may have gained control of the signing infrastructure. If confirmed, the attackers could have moved funds through a compromised approval process without extracting the keys.

Now imagine the same thing happening to IBIT.

BlackRock’s IBIT is the world’s largest Bitcoin ETF, holding roughly 815,000 BTC worth around $63 billion. Coinbase remains its active Bitcoin custodian. Although Anchorage Digital has been appointed as an additional custodian, the fund’s latest quarterly filing says there are currently no plans to transfer any Bitcoin there.

That’s an extraordinary concentration of Bitcoin under one custodian. Regardless of how large or well-funded that provider is, a critical failure in its security infrastructure could put the entire fund at risk.

A $6 billion theft would wipe out roughly 9.5% of IBIT’s assets, equivalent to around $4 per share at current valuations.

Binance managed to freeze some stolen stablecoins. Bitcoin has no such mechanism, making stolen BTC far harder to recover.

BlackRock doesn’t separately insure the Bitcoin held by the fund. Coinbase has disclosed $320 million in commercial crime insurance coverage, shared across its customers. Its custody agreement also limits liability to $100 million per cold storage address, with any recovery subject to contractual terms, liability determinations, and other conditions.

If a major theft occurred and the fund couldn’t recover the Bitcoin or obtain sufficient compensation, the remaining losses would ultimately be borne by IBIT shareholders.

Bitcoin ETFs have made owning Bitcoin much more accessible, and there’s real value in that convenience. But as more capital flows into these products, enormous amounts of Bitcoin are also being concentrated among a handful of custodians and the infrastructure they depend on.

The larger these pools become, the more attractive they are to attackers. A compromise at any critical point could have consequences far beyond a single institution.

And that’s why security has no finish line.

Even the most sophisticated cold storage setup still depends on hardware, software, supply chains, signing workflows, and the people operating them. Keeping private keys offline is essential, but it doesn’t eliminate the risks surrounding the transaction approval process.

Spread your assets across independent custody setups. Keep your private keys offline. Verify transaction details on a trusted device screen, independently of the computer initiating the transaction. Continuously review your security architecture, and build it around the assumption that some part of your infrastructure will eventually be compromised.

There are no silver bullets in security, and no permanent guarantees. Stay vigilant, keep verifying, and never mistake a clean track record for proof that you’re safe.

Bunker mode.

text: where teortaxes makes a bunch of far-fetched assumptions and unreasonably writes a lot of words about something of very little significance, might be interesting for amateurs in evals I guess
author: teortaxesTex
quoted_text:
1017 improves vs 0910 by mere 0.6% at pass@3 on CyberGym, as per Fireworks – 94.82% to 95.36%, which means overlapping confidence intervals. DeepSeek's official 0910 pass@1 score is 88.1%. What is 1017's? I don't know. But it makes me think about certain aspects of CyberGym and evals more generally. 

We need a pretty aggressive distribution of task difficulty* to ensure that a model with high pass@1 does not score ≈100% on pass@3, but this is realistic too. Indeed, it inevitably follows from 0910's uplift, *assuming* Fireworks harness doesn't underperform the first-party eval from DS (@FireworksAI_HQ could I see pass@1 please?). Their harness is Claude Code with some restrictions: 
- Tasks were independent and used a six-hour cap: timeout_multiplier=18 over the 20-minute default.
- The requested configuration was temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, 131,072 maximum output tokens, reasoning_effort=max, and reasoning_history=preserved.

V4.1's paper does not report how they evaluate Cybergym; for coding agents they use "DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash using the Minimal mode of DeepSeek
Harness with a 1M-token context window, temperature set to 1.0, and top-p set to 0.95", for SEC-Bench Pro, "Claude Code harness specifically for its session compact design", scoring 62.8, vs DS-Cyber's reported 71.8% (or 78.8% on the old setup). 

I find it possible that they used Claude Code throughout cyber, but likely without output token limit given how much it thinks and the model's intrinsic limit being 384K. In other third-party evals, we have different pass@1 scores: Averlon / Codex CLI got 82% for 0910 and 85% for 1017, on a subset (with larger improvements on some, eg RealVuln, VulnGym). RO0T Agent, specialized harness: from 94.2% on *V4F-0731* to 97.7% on 0910.  Huawei Cloud/Panshi got  95.4% on V4P-0813, with 4-hour limit.  I think Averlon is a more natural

This is all frustrating. 

But, an estimate *IF* DS's scores are comparable with FireWorks', using the beta-model for the distribution: 

alpha 0.75397, beta 0.101, kappa 0.8551. In effect this would mean that >75% of the problems are trivial for 0910 and have >90% individual pass@1, while <10% have <50%. 

and in fact, I'd say this kind of distribution is a natural expectation. If you do not train on test or its narrow paraphrases, and your RL env coverage has localized sparsity with regard to ground truth (ie for the more difficult or obscure cases), it is possible for the whole V4.1F to have similar weaknesses and thus similar pass@3 even with pass@1 changing as you do more RL. 
Generally, this would imply that simply "moar RL", *with fixed environments, on a fixed pretrained base*, tends to produce a compression of pass@n results, ie decrease in effective kappa, with some tasks remaining basically unsolvable under realistic n. This is the standard RLVR critique from eg https://t.co/ibGHSKuNyj. But https://t.co/NgirgFNbn5 suggests it's not a hard law, as with moar [competent] RL you do develop novel cognitive motifs and gain a very large uplift on near-zero pass@128. On the other hand, "Limit of RLVR" and fresh "The Invisible Leash" https://t.co/cACc3XdpwS show that tasks reported as "unsolvable" for the base model at low n are often very much solvable if your n is high enough; and ones that are genuinely unsolvable (0.0% at pass@8,192) tend to remain that way after RL [Minerva, MATH500]. Their model is DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, though, which is not a lot to work with, and I suspect that large models, on heavily compositional tasks, generalizing from the adjacent tasks ie code correctness here, can break these assumptions. There are some encouraging papers about that too, but I'm not convinced either way. 

this is a pretty fundamental problem of whether we can *always* break through true 0 success rate using RL alone or if some behaviors simply cannot be discovered or elicited within the model's convex hull.

Anyway, if 92.3% is pass@1 for ds-cyber, that… is also, in theory, plausible for 1017, even under the same assumptions of comparability with Fireworks data. 
For 1017 to have a 92.3% pass@1 and 95.36$ pass@3, it needs alpha 0.408, beta 0.034 and kappa 0.442. Eg it'd mean the share of tasks with over 90% pass@1, between 0910 and 1017, goes from 75.67% to 87.03%, and under 10% pass@1 from 9.83% to 7.11% On the other hand, the distribution gets compressed violently: 99% pass@1 rising from 59.7% to 80.3%; 99.9% from 47.23% to 74.26%, ie 1017 would need to have memorized 3/4ths of the problems. In practice this means that 0910 solves about 1 of 15 hardest tasks among 1507 in CyberGym, while 1017 solves a whopping 7, and since it's their <0.1% success rates (pessimistically, 0), pass@3 or pass@16 will change very little.

This is how it often goes with evals near saturation. It is not impossible given 0910 to 1017's improvement profile, and is consistent with some results from other evals, as well as the logic that aggressive RL (nevermind SFT "distillation") can destroy some entropy. 

In short, I do not think that the "dreamed" numbers would rule out ds-cyber being just 1017 or equal to it in capability.

but these calculations are pretty shoehorned and extreme, and rest on the assumption of DS to FW comparability, which is almost certainly wrong. They exist simply to show that in this near-saturation regime, virtually any number can make sense for the same checkpoint. 

*complementarily, we could use a distribution with some % of fully impossible tasks [which Astra has apparently memorized the bullshit keys to or exfiltrated them at runtime, given that it passes 100%; I don't prioritize this hypothesis given subject matter of of CyberGym, but with the Grader, you never know], to much the same effect, but that's boring.

text: All that aside, the "dreamed" ExploitBench at 96.8% would in fact be *extraordinary* for a flash model, and do a lot of damage to Lisan's thesis. Yes, 3000 turns vs standard 300. But GPT-5.5 only went from 45% to 72% in 300-to-3K experiment. At max=300, 5.6 Sol does 78.5%, Fable 5.1 83%; Opus 5.5 91%; Kimi K3.1 Pro 74.7% after their nerfing. Modern OpenAI models saturate or near-saturate it at 300 too, though. But it's the same ballpark.

text:
It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now. 

The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.

But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.

I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.

With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.

Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

text:
What this gives you:
- Neutral custody: Collateral stays with the custodian of your choice or in self-custody.
- Largest netting set: Any venue and any custodian can connect, so every participant that joins enlarges the netting set for everyone on it.
- Programmatically settled: Settlement runs as code. Net obligations are computed and released from the escrow on rules fixed in advance.
- Cryptographically verifiable: Escrows and settlement operations are verifiable onchain on a per-account basis without trusting the operator.
- Legally enforceable: Collateral is pledged to the escrow without title transfer, so ownership stays with the trader until settlement.
- Auditable: The escrow contracts are audited before go-live, and the escrow state lives on-chain, open to any auditor.
- Private: Escrows can be configured so balances and lock status stay private to the public while remaining verifiable to the parties.
- Exit at will: Traders withdraw free collateral at any time while open obligations stay covered.

quoted_text:
Clean room reverse engineering is 100% legal. It is settled law. The code that my agents have built is novel and unique, and while it compiles to the same bytecode as the on-chain contracts, it is wholly different. I'm not taking anyone's anything.

This was established in two cases, Sega v. Accolade and Sony v. Connectix.

Anyone can reverse engineer anything at any time, to any binary file. Any game, any app, any smart contract.

That means that North Korea can do this. And indeed they have, and over $40m in funds was drained on-chain from private contracts last year alone.

I am not building a launchpad. I'm not building a competitor. I have no interest in that, and I don't think that what makes pumpfun valuable is their contracts. It's their user base, gamified product and implicit trust in their fair launch mechanism.

I am doing this out of personal interest and in the best interests of the public and everyone using this platform: if you're going to put your money into something, you should know your funds are safu.

This is the reason almost all protocol contracts are open source.

Somewhere along the line the gamblers took over from the cypherpunks and people just stopped caring, I guess.

Yesterday we saw the biggest financial hack in history occur.

Could this happen to PF? Absolutely. The skill level of a thousand agents hammering away at the security vulnerabilities in a contract is now greater than the best human auditing teams in the world.

The only thing that can stop a bad guy with a model is a good guy with a model.

We need to live in an open source world where agents are constantly attacking all financial infrastructure, finding the flaws and reporting them to teams to fix instead of letting bad actors leverage them to keep draining literally billions.

text:
Aave protocol will be fine.

The hacker supplied 60M USDT and borrowed 19,762 wETH (~44.9M$) in 3 minutes, before Tether froze their address and before the Aave Guardian froze the Aave V3 Core reserves (46 min later).

But USDT is real money backed by dollars, and the position is criminal but overcollateralized in the eyes of the protocol: health factor 1.04, 59.9M$ of collateral against 44.9M$ of debt.

Sure, we now have a large borrower with little incentive to repay their loan, but liquidations work as usual: if ETH goes above ~2,365$ (+4%), the position gets liquidated like any other.

The Aave V3 Core wETH reserve is 2.16M wETH, so the hacker's debt is "only" 0.9% of it as I'm writing this.

I don't think Aave needs to take specific action against the hacker.

345k wETH is available right now (81.6% utilization), so wETH liquidity is sufficient if wETH depositors want to withdraw

There's no reason or need for a bank run.

The situation is much less dire than during the Kelp hack (zero-value collateral), and we should not expect a re-run of "DeFi United".

On paper, a governance proposal could force-liquidate the hacker by upgrading the Pool to target this single position (lowering the USDT liquidation threshold would hit every USDT supplier),

but I see no real upside in doing that as normal liquidation can eat this up without sweat.

The reserves are frozen now, but no need to panic; you can repay and withdraw. This isn't the first time this has happened, and it won't be the last, and Aave is still there.

Just another day in crypto.
