text:
"AI writing is bad"

I don't actually consider AI writing to be generally "bad" (except in the cases of egregious overuse of LLM-isms or vapid writing that doesn't convey anything).

But it does have limitations that seem hard to overcome.

Let me share my theory.

First, there is no such thing as universally good writing, except possibly for timeless storytelling like Harry Potter.

The way I would write to Terrance Tao (hypothetically) is not the same way I would write to a first year college student.

The way I would write to an American libertarian is not the same way I would write to a egotistical investor in Vietnam.

A banger on X is not written the same way a viral article in the WSJ is written.

AI can adjust its writing based on the audience.

But it cannot currently produce, *great* writing for any particular audience.

I *suspect* that one of the core reasons is that LLMs don't have empathy the same way humans do.

By "empathy" I don't mean "feel sorry" but "I have an accurate mental model of what's going through your head."

Example: I think I have "empathy" for what you experience when you eat ice cream. "ice cream" has adjacent thoughts that next-token-prediction cannot capture because the "real world next token" of "eating ice cream" isn't captured in the training data.

Now we can guess what the "next token" of eating ice cream is. I want more. My teeth feel cold. I feel good. I should have gotten a different flavor. This is captured in the training data LLMs are exposed to.

But many real-world experiences have "next tokens" that aren't written anywhere but humans universally experience, and can experience through "empathy."

Examples: the ups-and-downs of being a business owner in a particular niche. Marrying into a very different culture. The odd feeling a funny look in a certain context can create. These events create "next tokens" that aren't written, but humans can predict.

Humans can predict each other's "next token" quite well (whether due to biology or culture or both).

The LLM is generally smarter, but intelligence doesn't save you from not knowing key facts.

You can be the best quant in the world, but you'll never trade as well as the nephew whose rich uncle gives him advance warning when he buys or sells.

So that's (one of) the fundamental limitation of LLM writing. Humans have access to alpha LLMs do not, and a dummy with alpha beats a genius with weak signal.

When it comes to writing, humans have an empathy signal that LLMs (apparently) do not.

tldr; 7702 is safu. Binance is not.

"However, in order for the hacker to use 7702, they must have either 1) had access to the private key, or 2) tricked Binance into signing a 7702 authorization."
author: FigoETH
quoted_text:
Quick notes on 7702 to dispel fud and keep your funds safe.

First thing first -- 7702 itself isn't broken.  Don't panic if you are using a wallet that supports 7702 (MetaMask, Uniswap, Ambire, etc.).

To recap, 7702 is an account abstraction EIP that allows an EOA to sign a special message, called a "7702 authorization," that would insert a smart contract into the account, which enables the account to do powerful things like transaction batching, e.g. doing "approve" and "transfer" in one transaction so you can swap on Uniswap with one click.

But unfortunately the same feature also allows a hacker to efficiently move all your tokens in one single transaction.  In the Binance hack, the hacker moved ETH, USDT, and 62 other tokens in one transaction, whereas without 7702 they'd have had to send one transaction per token.  In this particular case, many of those transactions would've failed because Binance was still using the hacked wallet for withdrawals, so all transactions sent by the hacker would've had to compete with the legit transactions for nonces.  So using 7702 did help the hacker steal as much funds as possible, as quickly as possible.  Ouch!

However, in order for the hacker to use 7702, they must have either 1) had access to the private key, or 2) tricked Binance into signing a 7702 authorization.  The latter is very unlikely, as it's hard to imagine Binance being so incompetent as to expose an endpoint for signing 7702 authorizations or (even worse) for signing raw messages which the hacker could've repurposed for 7702 authorizations.  But I can't rule that out until the official postmortem.

What does all this mean for you?

- If you are a wallet developer, do NOT, under any circumstances, expose a way for third parties to request 7702 authorizations.  This is just handing your users a giant footgun to shoot themselves with.  No wallets I know of do this, so don't worry if you are a user.

- If you are a user, use a well-known wallet.  7702 does let wallet developers screw up in more ways than before, so use only well-known wallets whose developers' competence you can trust.

- If you are a company (e.g. an exchange) operating hot wallets, do NOT, under any circumstances, expose an endpoint (even if it's an internal endpoint) for signing 7702 authorizations or raw messages.

As a contributor to AA, I feel partially responsible for hacks like this, since by increasing the power of accounts, we've indeed also empowered hackers (not unlike how any new technology empowers both the good guys and the bad guys).  That said, it's important to note that 7702 was only a transitional EIP, and "endgame AA" such as Frame Transactions (EIP-8141) would allow wallet owners to set up their wallets much more securely.  For example, if Frame Transactions were available today, Binance could've:

- Set up their wallets as multisig contracts only (not EOAs).

- Set up "post conditions" for their `transfer()` functions, so that even if the multisig got hacked, the contract itself would perform sanity checks such as "no transfers of more than 1000 ETH without additional signers."

In short, the endgame of Ethereum UX is one with both optimal security and optimal UX, and users never have to trade off between the two.  But we still have a long way to go until we get there.  Back to work!

text:
being a neocloud can be a good business, but not a venture scale business

let's say you raised $40M and put aside $10M to buy hardware. you buy a 16 node B300 cluster, begin renting it out at $8 on-demand. your cash-on-cash payback is probably 12 months at best. if you buy nothing else, that investment returns like 2-3x over 5 years

maybe you decide to scale. you can put aside another $10M from your balance sheet for another 16 nodes, or maybe you decide to finance it this time. you get a 12% rate.

now you've got 32 nodes, you've broken even, and you're cash flowing.

but you also spent half your balance sheet on an asset that isn't making your product better

there's a world where you buy a much bigger cluster and sell $100M contracts to labs, but that's not the game you're playing - buying 16 nodes doesn't make you a mini CoreWeave

there's also a play where you become the best in the world at racking and stacking GPUs, and build your team around that

but if you're just buying GPUs as an investment asset off your balance sheet, it's pretty close to using your balance sheet to buy Bitcoin

it's not that it's a bad idea

it's just not really the bet a venture-scale startup should be making
author: mernit
quoted_text:
What's happening in the sub-scale neocloud world is concerning  

I'm seeing a lot of startups who raised money from VCs basically pivot into being neoclouds; the issue with that among many other things which I'll highlight in a minute is that neoclouds are not a natural fit for VC money. There is no 100x on the end of the magic rainbow for small cloud teams, at best they'll grow quickly but it's still a business limited by physics to a large extent and even the best teams will not scale valuations like true venture companies (not even close)  

They're pivoting into the neocloud space because it requires capital (which they have from their investors) and it seems like a good business (rental rates keep going up), and maybe their original business plan isn't finding crazy traction  

A lot of these teams doing this however are not equipped to handle the execution required to actually bring capacity online when it was promised to off-takers  It's "idea guy" meets the real world, and "idea guy" vs "local electrician" is not exactly a great matchup for ideaguy  

I see a lot of small teams "becoming a cloud" because it sounds good, but they're not close to being ready to really invest everything to ensure the RFS (ready for service) date they committed to their off-takers will be met by any means necessary. As a result I suspect there will be many lawsuits which actually will lead to the "Guppy Level Death" that Elon spoke about last week  

For off-takers, it's a dangerous environment at the moment - a lot of bad supply in the market, and "providers" who are inevitably going to let them down. Same for lenders.  I suspect the financing constraints will continue to tighten on smaller providers unless they're able to put the puzzle together in a way that sufficiently de-risks the counterparties involved (not so simple). Something we're very focused on at @computeexchange

To sum it up - Elon is probably right in that Guppy Level Death is on the horizon for many of the current sub-scale providers in the market. and what will force their demise imo will likely be lawsuits based on missed RFS dates and other forms of recourse. There will always be demand to work with smaller providers because 1. they can facilitate an RFS date that can actually support your business, and 2. they are more flexible on price than the big boys (which really matters)  

So the long tail of providers will ultimately still be there, it's just a question of who in this batch is going to survive. My guess is not a ton, because execution despite what people say, is still not a commodity at least when it comes to physical processes (like bringing a cluster online). Many aren't up to the challenge, but those who are are worth their weight in gold to off-takers and lenders alike

author: hongshen6666btc
quoted_text:
还是有高手的，解析出了币安这次是如何在以太坊链被攻破的，我大概看明白了

币安这次被攻破的地方，在签名这一步，不在私钥

以太坊有个功能叫 7702，允许普通钱包签一份授权，把账户交给一份合约去管

就像你写一张委托书，从今天起账户交给别人的程序管，钱一进来它就转走

签完之后，账户就不归你了

这份授权书是按编号生效的
每个钱包有个计数器叫 nonce，每发一笔交易加一

授权书绑死在某个编号上，账户走到那个编号才生效，用一次就作废

攻击者不知道币安那个钱包当时走到几号，因为它一直在发交易

于是他们让币安一口气签了 50 张连号的授权书，一张挨一张地签，碰运气

50 张里只要有一张刚好对上当时的编号，就生效了

结果中了一张

真正要命的是，这 50 张是币安自己签的
链上能看到编号是连着的，说明是在极短时间里批量签出来的

Blockaid 的判断是，这更像密钥被滥用，不是密钥被偷

私钥还在币安手里，但攻击者让签名系统以为，这 50 笔是该签的

授权一生效，那个钱包就不再是普通钱包了
它变成了攻击者那份合约的入口，而那份合约只有一个功能，扫所有币、所有 ETH 全转走，只留 1 个 ETH

留 1 个是为了让账户还能继续发交易，别人再往里打钱，照样被扫走

它不是只抢一次，而是一直持续扫钱

同一时间，币安在几条链上的热钱包也在往外流钱

这说明攻击者拿到的不是某个钱包，而是一套能同时对多个钱包生效的签名能力

过去十年交易所被盗，都是私钥泄露、助记词泄露、内部人

这次什么都没被拿走，是系统自己签的字

7702 之后，一个签名能干的事，比一笔转账多太多

text:
An a former $INTC Intel engineer I wrote my thoughts on the company back in December, 2024.
I advocated investors against Intel. 

Have my views changed? 

I never owned Intel. Not when the stock ran. I worked there. I knew the failures were never about demand. They were about management and execution.
Lately I bought a small number of 2028 calls. I talked to former colleagues. Under Lip-Bu Tan, the company was focused on profits. The old, inefficient guard was being cleared out. The fab was doing better. 18A yields were improving.
I've always been skeptical about yields. Not just at Intel, but at any US fab, given how much talent we've lost over the years. That skepticism is starting to ease.

Yesterday's call was rough. Supply is the ceiling. Substrates are short. A tragic accident shut Fab 28. The stock fell 21%.
After a lot of angst, I'm holding. Here's why.
Intel is two very different businesses. One designs CPUs for servers and PCs. The other is a fab that drains capex. Demand isn't the problem for either one. Execution is.
Intel still shows wear and tear. But it has a better CEO than it has had in a decade, and the US government owns a stake. It's more able to fix its mistakes today than at any point I've watched.Demand is robust.
And there's the bigger picture. Intel is the only leading-edge US fab, and the only one showing real signs of change. 
China is ahead in many ways. Depending on Taiwan is not a long-term plan. Trillions of dollars of US tech run on chips made on an island Beijing claims as part of One China.

Intel can't fail.

So I'll give it a chance. Call me foolish.
author: anni_sen
quoted_text:
$INTC I worked at Intel during transition of Brian Krzanich to its then CFO Bob Swan. Swan took care of closing loss making divisions but did little for innovation at Intel. Between inept management, work culture, lack of competitive moat, it was a broken company. 
In 2019 Intels revenue hit 71B and FCF ~14B. It squandered that loot into hiring more inefficient leaders like Murthy from $QCOM.
Gelsinger from VMWare was a good leader but inherited a company so behind in CPU processor architecture, unable to keep up in the AI compute race.
They had good engineers, sufficient capital  but lack of vision, in effective management, paying up for mediocre tech at high valuations from MobilEye to Altera to some AI outfits drained it’s resources 

Except Hock Tan, few non tech CEOs have successfully run big tech. 
I hope they will find a dynamic CEO to lead them, there’s a market out there in the AI compute race. 
They can learn from Hock Tan and aggregate good tech into a tech holding company with focus on vertical value chain like enterprise software. 
Oh and definitely spin out the FAB.
Two cents from an former Intel engineer

ANTHROPIC EXPECTED TO RECEIVE A “HIGH” JUNK CREDIT RATING AFTER IPO: FT

Blackstone has told investors Anthropic is likely to receive a credit rating in the double-B range after going public, below investment grade, reversing its earlier expectations for an investment-grade rating by year-end.

The lower rating could make it more expensive for Anthropic to finance its massive AI infrastructure expansion, while limiting access to pension funds and insurers that face restrictions on investing in junk-rated debt.

The warning comes as Blackstone participates in Anthropic's $63B financing deal, known as Project North Star, to support the leasing of 1.5 GW of Google's AI chips.

Under the deal:

• More than $42B in senior loans are guaranteed by Broadcom $AVGO.

• Another $18B in junior debt is backed by Anthropic's lease payments.

• Blackstone's funds invested $9B in junior debt, earning yields above 10%.

Anthropic's IPO prospectus outlined plans to spend more than $800B on computing infrastructure through 2045.

Without an investment-grade rating, Anthropic may need to continue relying on financially stronger partners to support its borrowing.

The major credit agencies, Moody's, S&P and Fitch, have not yet formally issued ratings for Anthropic, per FT.

text:
Kioxia Q2 was strong, but the guidance deserves a tougher read.

Q2 revenue reached ¥2.48T, operating profit ¥1.995T and net profit ¥1.356T. Operating margin rose to ~80%. Smart Device revenue grew 50% QoQ and SSD & Storage 37.6%.

Yet Q3 guidance is almost flat: ¥2.50T revenue and ~¥1.995T operating profit.

That looks weak in a NAND supercycle, but the details matter. Q2 had delayed Q1 shipments and strong smartphone seasonality; Q3 faces FX headwinds, restrained price hikes and limited shipment growth as capacity remains tight. Kioxia also keeps part of its output outside LTAs, preserving upside to market pricing.

The key question is whether Q4 re-accelerates as Kitakami K2 ramps. If bit shipments rise while ASP and ~80% margins hold, the “growth slowdown” thesis weakens sharply.

Positives: CY27 supply remains tight, CY28 LTA coverage is moving toward ~50%, FCF is extremely strong, and progressive dividends have begun.

Risk: if flat Q3 growth reflects weaker demand rather than supply limits, current margins are vulnerable.

My view: excellent Q2, conservative Q3, but no clear evidence yet that the AI/NAND cycle has broken.

#Kioxia #NAND #eSSD #AI #Semiconductors #285A

text:
英特尔这次是真的是跌懵了。

数据中心业务暴增78%，创下15年来最强劲的增长，结果股价盘前一度暴跌25%，创下两年多来最大单日跌幅。

更讽刺的是，美银刚刚把英特尔的评级从买入下调到中性，目标价从145美元砍到100美元，结果市场直接把股价砸到了70美元以下。

连华尔街分析师的悲观程度，都赶不上市场抛售的速度。

到底出了什么问题？

表面上看，是英特尔第四季度业绩指引太差。市场原本预计营收171亿美元左右，结果公司只给了155亿美元的中值。更夸张的是，每股盈利指引比市场预期低了四成多。

但如果再翻翻财报，信息量确实有点大。。。

比如，英特尔的代工业务。

三季度收入67亿美元，同比增长58%。
但是，这67亿美元里，真正来自外部客户的收入，只有4.11亿美元，占比仅仅6%。

剩下的绝大部分，都是英特尔自己给自己生产芯片产生的内部业务收入。

相当于一家餐厅宣布营业额暴增，结果大部分都是老板自己在店里吃饭。

更尴尬的是，代工业务这个季度还亏了18.5亿美元。

还有一个特别反直觉的地方。

英特尔最新18A制程的单位制造成本，相比年初已经下降了40%。
但18A生产的芯片，毛利率仍然达不到公司平均水平，产能利用率也不够理想。
英特尔甚至准备把部分原本用于18A的产能，重新调整去生产Intel 3服务器芯片。

为什么？

因为服务器芯片需求太旺盛，老一些的制程反而更有现实价值。

技术越先进，不代表赚的钱越多。

造得出来是一回事，能不能低成本、大规模地造出来，并且找到愿意高价买单的客户，又是另一回事。

且，AI一边在拯救英特尔，一边又在伤害英特尔。

AI数据中心需求爆炸，让英特尔的服务器业务收入暴增78%。

但另一头，AI数据中心正在疯狂抢占全球内存产能，推高存储芯片价格。

内存越来越贵，PC整机成本就越来越高。

结果就是，英特尔的AI PC业务明明增长35%，整个PC业务收入却下降了5%。

管理层甚至预计，第四季度PC业务还要环比下滑超过20%。

再往回看，三个月前的8月，英特尔还以每股95美元的价格大规模融资，募集了约230亿美元。结果短短两个月，股价就跌到70美元以下。

虽然英特尔账上还有约540亿美元现金及短期投资，但管理层已经明确表示，2027年依然是资本开支大年，自由现金流预计还是无法转正。

也就是说，英特尔可能还得继续投入巨额资金，去追赶台积电、争取外部客户、扩大先进制程产能。

对英特尔来说，最残酷的事情或许不是技术追不上别人。

而是好不容易把技术追上来了，市场却发现，这门生意未必有想象中那么赚钱。

text:
New challenge on Yukon: Circuit Breaker https://t.co/vpuIh2CnbR

It took 38 years to raise the best proven circuit lower bound from 3n to 3.1n. Days before this launch, an AI model pushed it to 3.5n.

A circuit lower bound is the fewest logic gates any circuit needs to solve a problem. Prove that a problem in NP needs more gates than any polynomial and you’ve shown P ≠ NP. That would settle whether every problem that’s easy to check is also easy to solve, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems.

We’re still far from that bound. Circuit Breaker, built with UCLA Math+AI, is where the push continues.

“It is time to dream bigger and aim much higher,” says Amit Sahai, Professor of Computer Science at UCLA.

Rough few days for prediction markets. Predictdotfun and Polymarket both lost user funds this week, and Binance is now investigating large outflows too. If you got hit, that genuinely sucks, and credit to the teams moving fast to make them whole.

Worth being clear about what actually happened in the prediction market cases: the smart contracts held. As far as it stands today, the money left through the web layer - a compromised third-party script in one frontend, a hacked docs site in the other. 

This is the part people underrate. Your contracts can be flawless and users still lose funds, because the browser loads code from a dozen places and the wallet signs what it’s shown.

We build money-moving infra at Fermah, so we are constantly paranoid about this. Our approach in short is: assume any frontend dependency is compromised, hold no user keys, re-verify every signature server-side, cap what any single signature or session can move, and ship immutable contracts that give no one a lever to redirect funds.

To be crystal clear, none of this makes a system unhackable. The goal is to keep the blast radius of any one failure small and visible.

We wrote up the full approach, including what we would recommend other teams do. It’s a hard week for crypto. Hoping this writeup is useful.

text:
Part 3: Measure once, cut twice: telemetry and Amdahl's law

Most people optimise their bot without ever measuring it. It's like trying to lose weight without a scale.

The bot from part 2 runs from my laptop in Singapore. It felt slow, and my first instinct was to dive into the Rust decision code and optimise the shit out of it. I was very wrong. It was nowhere near the bottleneck.

Then I remembered Kevin Bowers' @jump_firedancer  talks at Breakpoint, and measured first.

One trip, step by step

The bot now timestamps every step from a Binance price update to our new order resting on Bullet, and exports it all to Grafana. Averaged over 5 minutes:
1. Inside Binance: 0.4ms
2. Binance to us: 41.6ms
3. Waiting in our queue: 0.010ms
4. Our code deciding (tick-to-trade): 0.0057ms
5. Order to live on Bullet: 190ms
End-to-end: 232ms

Amdahl's law

Speeding up one part only helps as much as that part's share of the total. Our trading logic is 0.002% of the trip. Make it 99% faster and the whole trip gets about 0.002% faster. Days of work, basically nothing to show for it.

That's the whole point of measuring: know where to look before you spend your time, or Amdahl's Street Justice (as Kevin Bowers likes to call it) gets you.

And the numbers already tell us what to fix:
• Binance to us (41.6ms) is distance. Part 4 moves the bot next to the exchange. Hint hint, colocation.
• Order to live (190ms) is our naive executor. It cancels the old order, waits for Bullet to confirm, then places the new one, and waits on every request. Part 6 fixes that.

Two traps when measuring
• Use Rust --release builds. Debug builds skip the compiler's optimisations, and made our code look 3-5x slower than it really is. More on squeezing Rust in part 9.
• Sync your clocks. Binance to us compares Binance's clock with your laptop's, so if yours is off, the number is off. Mine drifted 433ms behind, so messages arrived before they were sent. That's why end-to-end only uses the exchanges' clocks. Details in the github

Now everything is timed and we have a target. Measure first, then fix the biggest number.

Tomorrow we move the bot to Tokyo, next to the exchange.
author: Tristan0x
quoted_text:
Part 2: Running a simple Rust market maker from your laptop in 5 minutes

Today: 2-sided quoting on SOL-PERP

Market making 101

The order book has bids (people wanting to buy) and asks (people wanting to sell). The gap between the best bid and best ask is the spread. Depth is how much size sits at each price. See attached image.

A market maker rests a bid below fair value and an ask above it, and earns the spread when both get filled. Fill too much on one side and you're holding inventory, so you skew both quotes to lean back toward flat. Get filled right before price moves through you and that's adverse selection, the thing that kills makers.

Fair value comes from Binance, where most price discovery happens: the Binance mid plus the average gap between Binance and Bullet. No trustworthy price, no quotes.

The design

The bot uses the actor model. Every input (a Binance tick, a Bullet book update, a fill, a timer) becomes an event on one queue. The market maker reads one event at a time and answers with intents: place this, cancel that. An executor carries them out and reports back as more events.

Why that fits a trading bot:
• One writer, no locks. Only the market maker touches its state, so there are no races between a fill and a requote.
• Quote on the newest info. If more events are waiting, read them first. Quoting on a price you know is stale is a gift.
• Testable. The market maker never touches the network, so its 48 tests run in milliseconds with made-up events.
• Dry run is real. Paper trading is just a different executor, so dry run runs the same code as live.
• Room to grow. Later parts move feeds and the executor onto their own threads without touching the strategy.

It's the same idea LMAX built a famously fast exchange on: a single thread owning the business logic, fed by a queue.

Why Rust

It's fast, close to C++. The compiler is strict, catching memory bugs (no manual memory mgmt with malloc) and data races before they ever reach production. The cargo crate ecosystem is extensive. And there's no garbage collector. A GC pauses your bot at random (see the orange spikes), and the worst time to pause is mid-move, with stale quotes resting. See the test below, same loop in Go vs Rust on my box: Go's worst tick was ~1ms, Rust's ~0.05ms (chart). That tail is where you get picked off.

To be clear, this strat rn has no edge. The defaults are deliberately wide and tiny, and it's slow: every order is synchronously waited on before the next event is read. It also measures no latency numbers yet.

Tomorrow we timestamp every hop, spoiler alert, our Rust trading logic won't be the bottleneck.

text:
Can we use any compilation pipeline we want to produce efficient machine code, then apply formal methods to show that this code behaves in a certain way? 

This has long been a dream – a gold standard of formal verification, verifying programs at the assembly level – but was considered to be too difficult due to the loss of structure when going from a high level language to machine code. 

Can AI bash through this problem? Apparently yes!

The basic idea I’ve been playing with is to write an interpreter of the target instruction set in an interactive theorem prover such as Lean or Bend. We can then prove that some compiled program conforms to a given specification by writing a proof that connects the machine code, interpreter, and some desired behavior of that code.

Why is this useful? It helps resolve 2 tradeoffs:

- When we write programs in a high level language designed for native execution rather than theorem proving, we get great performance, but are unable to formally reason about how that code behaves.

- On the other hand, when writing programs in a language like Lean, we can write proofs to reason about its behavior, but get poor native performance.

We can try and solve this tension by extracting a program written in something like Rust into Lean, but this tooling is complex, limited, and can introduce bugs! 

Or, we can develop theorem provers that can compile to efficient native code. This is what Bend hopes to accomplish. Today, both of these techniques are limited, so proving at the assembly or bytecode level seems like a good solution.

What is the downside then? Well, formally reasoning about an instruction set is much harder than high level code. You have to consider registers, stack machines, and other low level semantics that are not particularly relevant to showing the correctness of a given algorithm. You also lose a great deal of information during compilation, making reasoning about it more difficult. 

However, if you happen to be proving correctness over the instruction set you actually intend to run, you get *very* good correctness guarantees, as you don't even need to consider compiler bugs in your threat model.

So far, I have experimented with verifying simple algorithms compiled to both RISC-V and WASM32, and have gotten some surprisingly good initial results! LLMs handle writing tedious proofs, and all I do is verify a small set of invariants defining how the code should behave. Interestingly enough, WASM seems to be much easier to reason about, as the instruction set has some higher level semantics, such as local variables and functions. When proving RISC-V, we have to contend with reasoning about things like function dispatch and parameter encoding, which makes life much harder!

Anyways, stay tuned for some more updates on this as I try to see just how far we can push this technique!

quoted_text:
Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Are we actually measuring the things we ultimately want our voice AI models to achieve?

The best AI voices are becoming hard to tell apart.
From each other. Not from humans.

🚀 Introducing Turing TTS: an evaluation that measures how often human listeners mistake AI-generated speech for real human speech.

We tested leading TTS models against real human speech. Even the best model fooled listeners only ~10% of the time.

With Turing TTS, we hope to contribute to a broader discussion within the research community about how we measure progress in voice AI.

If one of our goals is to develop speech that is indistinguishable from human speech, how well do our current evaluation methods capture progress toward that goal?

We don’t claim that Turing TTS is the right way forward, or that human indistinguishability should be the goal of every TTS system.

Rather, we hope these findings encourage the community to collectively examine whether blind pairwise human evaluations of naturalness are sufficient, and what else we might need to measure.

Results are now live on @voicearena_ai.

text:
My friend @corbpage and others brought up the idea of shorting different parts and segments of a business. A good way to approach this could be by tracking different share classes, or even debt instruments tied to individual subsidiaries. Liberty Media did something interesting here with Formula One, SiriusXM, and the Braves. Beloved MSG, similarly...

But taking that a little further, you're essentially saying you don't trust large, bureaucratic organizations to allocate capital as efficiently as an open public market. That probably applies most directly to companies with multiple multibillion-dollar businesses within the same organization.

There should be indicators that give business managers better signals about where to allocate capital, beyond their own internal perspectives. But if that's the case, then we're also questioning whether these business managers should be business managers in the first place.

I'd actually love to figure out who they are and start voting them out instead. Which probably means taking some kind of activist position, something the average public market investor can't really do effectively.

One thing I've been thinking about is building a dashboard of organizational charts across public companies, where you could evaluate individual executives and vote them up or down based on performance, capital allocation, execution, etc.

Could be fun. Could also lead to the corporate Hunger Games, which is essentially what corporations are anyway.

Moving apart from that and to Corbin's point, if you believe in Google's leadership, then you have to hope they'll eventually recognize when Search is no longer the best place to allocate incremental resources and start rebalancing human capital, energy, compute, and financial resources toward alt/new business lines.

Which is essentially what they're starting to do now.

What's interesting is that Search is still an enormously profitable business. So there's an inherent tension in asking management to redirect resources away from something that's working today toward businesses that may be far more important tomorrow.

And over time, I suspect fewer of the best employees will want to work on legacy Search when they could be building entirely new AI products. That creates another pressure on management, because capital allocation is as much about where talent wants to go as it is about where the money goes.

Their success will depend on how quickly they make that transition, and how willing they are to rip apart parts of the existing organization to get there.

Blockbuster wasn't willing to do that. The taxi industry largely wasn't either.

Facebook, on the other hand, was willing to make those kinds of bets and reallocate enormous amounts of talent and capital toward entirely new businesses.

And behind the scenes, people forget how early some of that work actually started. FAIR was established back in 2013, and PyTorch came out of Facebook's AI research efforts years before the current wave of AI adoption. They were building foundational capabilities long before the market understood what those investments could become.

I think that's what's interesting about Google. They have extraordinary distribution, talent, infrastructure, and financial resources. The question is whether they're willing to reorganize those assets quickly enough, even when doing so disrupts the businesses and internal power structures that made them successful.

And bringing this back to the original point, perhaps the more interesting question is whether public markets can create better signals for how capital gets allocated within these organizations, and ultimately hold the people making those decisions more accountable.

LARPing fundamentally changed my life. If you're early career and maybe below average IQ you need to LARP oh and definitely find some smart people to listen to

At the start of 2025 while I was thinking about applying to business school a friend told me to go work at a startup like Kalshi instead. 

At the time it was much much much smaller company than it is today and also trailing far behind in volume and awareness to the larger prediction market at the time Polymarket. 

I had no clue why my friend was telling me he would drop everything to work for these 2 MIT founders.

I'm usually super skeptical person but this friend was claude before claude. He had the reading every wikipedia article type of autism, 4.0 GPA while taking all the hardest math courses in university.

So I read everything Kalshi had ever put out. Every interview, article, youtube video. 

And my conclusion was I had to work here. Tarek and Luana have always been obssessed about building a fundementally sound business. Something you read about in business school case studies. 

Why learn the theory when you can go experience it first hand.

So I wrote a 4-page Notion doc on every gap I could find, and how I’d fix each one.

The chief of staff was impressed enough by the homework and reluctantly took a call.

And when he was slow to respond to my emails… I just started doing the job.

Nobody hired me. I showed up anyway. For a month I did the work like I had the job, until they realized the hadn't actually hired me. 

Today Kalshi is worth $40B. I was just smart enough to join before the hyper growth.

I didn’t build that. I’m just a barnacle on the whale.

But here’s the biggest takeaway if you're early in your career:

1. You don’t need to be the smartest person in the room.
2. But you need to get in the room with the smartest people.
3. Then refuse to leave.

Find your shamu and hold on for dear life
author: salmanso_
quoted_text:
Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

text:
It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now. 

The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.

But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.

I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.

With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.

How We Are Fixing It
 To force the model to learn invariant epistemic structure instead of historical recall, we’ve launched a 3-arm generalisation experiment:

 1. Capacity pruning (XS size preset): Cutting parameter volume so the network physically cannot memorize individual rows.

 2. Aggressive regularisation: 10× weight decay (0.1) and higher stochastic dropout (0.2).

 3. Causal time-valid re-indexing: Strict separation between decision-clock availability and outcome resolution.

text:
Google 太空 AI 芯片第一次答题：卫星发射一个月后，在轨道上写了一首俳句

Google 放在卫星上的 AI 芯片，第一次在太空里完成了一次完整的提问和回答。Google CEO Sundar Pichai 10 月 30 日发推说，团队从地面把指令发到轨道，启动 TPU，跑完提示词，收回了第一份完整回复：一首俳句。

这颗卫星属于 Google 的 Project Suncatcher（“捕光者”计划），研究能不能把 AI 算力搬到太空，用太阳能供电。Google 给的理由是，在合适的轨道上，同一块太阳能板的发电量最多能到地面的 8 倍，而且几乎不间断。地面数据中心现在最缺的就是电。

卫星是 Google 和卫星公司 Planet 合作造的，10 月 1 日搭 SpaceX 的拼车发射任务 Transporter-18 升空。据《纽约时报》此前报道，上面装了 4 颗 TPU，设计寿命约一年。

升空后几周，团队按清单逐项给主机和 TPU 上电，跑了一些简单的机器学习测试。这周走到了“Hello World”这一步。程序员写第一个程序，惯例是让它输出“Hello World”，意思就是跑通了。

过程是这样的：卫星经过地面站上空时，团队把提示词传上去，让星上的 Gemma 4 写一首关于身处太空的俳句。卫星飞过挪威斯瓦尔巴群岛时，把诗传回了地面：

Blue marble below
Data streams in silent grace
Starlight feeds my core.

大意是：脚下是蓝色弹珠（指地球），数据在寂静中流淌，星光喂养着我的核心。最后一句说的正是这个计划要验证的事：靠阳光供电跑 AI。之后团队又让它写了几首太空主题的打油诗，还让它汇报设备的运行状态。

这首诗说明，芯片扛过了火箭发射的剧烈震动，在轨道上能开机、加载模型、算出结果、再把结果传回地面。Google 称这是“数据中心级 TPU”在轨道上的第一次 AI 回复。在太空跑大模型本身不算首次：英伟达投资的创业公司 Starcloud 去年 12 月就用卫星上的 H100 显卡跑过 Gemma，还训练了一个小模型。这次是 Google 自家芯片第一次过这一关。

更难的部分在后面。太空辐射会让芯片算错甚至损坏，散热也比地面麻烦，真空里没有空气帮忙带走热量。Google 接下来要测 TPU 在冷热交替和辐射下能不能稳定干活。下一个节点是 2027 年发射两颗互相连通的卫星。

对普通用户来说，这件事短期内不会影响你用的 AI 服务。按 Google 去年发布计划时的测算，要等发射价格降到每公斤 200 美元以下，大概 2030 年代中期，太空数据中心的成本才可能和地面数据中心的电费打平。

原文：Sundar Pichai 推文（@sundarpichai，2026 年 10 月 30 日）
Google 博客：https://t.co/zskk6ClI4l

text:
Some further clarity on Binance’s claim that customer funds are safe: The assets were drained from one of its hot wallets, which Binance controlled and is the legal owner of.

What does that mean? Generally, when you deposit crypto on an exchange, the exchange becomes the owner and gives you a claim on their assets. Retail customer assets are generally accounted for in an omnibus account with all other retail customer assets, and customers have a claim on a pro rata share.

A spokesperson confirmed this to Crypto in America and said the assets were technically Binance’s funds, and represented customers’ ownership claims for crypto on the exchange. Binance holds crypto in its wallets and credits customers’ accounts with the assets bought on their behalf.

Binance says it is replacing the stolen assets so customers’ account balances and values remain unchanged. Had Binance not had sufficient funds to account for the stolen assets, some customers may have had their recovery reduced, or received a “haircut.”

The exchange says it has reserved more than $6.34 billion in company funds to cover the incident.

🚨NEW: Lots of people are asking: “Binance just got hacked for $6 billion. How can they say funds are safe?”

According to a Binance spokesperson, customer funds were not affected. The money drained came from one of the exchange’s own hot wallets. Binance says most customer funds are held in cold wallets and moved to hot wallets only when users make withdrawals.

“Most of what we earn from day-to-day operations is held in crypto assets. We have kept a lot of them in the company, and reinvested them — into the business, and into security. Because we believe in crypto, and in the long-term value of this industry,” the spokesman said. 

“That is precisely why we are able to absorb a loss of this size, immediately, with our own money.”

quoted_text:
Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

We've spent years asking which AI voice sounds better. 

Voice Arena is asking something different: can listeners actually mistake it for a human? 

The gap between those two questions is worth studying.
author: hamptonism
quoted_text:
Drop 2/15 

Are we actually measuring the things we ultimately want our voice AI models to achieve?

The best AI voices are becoming hard to tell apart.
From each other. Not from humans.

🚀 Introducing Turing TTS: an evaluation that measures how often human listeners mistake AI-generated speech for real human speech.

We tested leading TTS models against real human speech. Even the best model fooled listeners only ~10% of the time.

With Turing TTS, we hope to contribute to a broader discussion within the research community about how we measure progress in voice AI.

If one of our goals is to develop speech that is indistinguishable from human speech, how well do our current evaluation methods capture progress toward that goal?

We don’t claim that Turing TTS is the right way forward, or that human indistinguishability should be the goal of every TTS system.

Rather, we hope these findings encourage the community to collectively examine whether blind pairwise human evaluations of naturalness are sufficient, and what else we might need to measure.

Results are now live on @voicearena_ai.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

Almost 5 years ago, after one of our first trader events, I joked to @luanalopeslara that working at Kalshi felt like a class project. The team was tiny but motivated, and our most passionate traders could fit with us in our cramped SoHo office.

$40B later, our relationships with each other, our product, and our traders feel just as close. There are just a lot more of us now.

Back then I had a quiet deference for large institutions. When we started working with partners much bigger than us, I honestly wasn’t sure we could bring event contracts mainstream without them.

Along the way, I watched companies that looked untouchable come and go, and I watched us keep building. Today we're right alongside the giants I once feared we couldn’t do it without.

What I’ve learned is that every great company starts as an underdog. Up close, even the biggest ones are just people you can admire, learn from, and compete with.

These days, one of my favorite things is walking around the city in my Kalshi hoodie and meeting people who tell me how much they love our product. It never gets old.

None of this happens without our community or the people who have joined this team to make Kalshi better for them. I’m grateful for both, and we’ll never take either for granted.

@mansourtarek_, you wrote that we believed when there was little to point to. Believing was the easy part. You and Luana gave us something to believe in.

We’re still growing, and it still feels like that night in SoHo. Come see for yourself.

text:
有些话憋了半年，一直没说。

倒不是不能说，也不是不愿意说。只是金融市场有个很有意思的现象：看不见的风险，大家总觉得不存在；没发生的事情，说得再多也没人信。

金融市场本质上就是一场合法的财富再分配游戏。

所有资产都打着投资的旗号，但我一直认为，所谓投资，本质上也只是交易中长期做多的一种策略，没什么神圣的。

如果非要说有什么优势，那就是收益与亏损的不对称：理论上盈利没有上限，亏损最多归零。这种数学结构，加上长期经济增长的预期，很容易让人产生一种只要长期做多就能赚钱的幻觉。

但市场从来不负责兑现每个人的预期。

这些年见过太多人追高、杀跌、接飞刀抄底，一套操作行云流水，账户余额一泻千里。

当然，也包括曾经的我。

毕竟自己也是真金白银交过几十 M学费的老韭菜，论犯傻，我可能比很多人更有发言权。我以前真的是一个大傻逼！！！

所以过去一直愿意分享自己的交易观点和市场预判。初衷其实很简单：自己走过的弯路，希望别人能少走一点。

但慢慢发现，我的初衷可能高估了分享的意义。

交易这件事，很多道理只有亏过钱才听得进去。认知相近的人，点到为止就能心领神会；认知不同的人，你把答案写在黑板上，他也未必愿意抬头看。

何况我自己也远远谈不上什么标准答案。

今年就是个很好的例子。

年初那波行情做得不错，后来也比较准确地预判了纳指的阶段性低点并且分享了出来，及时平掉了空单。

结果人一顺，就容易飘。

纳指刚创新高，我又急着左侧做空。更要命的是，后续没有严格执行自己的止损和反手纪律，最终导致最大浮亏一度达到 2M。

方向判断是一回事，交易执行又是另一回事。

道理讲了这么多年，轮到我自己，照样会犯错。

偏偏那段时间，家中长辈又意外离世。行情、亏损、生活里的变故接踵而至，也让我沉寂了很长一段时间。

回头想想，这半年最大的收获，可能就是终于接受了一件事：

市场不需要谁来证明自己是对的，每个人也都有权利为自己的判断付费。

我不是神，也没有义务每次都看对。分享观点从来不是为了证明什么，更没必要把自己活成一个天天喊多喊空的市场天气预报员。

这段时间，无论行情好坏，都感谢一直关注我的朋友。

尤其是在亏损、质疑甚至人身攻击的时候，依然有不少朋友愿意理解和支持。患难见真情，这份情谊比任何一次交易盈利都更值得珍惜。

接下来准备暂时停更一阵交易相关的观点。

出去走走，看看山水，陪陪家人，也重新找找交易之外的生活。

市场永远在那里，机会也永远不会缺席。

钱是赚不完的，人生却是有限的。

感谢大家，江湖再见。❤️

text:
Founders Tarek and Luana dated before starting Kalshi

- Tarek grows up in Lebanon, surrounded by war
- Obsessed with finance, makes it into MIT
- Meets Luana, a Brazilian former ballet dancer
- They start dating
- Eventually break up

- Start Kalshi together anyway in 2018
- The idea: let people trade on real-world events
- Spend two years dealing with US regulators
- Can't launch the product, burning money the entire time
- Finally approved, launches 2021
- Almost no customers, barely any liquidity
- Lays off half the team

- 2023, Kalshi wants to list election markets
- CFTC blocks them
- They sue their own regulator
- September 2024, Kalshi wins in federal court
- CFTC appeals to keep markets blocked
- One month before the US election, Kalshi gets the green light
- Election markets launch, trading takes off

- June 2025, raises Series C at $2b valuation
- Market share grows from 10% to 80%
- Annualized revenue hits $6b this month
- Today, announces Series G at $40b valuation

Truly insane story

text:
In 2014 I went nearly a week without sleep. I was running PayPal and attackers were inside our corporate network. They'd compromised an eBay employee's laptop, got onto the VPN, taken over a domain controller and made themselves domain admins. eBay and PayPal were one company then, on one Windows network. They stole 145M eBay user records, then came for the segregated vault holding PayPal's card credentials. We fought them off. They never got in, but they got close. Too close.

Yesterday Binance lost ~$6.3B in what looks like the same way. A DevOps engineer's laptop, then a service inside the withdrawal stack, then withdrawals the signer approved because they came from a trusted source. Hot wallets emptied in under four hours. No key was stolen.

Nobody broke cryptography or a ledger. They found someone with access and used the trust that came with it. Banks get hit exactly the same way.

2016: attackers inside Bangladesh Bank used its own SWIFT access to send $951M of payment orders to the NY Fed. $81M was lost. The rest was held because an unrelated sanctions filter tripped on the word "Jupiter". That was luck, and it only worked because wires took days to settle.

June 2025: an IT employee at C&M Software, which connects Brazilian banks to Pix, sold his credentials for about $2,700. Attackers used them to send fake Pix transfers out of six institutions' reserve accounts at the central bank. ~$140M in under three hours.

August 2025: stolen vendor credentials at Sinqia, another Pix connector. ~R$710M out of HSBC and one other institution in a single afternoon. The central bank froze most of it, after it had already moved.

Same attack every time. Speed is what changed. When settlement took days, a filter, a correspondent bank or someone in ops could catch a bad payment. Pix, FedNow, SEPA Instant and blockchains settle in seconds. Payment security was mostly built for the slow world.

PayPal's card and user data survived 2014 because domain admin on the corp network couldn't unlock it quickly enough, and our alerting caught the unusual activity on the network. That's the model. Approval policy no laptop or vendor login can reach. Velocity and anomaly limits enforced outside the system that sends. Dynamic caps on what any one wallet, account or service can move per hour. All of it in real time.

About $3B of what left Binance has been frozen, almost all of it stablecoins. The $1.4B in bitcoin is sitting in 19 wallets and nobody can touch it. I don't think that's the problem. For decades the ability to reverse a wire or a card charge let a lot of weak security slide. You either stop the transfer before it's signed or you eat the loss.

Nothing about the technology failed here. The chains processed exactly the transactions they were handed. Binance's own systems handed them the wrong ones because an engineer's laptop was compromised. That's operational security. eBay in 2014, Bangladesh Bank and two Pix connectors all failed at it on their own rails.

In 2014 the attackers never reached the vault. If they had, the fraud losses would have been the small part. PayPal existed so people could pay without handing their card details to every merchant on the internet. We held those details so they didn't have to. Losing them would have broken the one thing the company was built on, and I'm not sure we would have recovered.

I expect blockchains and digital assets to become the standard way money moves. Every custodian of digital assets, or of fiat on a real-time rail, is in that position now. The controls have to adapt to settlement in seconds, crypto or not.

text:
🚨 @Binance was hacked for roughly $6.3B, the largest theft from a single entity on record. This animation shows how it happened 🚨

The exchange lost roughly $6.3B in under two hours on 29 October, and its main hot wallet never signed the transfer that emptied it.

The attacker used EIP-7702 delegation. With a copied key, they pre-signed 50 authorizations, one for each upcoming nonce on a wallet that handles thousands of withdrawals a day. One matched, and from that moment the wallet ran the attacker’s code. A single call then swept about $2.5B in $ETH, $USDT, and around 60 other tokens.

Rotating the key didn’t stop it. The delegation stays live until the same key signs a new authorization, so new deposits were swept again at 21:04 and 21:44 UTC.

The animation walks through every step, from the mixer-funded setup the day before to the final sweep, and then shows where a policy check in the signing path would have stopped it.

@Blockaid has worked with #Binance and the wider ecosystem since the first alert. We’re tracing and freezing funds, and we notify teams as soon as tainted funds reach their platforms. We’ll keep this updated as the story develops.

The research team and I are in the comments, so ask anything about how the attack worked 👇

Therapy doesn’t work for me, and I’m not convinced it was built with autistic people in mind.

The second I walk into that room, I start masking on autopilot. It’s like my face has a “Customer Service Mode” button.

I can hear what she’s getting at beneath the words. I spot the technique. I can practically see the flowchart. So I leave feeling worse, not better: analysed, not helped.

To be fair, she’s doing her job. I get it. She’s trained to sound like she understands, warmly and thoughtfully, with the right pauses in the right places. But it feels like she’s performing empathy, not feeling it.

Meanwhile, I’m sat there thinking: Brilliant. I’ve just paid money to watch someone try to reverse-engineer my brain with a toolkit that doesn’t fit.

By the end, I’m the one doing the heavy lifting. I walk out knowing more about psychology than anything that actually helps with my daily struggles.

Anyone else feel the same?

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

text:
New Google DeepMind paper says AI is already changing the economy, just not in the way people look for.

Its changing through leaner startups, flatter org charts and slower hiring for some entry-level jobs, but not through mass job losses.

The paper argues that big economic change from AI depends on agents learning to coordinate, not on each model getting smarter.

AI models already match experts on many solo tasks, yet jobs and productivity numbers have barely moved. Most benchmarks test 1 model alone, but firms compete as teams.

They built an economic model that tracks 2 abilities separately: competence on single tasks and coordination between agents. More competence moves wages gradually, but coordination past a tipping point lets a few large AI firms suddenly take over big, standardized markets.

In a quiz of 100 people, pairs matched to cover each other's weak spots beat random pairs by 32%. AI copies share the same weak spots, so a model that beats every person alone can still lose to a well-matched human team.
author: Scobleizer
quoted_text:
I joined @GoogleDeepMind to develop a research program on the economics of AGI. Today, together with Andrew Koh (@andrewjkoh) and Shane Legg (@ShaneLegg), we are incredibly excited to release The Economics of Intelligence, the first in a series of projects from our group on how AGI will change the economy.

How do capability improvements transform the economy, and when? In this project, we define thresholds of economic capabilities, e.g., minimal AGI, based on how they transform the economy. We then track how the economy–market structure, employment, and wages–changes during the transition across capability regimes.

We have seen exponential increases in what AI agents can do but the broader economy seems almost remarkably unchanged. Part of the reason is that the solo AI agent is the wrong economic object; economic transformation is an equilibrium outcome where organizations compete. Looking at how intelligence functions within organizations, transformation will depend on when two key capability thresholds are crossed: competence (gains on individual skills, e.g., coding, math) and coordination (gains on ability of agents to cooperate and work together).

We show that what economic transformation looks like depends on whether AI becomes supercompetent, supercooperative, or both—the regime of artificial superintelligence (ASI). Tracking this transition shows why the real visible transformation may come from improvements in coordination—a capability most benchmarks don’t yet track. Past a certain threshold, AI capabilities can break the Coasian ceiling on firm size and lead to an economy that looks drastically different than the one we see today.

Two main takeaways:
1. To understand the path of transformation, we should be tracking agentic coordination more closely.
2. The impact of AI will likely show up in wages before market structure or employment.

We are really excited about this paper. Excited to hear people’s thoughts.

text:
我不太建议把个人 portfolio 的主要资金再放在 crypto。

主要原因是，就这短短半个月以内，已经出现 4 个采用率极其广的操作系统/编程语言的重大安全漏洞了。只要是人写的代码，只要可被逆向、bytecode 可以被分析，那就一定存在被注入以及漏洞挖掘的风险。很多底层的程序语言以及多年前开发的程序，中间经过了不知道多少代人的维护，早就已经是代码屎山了。

在这种情况下，crypto 的很多资产管理方式都非常不安全：多签可以被篡改，前端也可以被劫持，设备可以被入侵。更别提很多人拿一个手机设个 8 位数密码，或者用个浏览器插件，就敢在里面放几百万美金。很多人觉得用苹果的设备就绝对安全，但请别忘了多次的重大安全事故里面（包括这次的 Binance，以及之前的 Bybit，包括之前出现过的大大小小事故里面），工程师用的也是 Mac 系统和IOS工作手机。冷钱包也并非绝对安全，即使是从未联网的冷钱包，也有可能因为前代留下的傻逼假随机数被攻破。现在在 AI 的加持下，尤其是开源模型非常强大、且支持私有化部署的前提下，攻防逐渐不对等了。所谓“道高一尺，魔高一丈”，动态攻防那也是要等先发现了漏洞再防，但是中途被牺牲的，其实是用户的资金安全。我觉得零日漏洞之后会越来越多。Crypto 领域依然有很多非常有趣的机会，不管怎么样，meme也会一直存在，洗钱和支付也是原生需求，套利也是一直存在的，只是crypto的利率要重新算风险溢价了。

 Crypto 的 venue 够多，但 venue 够多也意味着可被攻击的节点更多。因Crypto 资金要是丢了，像 Binance 这样的体量是可以完成赔付的；但很多其他交易所、很多其他 venue 是做不到赔付的，甚至会直接跑路。维权之路是非常艰难的，你把钱放ibkr买美债，收益可能只有1/3，出事了起码有存款保险给你赔。作为一个每天在做服务器运维和跑量化策略的人来说，一直把所有资金放在无法控制的随时可能被零日漏洞攻击的环境里，不是一个明智的选择。

quoted_text:
AI is slowly changing how people trade

You’ve probably seen people using AI to analyse crypto, stocks, forex and prediction markets like Polymarket

But how does it actually work?

Basically, AI can help traders process information, study market data, monitor price movements, follow news and identify possible trading opportunities

Some tools only provide analysis and suggestions others do combine AI with automated trading systems to take things further

When connected to a supported trading platform through an API, these systems can place orders, open or close positions and manage trades based on their instructions and permissions

For example, a trader could set up a system to monitor multiple markets, look for certain conditions and execute trades when those conditions are met. This can reduce the need to watch every market and place every order manually

But it’s also important to understand that AI doesn’t automatically mean better trading or guaranteed profits

It can misinterpret data, make poor decisions or follow a strategy that stops working when market conditions change Automated trades can also fail because of technical issues or poor execution

That’s why human oversight and proper risk management still matter

I think we’ll see more traders experimenting with AI as these tools become easier to access

But the big question is: would you trust an AI trading system with your money?

text:
Fighting abuse & spam on a consumer app is a perpetual cat-and-mouse game: 

Every solution you create is a bandaid for 3-12 months -- until the adversaries find a workaround. When money is involved, people are tenacious to circumvent your patch and keep the money flowing.

While large language models have made attacks more intractable, there are tools you can build to protect your product:

(1) An in-house Risk Scoring stack that assigns a 0-100 score of likelihood someone is a spammer or bot. This should be informed by machine learning, IP & email reputation data, device telemetry, among many other signals.

(2) A near-bulletproof method to "checkpoint" your highest risk users, such as liveness verification or phone number auth. This will have to be reinvented every year (e.g., CAPTCHA tests are obsolete now with today's models).

As new attacks emerge, you can move the risk threshold lower to checkpoint more people. However, you want to be cautious so you don't add unnecessary friction for too many people and impact usage.
