Sequoia's thesis that the next $1T company will sell work, not software, is the most important reframe in AI right now.

The argument: if you sell a copilot, you're competing with every new model release. But if you sell the outcome, books closed, contracts reviewed, claims handled, every AI improvement makes your margins better, not your product obsolete.

The key insight most people miss: for every $1 spent on software, ~$6 is spent on services.

The entire SaaS playbook was about capturing the software dollar. The AI playbook is about capturing the services dollar, at software margins.

Not "AI for accountants." The AI accounting firm.
Not "AI for lawyers." The AI law firm.

The companies that figure this out won't look like SaaS companies. They'll look like services firms rebuilt on software infrastructure.

That's a fundamentally different company to build, fund, and scale. And most founders are still building copilots.

quoted_text:
Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

text:
On Variational you can't withdraw your own funds permissionlessly

Read their contracts. As far as I can tell:

- Collateral sits in per-user usdc pools on arbitrum, ~$224m across ~208k pools
- You can deposit into your pool but you can't withdraw from it yourself. Every withdrawal goes through their oracle contract and only addresses with PROVIDER_ROLE can trigger it
- 17 addresses have that role, 16 of them plain wallets (EOAs). as far as i can read the code, any one of them can move usdc out of any pool on its own, and the contracts don't cap the amount
- The admin that hands out these roles and can pause the oracle is a single EOA: 0x8e4d1ad423e4f37600cda314fd3d99629ceaeabf. role changes take effect immediately
- Docs describe the olp vault as "a smart contract where the capital that powers OLP (USDC) is secured". the address they list for it, 0x74bbbb0e7f0bad6938509dd4b556a39a4db1f2cd, has no code. It's an EOA 
- the protocol treasury, 0x5e91b40467fb8902c46a7b6cb90482363188d645 (~$12m usdc), is one of the 17 provider keys

Docs say the keys live on fireblocks. If there are policies on them (limits, quorum) that answers most of this, but none of it is visible onchain

@variational_io how is the admin key secured, do provider keys have limits, and how does a user get funds out if your backend is down?

Correct me if I'm wrong

text:
Our firm’s back of the napkin math shows that Nvidia’s $NVDA ACIE segment could potentially overtake hyperscalers in two to six quarters. This is an important development as it results in Nvidia’s revenue being more resilient as hyperscalers shift capex toward designing and deploying their own custom chips.

ACIE revenue grew faster than hyperscaler revenue last quarter at 138.5% compared to 101.2%, respectively. After reclassifying one company, the QoQ growth for ACIE was 25% compared to hyperscalers at 13%.

Depending on how you model the two-quarter lumpiness, ACIE can conservatively overtake hyperscalers in 5-6 quarters at a 14% QoQ growth rate versus 10% QoQ growth rate for hyperscalers, or as soon as 2 quarters if the Q2 pace continues.

In early September, Dell $DELL was in agreement with Nvidia’s results, stating that enterprises and neoclouds could contribute half of AI data center capacity growth through 2030, creating a $1 trillion total addressable market (TAM):

“We’re expecting AI to be 75% of all data center demand by 2030, adding 200 gigawatts of power over that same time frame. And half of that, we believe, is right in our sweet spot with our customers, the Neoclouds, sovereigns and enterprises. And if you look at that math, we think the opportunity in front of us is more than $1 trillion over that time frame.”

Although it may seem counterintuitive for Nvidia, Dell or Super Micro $SMCI to emphasize enterprise and neocloud customers over the hyperscalers and their $1 trillion capex next year, the reason is simple.

Unlike the hyperscalers, these customers do not have those budgets to splurge tens of billions on custom chips. Instead, demand is more concentrated in ready-to-deploy servers that can immediately be brought online to generate revenue for immediate ROI, which Dell and Super Micro can do in as little as six hours to one day.

Tin foil hat time.

My theory is that Binance has had a hole in their balance sheet for a while now.

Today was their last-ditch effort to nuke crypto prices so they could buy back way lower, fill the hole, and maybe even make some money off the top.

They saw prices going up, realized the hole was going to get WAY bigger, and decided to nuke it.

Unfortunately for them, prices didn't drop nearly as much as they needed.

And I'm not buying this story about some random DevOps developer getting hacked and compromising the entire operation.

I've worked in enterprise software engineering. Nobody at companies of this size should have that kind of unilateral access.

Changes to critical infrastructure typically have to go through multiple layers of review. Engineering, security, DBAs, org leadership, etc.

In a properly secured Kubernetes environment, you aren't be able to just waltz into production pods and do whatever. 

You're telling me one compromised DevOps engineer had enough access to cause BILLIONS in losses, and there wasn't a single additional control in place to stop it?

You expect me to believe that shit?

Something doesn't add up.

This is speculation, obviously.

Mayne reveals his two-timeframe rule for every trade, using higher timeframes to identify key price levels and lower timeframes to find precise entries and stop losses

“When you understand that these patterns are the same across all time frames, really the magic, at least for me, comes when you combine two time frames together”

“I have a two time frame rule for all trades that I take. I don't take any trade off of a singular time frame. It's always two”

“The higher time frame, whatever it is, it could be the monthly and weekly, it could be the four hour if you're a lower time frame trader, that's where you're looking for your levels, your demand, your area where you think price is going to get a reaction”

“Once price gets to that zone, that's when you scale down to the low time frame and you look for that fractal to play based on what you think is going to happen”

“When you start to get good at that pattern recognition, it helps you turn what a lot of people believe is noise on the low time frame into exactly how I get into my setup, why I know where the entry is, and why I know where the stop loss is”

if u wanna know what crypto to hold for the next bull run, apparently all u gotta do is look at today’s reported $5.6B Binance hack

guys no wonder $ETH is Kim Jong Un’s favorite pookie 

So bullish on my ETH babies😭

but jokes aside, I’d keep a very close eye on the market over the next 72 hours. wouldn’t be surprised if we get another leg down. I’m already getting ready to DCA.

this whole thing reminds me of 2022.

remember, LUNA collapsing in May wasn’t the bottom. Celsius and 3AC blew up in June, BTC flushed to around $17.6k, and then FTX happened in November and took us down to ~$15.5k.

looking back, those were some of the best accumulation opportunities of that entire cycle. but they didn’t all happen at once.

major blowups tend to cluster around periods of forced deleveraging. when institutions are scrambling for liquidity, they sell whatever they can, not necessarily what they want to. that’s when prices can temporarily disconnect from fundamentals.

now, I don’t think it’s fair to call this FTX 2.0 just yet.

FTX was fundamentally a solvency and credit contagion crisis. so far, the Binance situation appears to be a security breach, with roughly $2.4B in stablecoins reportedly frozen and Binance saying user funds are safe.

that’s encouraging, but we still don’t know the final losses or whether there are any second-order effects. frozen funds aren’t necessarily recovered funds either.

and remember, BTC was already under pressure before the hack news broke. we’ve got a hawkish Fed, weakness in tech stocks, and a market that’s still extremely sensitive to liquidity.

the hack just added another layer of uncertainty and triggered a pretty brutal long liquidation cascade.

so over the next few days, I’m watching withdrawals, any signs of contagion, whether futures leverage gets properly flushed out, and most importantly, whether real spot demand starts absorbing the selling.

a big red candle alone doesn’t mean we’ve found the bottom. I wanna see whether the forced sellers are actually running out.

I’m not interested in catching the exact bottom or levering myself into another disaster lol. just keeping dry powder and preparing to DCA in stages if we get another proper liquidity sweep.

and please, every time something blows up in crypto, people start screaming that the entire industry is finished.

we heard enough of that shit in 2022.

the industry survived, but plenty of individual companies and tokens didn’t. there’s a difference.

anyway, I’m watching closely and getting ready to buy the fear, fam. 🥒

text:
I’m keeping a close on eye on @tapeupio that’s launching their token $UP tomorrow. I’ve staked a good portion of my $BEM on @tapeupio and i’ve been publicly bullish on it and its team since the protocol launch. 

@tapeupio id one of the biggest protocols on @TapeOutWorld and what’s interesting with their token launch is that they’re experimenting with a completely new trading mechanism called PoB (Proof of Build) designed to encourage long-term ecosystem participation rather than short term speculation and align community incentives.

$UP is going to be paired with $BEM, and instead of spending your entire buying budget with $BEM immediately, PoB spreads most of your purchases over 25 days. the idea is to create sustained buying demand and incentivise long term community participation. 

unlike PoW or PoS, PoB isn't a blockchain consensus mechanism. It's a token launch and trading model.

here’s how it works:

1. supply: 21 million $UP tokens, with 100% initially allocated to trading liquidity. no team allocation is mentioned.

2. gradual buying (PoB): When you buy $UP, only part of your $BEM is spent immediately:

first 24 hours: 10% immediately, 90% over 25 days.

after 24 hours: 30% immediately, 70% over 25 days.

3. sustained buying pressure: the remaining $BEM is locked into future $UP purchases. It cannot be withdrawn, creating a pipeline of potential buying demand over time.

4. builder code: users can enter another user's code to accelerate purchases for both participants using their respective locked $BEM. This also earns them a share of $UP rewards.

5. fees and rewards:
- 1% trading fee in $BEM, distributed among staking participants, $UP buybacks, and the team.
- 1.5% tax in $UP, redistributed to users participating in builder code acceleration.

6. crosschain expansion: once $UP reaches a 10 m market cap, it automatically enables conversion to BEP20 $UP on BNB chzin without increasing supply.

It’s a completely new trading mechanism intended to discourage purely short-term speculation. It’d be interesting to see how it’ll work.

special thanks to @BruceBlue and @tapeuptony for their help dd’ing this. i think it’s the definitely worth to keep an eye on this launch 👀

text:
支持币安。刚才我把时间线上几种人mute了：说币安这次被盗是在替 10·11 偿债的，幸灾乐祸的，以及借机唱衰整个加密行业的。在这样一个悲伤的时刻，行业需要的是同舟共济，而不是落井下石。想说几点。
第一，加密没有想象中脆弱。 大家可以去看一下数据：被盗之后，整个加密资产的跌幅其实还不到隔壁 AI 板块几个重要 ticker 跌幅的一半。在最坏的消息面前，这个市场展现出了超出预期的韧性。

第二，关于 EIP-7702。 很多人把矛头指向 7702，认为账户级授权给黑客开了方便之门。需要阐明的一点是，7702 让一个 EOA 可以把合约逻辑挂载到账户上，从而实现交易打包——比如把 approve 和 transfer 合成一笔，一键完成 swap。这次黑客确实利用了同样的能力，在一笔交易里把 ETH、USDT 和另外 62 种代币全部转走。如果没有 7702，他得一种资产发一笔交易，而币安当时还在用这个被盗钱包处理提币，黑客的交易要跟正常提币抢 nonce，很可能有一部分会失败。所以客观地说，7702 确实帮黑客”偷得更多、更快”了。但它是放大器，不是漏洞。黑客能用 7702，前提是已经拿到了私钥，或者骗到了币安签的一个 7702 授权——后者几乎不可能，除非币安暴露了一个可以签任意消息的接口。以太坊基金会和账户抽象方向的几位核心研究员都给出了同样的判断：7702 本身没有大问题，真值得复盘的是：一台 DevOps 的个人电脑，是怎么一路穿透到生产环境的？为什么能调用签名器做任意签名，连 BTC 的签名都能过？整套流程又为什么能完全绕开提币的安全审计？

AI时代的资产安全攻防战能否打好，我能看到很多行业内的 player 都在努力。矛越来越锋利，盾也会在一次次阵痛中越铸越厚。加密从未死去，只会在一次次阵痛中变得更强。

第三，BNB Chain 一直在认真布局新东西。 之前以太坊香港期间，我和@nina_rong 沟通后，邀请 BNB Chain 的 CTO David 参加了我组织的与 Vitalik 的小型座谈会。会后我帮忙David老师和BNB对接了耶鲁的一个抗量子团队，正在推进抗量子账户的部署。至少在技术层面，我能看到BNB对 AI security 这些 concern 非常上心。

第四，币安作为行业的最大玩家，我很反感有一些尬黑号发黑帖说它是靠一路抢掠、跑马圈地走到今天的。能成为头部，一定有它背后的原因。@heyibinance 有多劳模我就不赘言了。一件小事我一直记得：去年在阿根廷参加 DevCon，我们和 Vitalik 同桌吃饭，他说起自己当时问了一圈人愿不愿意捐助他支持的一个 biotech initiative （NGO）——@cz_binance 是第一波响应的人，毫不犹豫地捐了 1000 万美金。

最后之所以想发这条，是因为刚看到《晚点 LatePost》对一位国内VC 投资人的采访。对方说，在中国 VC 投资的顶峰时期，一年也不过投出四五十亿美元。这不正是黑客一把偷走的钱吗。这笔钱如果投在真正有意义的方向上，不知道能成就多少事。想到这里，我是真的心痛。

我相信币安的格局，自己也买了一些 BNB以示支持(这么大的hack才跌了百分之七），也了解到目前币安的资金储备能很好cover这次危机。

希望经此一役，我们能真正建立起一整套危机预警机制——在重大黑客风险面前，这个行业能够团结一致，而不是各自为战。

author: HarryStebbings
quoted_text:
Very few podcasts will actually make you smarter AND make you laugh.

No politics, no egos, just tech.

The biggest news this week:

- Anthropic Files S1 Ahead of $2TRN IPO
- Instinct's Rumoured $30BN Fundraise
- Microsoft Lays off 27,000 While Meta Taps Equity Markets for $95BN Capex Spending Spree

My notes with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. Analysis of Anthropic S1

Anthropic's S1 beat expectations on margins and operating income, even after stock-based compensation, leaving the burden of proof on the naysayers. It also looked strong on customer concentration, compute efficiency and cash. Some questions remain, including the undisclosed Q3 revenue number.

2. Is the Value Extraction Requirement From the Latest Models a Benefit or a Curse of Anthropic?

Eighty percent of Anthropic's revenue comes from models less than six months old, and 70 to 80% of compute costs go to training. Models are expensive to build and highly profitable to serve, but only for six to twelve months. Few companies can write a $10 to 12BN compute check, so this short shelf life can favour Anthropic if it stays aggressive.

3. Brutal Reality Is Microsoft Have Just Admitted They Don't Want 27% of Their Workforce

Whatever gets said on LinkedIn, Microsoft's move says it does not want 27% of its people. That is a worse scarlet letter than a pure layoff, because the company has told these employees they do not meet its minimum bar.

4. Chinese Open-Source Models Have Peaked and Will Decline From Here

Chinese open-weight models are close to finished in the US, and this is the beginning of the end for them. Despite DeepSeek's latest raise, it is starting to be banned across all federal agencies.

5. Why No CIO Will Take a Chance on a Chinese Model

Even if confidential data reaches Alibaba servers in Asia only one time in 100,000, without consent, no CIO or CISO will approve the model. If it keeps happening and Alibaba stays silent, anyone using these models will lose their job.

6. Why OpenAI Is an Underappreciated Asset to Invest in Today

OpenAI is mispriced at the $1.25 TN round. Brief market panic has created a dislocation like Anthropic's round at around $183BN, even though OpenAI has closed all its competitive gaps.

7. What Is the Upside of OpenAI at $1.25 Trillion?

OpenAI and Anthropic are both expected to become $10 to 20TN companies. Anthropic takes only 0.1% of Fortune 500 budgets today, and even conservative estimates put that at 2 to 3%. Because OpenAI is not priced to perfection, the worst case is doubling the money.

text:
看见币安被盗的快讯之后第一反应是不相信，第二反应是把放着理财的 USD1 卖了换 USDT，当时还没有很多人反应过来，USD1/USDT 只砸到了 0.9997。北京时间 4:43 消息发酵并且确认大概是真的被盗，想了想 EVM 链应该已经有很多人提了，4:45 从 APT 发起了提币，果然，已经提不出币了

黑客在链上的操作导致了 ETH 的巨大溢价，当时是 2800-2900，gwei 145 左右，本着醒都醒了的原则把之前在 Robinhood 和 Base 上冲土狗的几万 u 跨到了 ETH 主网上，最后没赚多少钱，因为交易失败卡住了

再看了眼时间，迪拜时间币安的团队大概率都还醒着，反正也提不出币了，慌也没什么用，又把 USD1 在 0.9990 左右买回来了。本金都被威胁了，当时我也没什么心思想着到底多哪个空哪个了。事后想想应该有聪明人猜到币安一定会把这些代币买回来，去中心化程度较高的 PEPE、UNI 和 ENA 不一样，很难从项目方那里以一个较低的价格 OTC 买回来，只能从二级市场买，于是也看到了 PEPE 有了个较好的涨幅

有件事不知当不当讲，ENA 项目方应该是本次被盗事件中的最大赢家。被盗的是用户资产，需要掏钱买回来币的是币安，结果 ENA 还能一次性出这么多货不承担任何道德风险，哈哈哈

思考一件事直到 8AM 都没睡着。以前有个不太政治正确的共识吧，就是存在 CEX 尤其是存在币安这样的龙头老大交易所，对绝大多数普通人来说是远比硬件钱包安全的最优解。结果这次发现，首先硬件钱包不安全，其次 CEX 在 AI 时代也没想象中那么安全了。有种鸡蛋不要放在同一个篮子里，于是分别放在了 Bybit Bitget 硬件钱包和币安里，最后都分别出事儿了，尽管用户资产都没有遭受 FTX 级别的损失，这点华人交易所说明在危机处理上还是反应快的、经验老到的，还算值得称赞的

有关钱放在哪里最安全的问题，昨晚跟几个朋友电话聊了聊。稳定币一度被认为是集抗监管（主要体现在中国人不交加密税维度）与一定程度跑赢通胀（因为高利息），为一体的最优解，普通人拿着 USDT 多爽啊，经常能白嫖各种 CEX 远高于美债利率的利息，而经此一役，多少有点内心难安。黄金？也早成风险资产了

这时候我寻思着，那再往前推一点呢，优质公司的股权？朋友说，这年头，如何定义优质，版本迭代太快了，你不看 INTC 都能一天跌 30%。还别说，确实挺对的，很难预测下一个版本什么东西能一定 outperform，除非这事你真自己在干，你有 conviction。我再换了个思路，说，那从政？（不经过严谨思考想了半天想不出什么方向还有效了，瞎说的一个选项，显然对普通人来说是走不通的）朋友说，那死得更快。于是又陆续排除了包括并不限于房子、实体、基金等选项，最后得出答案，还是明明白白的软妹币和美钞拿着不烧心啊，尽管也有被税的可能性，但至少不至于哪天一锅被端了。当然这也有要点，比如单银行不超过 50 万人民币，在存款保险的限额内存款等等。这又回到了最开始选择加密货币的理由，抗通胀资产，法币有通胀啊。。。这下死循环了

只能说，恐怕普通人对于资产存放的不安全感会是接下来几年十几年的问题，直到 AI 彻底接管普通人类前都会存在的一个问题，那么对普通人来说，只能谨慎谨慎再谨慎，做好人只能富一次并且很难富第二次的心理准备保护好本金。而在人力资本投入的维度，群里有一些 05 后甚至刚 17 岁的小孩，还比较迷茫，于是魏神在群友讨论未来应该从事什么行业的问题时，给出了一个非常有建设性的意见：现在卷很多东西未来可能都逐渐没用，必须谨慎筛选方向。只有卷健康是投入 100% 必长期复利的。高效地花钱，并把它投入到身体健康的维度，这投资不会输

很久没有分享这么长的杂谈了，也是想记录一下历史事件发生时没有营养的一些思考和记录，也尤其好奇有关资产安全性的问题到底有没有什么更好的答案，虽然大概也没有什么更好的答案，有的话那不早就直接梭了。但至少一个毋庸置疑的事实是，做多长寿的必要性又增加了

quoted_text:
Do NOT buy a 512GB Mac Studio ‼️

Two 256GB Mac Studio M5 Ultras are ~$700 cheaper and have ~1.7x faster prefill and decode

Price: $22,299 vs $21,598
Both are the 36-core CPU / 80-core GPU

You can connect 2x 256GB with one Thunderbolt 5 cable + RDMA, which is fast enough to run one model across both

Prefill (compute)
- 1x 512 does ~135 TFLOPS
- 2x 256 does ~215-245 TFLOPS
- Apple claims up to 3x for a 4-Mac cluster, which works out to ~1.7x for two

Decode (bandwidth)
- 1x 512 has 1.2 TB/s
- 2x 256 gets ~1.9-2.2 TB/s effective
- With tensor parallelism each box reads its half of the weights at the same time, which works out to ~1.7x for two

GLM-5.3 goes from ~33-40 tok/s to ~55-70
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash goes from ~45-60 tok/s to ~75-100
Both are 4-bit with spec decode on, estimated from M3 and M5 Ultra benchmarks

If you want Qwen3.8-Flash-Next or GLM-5.3-Flash, a single 256 already runs them well and you don’t need either setup. The 512GB question is about DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (552B) and GLM-5.3 (753B), tied as the best open models on Artificial Analysis v5. They need 310-420GB at 4-bit, so neither fits on one 256

text:
I first heard about Kalshi as a senior in college, 6 years ago, and I loved the idea immediately: I felt like prediction markets solved an urgent need in the world. But I still wasn’t sure that joining the company was the right next step for me. Instead of going to a ~10 person startup, I could instead take a job at a big tech or trading firm.

My view changed as soon as I met the team: everyone I spoke to - among them @mansourtarek_ , @luanalopeslara , @luishusier , and @_rainerds  - was so passionate, curious, and thoughtful. It became clear to me that even if the company didn’t succeed - if I gave it my all, I could learn a lot by working with such talented people.

Kalshi has had its ups and downs, but that first impression has held true for every day of my last 6 years. Remarkably, as we’ve grown, the challenges have grown too. I have felt at times incredibly stressed, but that all is 100x easier to bear with the right people around you and the knowledge that you’re working through difficult, worthy problems together.

With an announcement like this one, it’s easy to look back in hindsight and say that I made the right choice. But I’d feel the same way even if today’s news was very different, and we were still 10 people grinding away.

I’m so grateful for having had the opportunity to build with this team, and I look forward to many more years and even tougher problems to solve together. If you’re interested in joining us, send me a message!

“It's a dangerous business, Frodo, going out your door. You step onto the road, and if you don't keep your feet, there's no knowing where you might be swept off to.”
author: mansourtarek_
quoted_text:
Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

Update on the Binance exploit and RSR:

Binance confirmed the attacker drained one of its hot wallets and that it will cover all losses with company funds, including the stolen RSR. We've been in direct contact with Binance's team since our last update, and they've moved quickly and responsibly, confirming that they will be re-purchasing the missing 3.38B RSR promptly.

New from Binance co-CEO @_RichardTeng's video update:

• Binance has set aside over $6.34B of company funds to cover the stolen assets. About $5B of that is already held in the exact tokens affected (he named USDC, USDT, BTC, ETH and BNB).
• It's buying the remaining assets through market and OTC channels. Because the Reserve treasury does not have an appetite to reduce its RSR position, in the case of RSR we believe Binance will acquire on the open market through a professional market maker.
• Binance withdrawals are paused while the team rebuilds and retests its withdrawal system. It hopes to reopen them before Sunday. Until then, RSR on Binance can't be withdrawn.
• A full proof-of-reserves report has been promised by Monday. That's where you'll be able to check that RSR balances are fully backed. We infer from this that the RSR re-purchase will be completed by Monday.
• Binance is working with law enforcement, blockchain analytics firms, token issuers and other exchanges to trace and recover the stolen funds.

On Reserve's side, nothing has changed since our last update. We'll keep monitoring and share more as Binance does.

text:
RAG 又杀回来了。

最近 Agent Memory 越做越复杂，但这篇《Memory Tax》发现了一个挺尴尬的结果：

很多专门设计的 Memory 系统，最后还不如直接对 raw history 做 RAG，而且成本更高。

作者把 Memory 的价值拆成两部分：

Memory Benefit：RAG 答错，但 Memory 答对的问题。

Memory Tax：RAG 本来能答对，经过 Memory 处理后反而答错的问题。

问题就出在「整理记忆」这一步。

历史被摘要、重写和结构化以后，一些细节会直接丢失；另一些虽然还在，却变得更难检索。

比如在 LongMemEval 上，Qwen3.6-27B 用两轮 RAG 能做到 81.4%，GPT-5.6 Luna 达到 90%，都高于对应的复杂 Memory 方案。

一个简单的修补反而很有效：

Memory 继续用，但同时保留 raw history 的检索通道，再把两边结果一起 rerank。

这篇工作也给我们做了一个提醒，给 Agent 加 Memory 之前，最好先拿最简单的 raw-history RAG 做个 baseline。

有时候，真正昂贵的并不是「没记住」，而是过早把原始信息总结掉了。

text: Bill Gates is the pure, sick product of our era. A society that rewards the appearance of goodness over goodness itself. That prefers the press release to the result. The charity gala to the factory.
author: CryptoScoopOG
quoted_text:
Today, two visions of the world are colliding. And Bill Gates is probably the clearest example.

On one side, the people who build. On the other, the people who manage.

For 30 years, Gates has presented himself as the man who wants to save the world. But look closely at how it actually works.

His philanthropy is first and foremost a reputation machine. Millions poured into media, massive funding for supranational organizations, a presence everywhere the narrative gets written. When you fund the people who write the story, the story is rarely hard on you.

Then there's the model itself. Foundations, NGOs, grants. A system where money flows, reports pile up, conferences follow one after another, but the problem never actually needs to be solved. Because a solved problem is a cause that disappears. Grants keep the problem alive. Entrepreneurs kill it.

The Elon Musk episode sums it all up.

In 2022, Gates reaches out to Musk to talk about philanthropy and climate. Musk asks him one question: do you still have a half-billion-dollar short position against Tesla? Gates replies: sorry to say I haven't closed it out.

Read that again. The man who wants to save the planet from climate change was betting hundreds of millions on the collapse of the company that did more than anyone to electrify global transportation. And he was asking its founder to back his climate vision.

Musk said no. Obviously.

Because underneath, these are two irreconcilable philosophies.

Musk believes we need more. More energy, more humans, more planets. Abundance as the answer.

Gates believes we need to manage. Consume less, emit less, have fewer children. Ration, regulate, control. It's Malthus for the modern age: the conviction that humanity is a problem to contain rather than a force to unleash.

Bill Gates is the pure, sick product of our era. A society that rewards the appearance of goodness over goodness itself. That prefers the press release to the result. The charity gala to the factory.

And deep down, I find this man profoundly sad. To have had so much money, so much power, and to choose to manage the world instead of building it.

A de facto power struggle has erupted within one of Poland’s most important state institutions in Warsaw today. For now, the outcome of this confrontation remains uncertain.

Police did not enter the building, but a significant number of officers have been deployed in the surrounding area.

Korwin-Piotrowska suspended Tribunal President Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, for one month, temporarily taking charge of the institution herself.

Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, called the developments a “coup” and urged Polish President Karol Nawrocki to intervene.

Nawrocki has cut short his visit to Senegal and is returning to Poland.

The conflict stems from a deep division over the composition of the court. Donald Tusk’s government refuses to recognise the Tribunal’s rulings because of judges appointed under the previous PiS government.

Meanwhile, Nawrocki and Święczkowski refuse to recognise judges elected by the Sejm in 2026.

quoted_text:
Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

Let me show you why: 
- Anthropic subsidises subscriptions (and leads in SemiAnalysis subscription value chart) 
- OpenAI subsidises API (hence, dominates at the Pareto frontier)

There is a very good reason why Anthropic's subscription plan seems so "cheap" (gets more tokens), cheaper than even the nearest competitor OpenAI: 
it is deliberately chosen to be a "loss leader" because so few people use it compared to rest of the business (Claude API, Claude Enterprise). This is something OpenAI can not do, but they have their own loss leader.

A loss leader is a product or service that a business intentionally sells below its production or market cost to draw in customers, with the goal of making a profit on additional, higher-margin items bought at the same time. People who use cheap Claude subscriptions for personal use end up loving it and recommending it at work, and there is where Anthropic makes profit.

Other Anthropic subscription products are not at all subsidised. For example, for "Claude Enterprise" you pay a base price and then you pay for tokens at API price. No subsidy!

Let us look at the revenue mix
- for Anthropic 80% revenue is direct API, and 20% subscriptions (individual and Enterprise).
- for OpenAI 20% or less revenue is direct API, more than 65% is individual subscriptions and rest in Enteprise subscriptions. 

That is why OpenAI can not afford to heavily subsidise consumer subscription because this is where they make most money!!!

This is also why OpenAI can afford to sell their API cheap, because it doesn't contribute the most to revenue - that is exactly why OpenAI are Pareto frontier leaders

quoted_text:
Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

text:
The real story here is that the market wanted cheap onchain data that applications could actually use.

The industry spent years making blockchain execution cheaper and data availability cheaper, but largely neglected making data useful to execution.

The focus on data availability never really captured that demand. It made L2s cheaper to operate, but did little to enable new classes of applications. Meanwhile, scalable L1s like Solana demonstrated that execution itself could become much cheaper.

Data availability should have helped unlock an entirely new class of data-centric applications. But the fundamental limitation was that execution layers couldn't directly access the data being made available.

Even Ethereum's blob storage illustrates the problem. Contracts can verify commitments to blobs, but they can't read the contents of those blobs.

So data availability largely became a way to reduce the cost of securing and scaling existing applications, particularly financial applications on L2s. It didn't make large amounts of application data useful to smart contracts.

EigenLayer was moving in a more interesting direction, extending Ethereum's economic security to the validation of entirely different types of services.

But I think even that is the wrong affordance.

Developers don't want to assemble separate systems for storage, availability, validation, and execution.

They want cheap onchain data that's verifiable and directly accessible to the execution layer, without paying the cost of executing every data update through a VM.

That's what we're building towards with Irys.

text:
有人发现了一种非常离谱的 JavaScript 混淆技术：通过在代码里塞入大量生物武器、毒药和致死剂量相关的函数名，让 AI 因为安全限制而拒绝分析代码。
安全研究员 veritas 在分析浏览器指纹脚本时，发现一段来自 ServicePipe 相关域名的 JavaScript，里面充斥着极其诡异的函数名：
computeRicinLethalDosageForWaterSupply
calculateDeadlyLethalSuicideAspirinDosage
光看名字，仿佛在研究生化武器。但实际上，这段代码只是在收集浏览器指纹，包括 User-Agent、GPU、Canvas 等信息。
研究员怀疑，这些名字是开发者故意设置的陷阱，专门用来阻止 AI 辅助逆向工程。
于是他做了个实验：
• Astra：拒绝分析
• Astra + Daybreak Blue：仍然拒绝
• GLM-5.3：成功分析
这就有意思了。
传统代码混淆是通过复杂控制流、加密字符串、无意义变量名，让人类和工具难以理解代码。
而这种新思路，直接瞄准了大模型的安全机制。
代码本身可能完全无害，但只要在函数名里塞进足够多的危险词汇，部分 AI 就可能主动放弃分析。
更讽刺的是，模型越严格遵守某些安全规则，面对这种混淆时反而可能越容易受到干扰。
当然，目前还没有证据证明开发者一定是故意这样设计，也不能说明这种方法对所有模型都有效。
但它揭示了一个值得关注的趋势：随着越来越多的逆向工程依赖 AI，未来的代码混淆技术可能不再只针对编译器、反编译器和人类研究员，还会专门针对大模型的安全判断机制。
以前是让代码难以理解，现在甚至可以尝试让 AI 不敢理解。

quoted_text:
.@ThinkingUSD once said, if you ask candidates during interviews about how much revenue binance generate per year and they are off by magnitudes, you shouldn't hire them. for trading / defi adjacent things, i think this is absolutely crucial. i've been doing this and you would be surprised how many "crypto ppl" have no fucking clue. 

The CEX game was very tough and competitive since 2013. You are a goober if you think @coinbase @binance won their position at the top bc they were "early" and "benefited from first mover advantage in a nascent industry". Esp binance, which was started in 2017 so 4-6 years late. I've always wanted to figure out WHY and HOW binance became so successful, and learn about how some great runner-ups like @bitfinex, @BitMEX gradually lost their top positions. 

The following is a summary of my findings based on conversations with traders with 9/10 fig volume, MMs, binance board member since 2018, CZ's poker friend since 2011, ex-listing lead, and reading CZ's recent book.

Disclaimer: Some love binance and others hate them. This post is not judging the right and wrong - only an analysis on the six months, two quarters period during which they became the no. 1 cex by size.  

early reasons (2017 Q3)  

> ICO heat: Binance started in July 2017 with its ICO bc it couldn't raise VC capital due to the competitiveness of CEX sector back then. They raised $15m in the ICO. They did that in July and China banned ICO and CEX that September 4th. There will be no Binance if they were 6 weeks slower. 

> All publicity is good publicity: OKX and Huobi banned users from withdraw to hinder Binance's ICO, which accidentally drove a lot of traffic and eye balls to Binance while they damaged user trust. 

midterm reasons (2017 Q4)

> The few that caught the 2017 Q4 Bull: After 2017/9/4 ban, OKX and other leading CEXes based in China got significantly slowed down. Binance moved their entire team out to Tokyo and functioned without interruption during the 2017 Q4 bull market. BTC 5x ed during that 3 months and they were on-boarding 100k+ users PER DAY. 

> PMF / fast listing is more important than Compliance: After 9/4 ban and while in Tokyo, BTC exchange was viewed as more compliant while policies around ERC-20 exchanges weren't clear. They went ahead with listing ERC-20s off the ICO market heat and became the largest CEX in 6 months bc ppl couldn't trade alt-coins elsewhere. 

long-term reasons (2018 onwards) 

> USDT wave: Before Binance/Bitfinex, most CEXes were fiat-pair based. Binance caught the wave of USDT @tether growth in 2018/19 

> 300 Binance Angels for international markets: 300 grassroot users from all over the world who bootstrapped adoptions in some emea / third world markets that no other CEXes have successfully penetrated through with in-house teams. This is different from ride-sharing apps' international growth, which were all done by in-house teams 

> 1hr reply customer support: sounds simple but lots of CEXes weren't doing it back then 

> Liquidity moat: Once this is established, it's very difficult to outcompete unless there's a huge influx of 1. new liquidity; 2. new traders; 3. new, demanded assets that incumbents somehow don't list fast enough; 4. or, no KYC and US users in @HyperliquidX 's case 

= my biggest takeaway =  

due to the high growth / frontier nature of startup / tech, some quarters are much more important than other quarters. if you did the right things during those quarters, you set your company up for years or even decades after. if you messed up those quarters, it will take decades and billions, and highly likely never, to outcompete again.

author: joemccann
quoted_text:
It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now. 

The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.

But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.

I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.

With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.

‼️ A COUP IS HAPPENING IN POLAND 🇵🇱

Poland's Constitutional Tribunal is being subjected to an extraordinary takeover operation by pro-EU Prime Minister Donald Tusk. 

Its official website has been taken over, an announcement has appeared removing its president and vice-president from their duties, and police have been deployed around the institution.

The Tribunal's existing leadership has declared the operation illegal and accused those responsible of committing a coup d'état.

The Constitutional Tribunal is the institution responsible for reviewing whether laws comply with the Constitution. It is broadly comparable to the constitutional-review function of the United States Supreme Court.

Today, its website announced that President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański had been suspended for one month. 

The person now claiming authority over Poland's Constitutional Tribunal is Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, elected to the Tribunal by Donald Tusk's parliamentary majority in March 2026.

But there is a fundamental legal problem: she has never taken her judicial oath before the President of Poland, Karol Nawrocki.

Under Article 4 of the Act on the Status of Constitutional Tribunal Judges, newly elected judges must take their oath before the President of the Republic.

Nawrocki refused to receive her oath. Instead, on April 9, Korwin-Piotrowska participated in an alternative swearing-in ceremony organised inside the Polish Parliament, without the President's presence or participation.

The Presidential Chancellery explicitly declared that this procedure had no legal basis and could not confer judicial authority. The existing leadership of the Constitutional Tribunal maintains that she is therefore not legally a judge of the institution.

And now, a woman whose authority to serve as a constitutional judge is rejected by the President and the Tribunal's existing leadership is being presented as the person entitled to take control of the entire court.

Poland's Constitution does not give the prime minister or his government the power to dismiss the Constitutional Tribunal's leadership.

Article 194 establishes the Tribunal's composition and the procedure for appointing its president. Article 195 guarantees the independence of its judges. 

The announcement of a suspension relies on Article 130 of the law governing ORDINARY COURTS. Invoking this article to suspend the leadership of the Constitutional Tribunal is a legally indefensible distortion of the law, revealing a staggering disregard for elementary constitutional principles.

HOW DID POLAND GET HERE?

Donald Tusk returned to power in December 2023, promising to reverse the judicial reforms introduced under the conservative Law and Justice government.

Those reforms had been fiercely opposed by the European Commission, which initiated rule-of-law proceedings against Poland and linked access to European funding to judicial conditions.

Tusk's government subsequently presented Brussels with a programme for restructuring the judiciary, including the Constitutional Tribunal. The European Commission welcomed that programme and ended its Article 7 proceedings against Poland in 2024.

The methods used by the EU and its supporters undermine the very constitutional principles they claim to restore.

President Karol Nawrocki has reportedly interrupted his journey to Senegal to return to Poland.

author: Alchemy
quoted_text:
Binance’s update is a useful case study in what incident readiness requires once funds are already moving.

A compromised endpoint reached the withdrawal path. No private keys leaked, yet ~$6.3B left across more than ten chains in ~20 min.

Freezes started in less than 1 hour after funds first left Binance. Ability to respond fast depended on three things that had to already exist: fresh on-chain data, relationships with issuers and blockchain teams that can trace and freeze funds, and the operational authority to pause the service and revoke access.

The educational takeaway for infrastructure teams is that the speed of the freeze is downstream of the quality of the preparation. Detection alone is not enough if the escalation path, the data, and the permission to act are still being negotiated while the drain is underway.

Silver Lining: crypto industry worked together quickly to cauterize the attack!

text:
with all due respect, that is not what agents need.

agents need a way to RELIABLY EXECUTE ON HUMAN INTENT. 

i’m bearish on all companies that are giving agents human identifiers. they all seem to think the pain point is that agents are being blocked by all these institutions, websites and merchants, so they make it easier for agents to bypass them.

but we need to think why this is happening! 

every one of those blocks exists because a human identifier in the wrong hands is the oldest fraud vector there is:
- the FTC logged $15.9B in reported fraud losses in 2025, up 24% YoY
- identity theft reports hit 1.36M and credit card identity theft alone was up 33%
- javelin puts identity fraud losses at $27.2B
- the FBI flagged account takeover as a rising vector, with $893M in losses already tied to AI

step-up auth, device checks, bot detection. institutions spent decades building these to answer one question: is this really the person who owns this identity? 

handing an agent your card number, your login or your SSN doesn't answer that question. it makes the agent indistinguishable from the fraudster.

quoted_text:
Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

Claude 200 美元档改名 Ultra，已验证账号取消 5 小时限额，价格和周额度不变

Anthropic 10 月 30 日宣布给 Claude 的两档 Max 套餐改名：每月 100 美元的 Max 5x 改叫 Max，每月 200 美元的 Max 20x 改叫 Ultra。价格不变，现有订阅自动换成新名字，用户什么都不用做。

同时，Ultra 的已验证账号不再有 5 小时限额，当天先对大部分现有订阅者生效。较新的账号在通过验证前保留一个临时限额，官方说这是为了防止欺诈和滥用，限额取消时会收到邮件。周限额不变。

【取消 5 小时限额，对我有什么用】

Claude 付费套餐原本有两道限额：一个每 5 小时重置一次的窗口，一个每周的总上限。重度用户，特别是用 Claude Code 长时间写代码的人，常遇到周额度还剩不少、却被 5 小时窗口卡住的情况，只能停下来等它重置。

Ultra 去掉这道限额后，一周能用的总量没变，但可以连着用，不用再每隔几小时停一次。每周本来就把额度用光的人，总量上不会多拿到什么。

100 美元的 Max 还是两道限额都有，每 5 小时和每周的用量都是 Pro 的 5 倍。200 美元的 ChatGPT Pro 一直只有周限额，Ultra 现在在这一点上和它一样。

【我的账号验证了吗】

验证由 Anthropic 自动完成，依据账号和付款记录等因素，用户不需要提交任何东西。订阅时验证手机号是另一回事，不会取消这个限额。帮助页没说验证要多久。

自己查的方法：打开 Claude 设置里的“用量”页面，如果看不到“当前会话”（Current session）这条进度条，账号就已经验证，5 小时限额已经取消。

【名字里的“20x”去哪了】

旧名字里的 20 倍，指的是每 5 小时窗口能用 Pro 的 20 倍。新的 Ultra 帮助页写的是，每周用量是 Pro 的 10 倍，另有一个单独的 Fable 周限额。SemiAnalysis 10 月初的实测也是这个比例：200 美元档每月可用量约是 100 美元档的两倍。

Anthropic 没解释为什么改名。5 小时窗口取消后，按窗口算的“20 倍”对 Ultra 不再适用，新名字里也就不带倍数了。

text:
Ask your local library to order Unelected.
Most NYT bestsellers get a quiet boost from institutional buyers and library systems. This one didn’t. It hit the list on reader demand through Passage Press. That makes library requests a high-leverage way to expand its reach beyond people who already follow the authors or buy directly.
Why it matters
Libraries buy multiple copies once a title is requested enough times.
It puts the book in front of people who wouldn’t otherwise see it.
It reduces the relative advantage of titles that arrive with pre-arranged institutional support.
Public libraries are still one of the few remaining open distribution channels that don’t require a platform algorithm or a retail buyer’s approval.
How to request it (takes 2–5 minutes)
Go to your library’s website (or the app) and search for “request a purchase,” “suggest a title,” or “recommend a book.” Most systems have a simple online form.
If you prefer in person, ask at the reference or circulation desk. They handle these daily.
Give them:
Title: Unelected: How You Paid a Sinister Elite to Take Over America
Authors: Jennica Pounds & Joshua Lisec
Publisher: Passage Press
ISBN: 979-8-90116-062-6 (hardcover)
Add a short note if the form allows: “New York Times bestseller; high local interest.” That’s often enough.
Many libraries will order it if they get even a handful of requests. A few more from the same system strengthens the case.
If your library already has it, check it out. Circulation numbers matter too.
Do it once, then mention it to one or two other people. That’s the whole ask.

author: hashcoin0
quoted_text:
is Variational telling half-truths about fund safety?

interesting take from Degen Guy
Variational’s statement on the Binance hack sounds reassuring - “user money is on-chain, doesn’t go to external hedge exchanges, 100% withdrawable anytime”

technically true, collateral sits in isolated on-chain settlement pools and isn’t sent to CEXs

but there’s a nuance they didn’t mention

on Omni you don’t trade against other users - you trade against a single counterparty, OLP (their internal market maker). All trades go through RFQ, and OLP is the one that has to pay you your profit

OLP hedges its exposure with its own capital on external exchanges (including Binance and others). If OLP loses money on hedges and becomes insolvent:

- your original collateral can still be withdrawn
- but unrealized and realized PnL turns into bad debt and doesn’t get paid

so the platform really doesn’t touch your deposits, but your profit depends on OLP’s solvency, which is directly tied to the risks of the same external exchanges they hedge on

the statement is technically correct, but it creates a feeling of full safety that doesn’t actually exist

to really reassure users they should show OLP’s current external exposure and capital buffer, not just say “collateral is on-chain”
until then it looks like a careful half-truth

I recommend subscribing to his TG channel - justdegenguy

My take on the current AI trade "bear narrative in a fear driven market": "Nasdaq is KOSPIfied."

$INTC beat on EPS by 30% and still lost a fifth of its value after hours. Disclosure: I don't own Intel and never saw it as a pure AI trade (too much PC, too much foundry capex), but the reaction is worth studying.

The miss came from PCs, data center supply and an Israeli fab, not from AI demand. Everyone sold the AI story anyway. A stock valued on 2028 dies on anything that threatens the funding of 2028.

Now look at the beats, the one-day wonders:

$MU in June: revenue more than quadrupled, +15% on the day. Two weeks later 22% off the high, below its pre-earnings price.
$MU in September: revenue +380%, 87% gross margin, 7x forward P/E. A month later down ~20%.
$SKHY this week: record quarter, 80% operating margin, ~$75B in shareholder returns. +13%, then -2% the next day and -7% in Asia today. Let's see where it is in two weeks.

The bear read: this is what a peak looks like. 80%+ margins, capex doubling, 7x earnings because nobody believes the earnings will last. And the cycle is already hitting customers: memory costs are pushing up PC prices and PC units are falling. That's part of Intel's miss.

The bull read: an early supercycle, not a peak. HBM sold on long-term agreements, SK Hynix seeing shortages through 2030. Not a smooth ride: capex doubling, demand destruction at the edges, and it all depends on the AI buyers continuing to pay.

Both sides trade the same numbers. They disagree on how long the cycle lasts. However when the market is in fear or extreme fear like last week bears win.

That's the asymmetry right now. In a crowded trade a beat brings out sellers waiting for an exit, while a miss tells everyone the exit has arrived. Good news fades. Bad news compounds.

The AI trade still moves as one block on narrative days and sorts violently on earnings days. Being right on the theme no longer pays by itself. What pays is owning the bottleneck when the narrative wobbles.

My take is that the AI trade over time will stop trading as a block and the real winners will be more and more visible over time when fear moves to neutral territory and above.

저는 전 $INTC 인텔 엔지니어로서 2024년 12월에 이 회사에 대한 제 생각을 썼습니다.
저는 투자자들에게 인텔을 반대하도록 주장했습니다.

제 견해가 바뀌었나요?

저는 인텔 주식을 한 번도 소유한 적이 없습니다. 주가가 급등할 때도요. 저는 그곳에서 일했습니다. 실패가 수요 때문이 아니라는 걸 알았습니다. 그것들은 경영과 실행에 관한 것이었습니다.
최근에 저는 2028 콜 옵션을 소량 매수했습니다. 전 동료들과 이야기를 나눴습니다. Lip-Bu Tan 아래에서 회사는 수익에 집중했습니다. 오래되고 비효율적인 경영진이 청소되고 있었습니다. 팹이 더 나아지고 있었습니다. 18A 수율이 개선되고 있었습니다.
저는 항상 수율에 대해 회의적이었습니다. 인텔뿐만 아니라, 우리가 수년에 걸쳐 잃어버린 인재 때문에 미국의 어떤 팹에 대해서도요. 그 회의가 점차 누그러지고 있습니다.

어제의 컨퍼런스 콜은 힘들었습니다. 공급이 한계입니다. 기판이 부족합니다. 비극적인 사고로 Fab 28이 중단되었습니다. 주가가 21% 하락했습니다.
많은 고뇌 끝에, 저는 보유하고 있습니다. 이유는 다음과 같습니다.
인텔은 두 개의 매우 다른 사업입니다. 하나는 서버와 PC용 CPU를 설계하는 것입니다. 다른 하나는 자본 지출을 소모하는 팹입니다. 어느 쪽도 수요가 문제가 아닙니다. 실행이 문제입니다.
인텔은 여전히 마모와 손상을 보여줍니다. 하지만 지난 10년간 가졌던 최고의 CEO를 두고 있으며, 미국 정부가 지분을 보유하고 있습니다. 제가 지켜본 어떤 시점보다 오늘날 실수를 고칠 수 있는 능력이 더 있습니다. 수요는 견고합니다.
그리고 더 큰 그림이 있습니다. 인텔은 선도적인 미국 팹으로 유일하며, 실제 변화의 징후를 보이는 유일한 곳입니다.
중국은 여러 면에서 앞서 있습니다. 대만에 의존하는 것은 장기 계획이 아닙니다. 수조 달러의 미국 기술이 베이징이 하나의 중국의 일부로 주장하는 섬에서 만든 칩으로 작동합니다.

인텔은 실패할 수 없습니다.

그래서 저는 기회를 주겠습니다. 저를 어리석다고 부르세요.
author: mindmoon_108
quoted_text:
An a former $INTC Intel engineer I wrote my thoughts on the company back in December, 2024.
I advocated investors against Intel. 

Have my views changed? 

I never owned Intel. Not when the stock ran. I worked there. I knew the failures were never about demand. They were about management and execution.
Lately I bought a small number of 2028 calls. I talked to former colleagues. Under Lip-Bu Tan, the company was focused on profits. The old, inefficient guard was being cleared out. The fab was doing better. 18A yields were improving.
I've always been skeptical about yields. Not just at Intel, but at any US fab, given how much talent we've lost over the years. That skepticism is starting to ease.

Yesterday's call was rough. Supply is the ceiling. Substrates are short. A tragic accident shut Fab 28. The stock fell 21%.
After a lot of angst, I'm holding. Here's why.
Intel is two very different businesses. One designs CPUs for servers and PCs. The other is a fab that drains capex. Demand isn't the problem for either one. Execution is.
Intel still shows wear and tear. But it has a better CEO than it has had in a decade, and the US government owns a stake. It's more able to fix its mistakes today than at any point I've watched.Demand is robust.
And there's the bigger picture. Intel is the only leading-edge US fab, and the only one showing real signs of change. 
China is ahead in many ways. Depending on Taiwan is not a long-term plan. Trillions of dollars of US tech run on chips made on an island Beijing claims as part of One China.

Intel can't fail.

So I'll give it a chance. Call me foolish.

text:
What if you could hold a stock only while the market is closed, without buying and selling every day?

That's the idea behind Isolated Exposure Tokens (IETs), proposed by @0xbeans and The @standard_rsv.

Deposit one tokenized share and receive:

• OVERNIGHT: exposure from the close to the next open.
• SESSION: exposure from the open to the close.

Hold both and redeem for one share. Sell one to keep only the exposure you want. Each series has an expiry; exiting one side earlier requires a buyer.

A simple example:

• A $100 share starts with $50 allocated to each token.
• It opens at $110: OVERNIGHT rises to $60.
• It closes at $105: SESSION falls to $45.
• Together, they're worth $105 at the accounting level.

Why it's interesting and why we're at @paboxoxyz also loves it as it align with our off-market lending features.

• Could support overnight-only vaults and targeted hedges.
• Splits exposure without requiring the issuer to trade the underlying every day.
• Gives DeFi another building block, similar in structure to Pendle's split claims.

But something that still needs some works and detailed explanations:

• Each token starts with roughly 2× exposure at its initial accounting value.
• Balances accumulate dollar moves, so they don't reproduce the compounded returns.
• Expected overnight gains can already be priced into the token.
• Overnight exposure existed before through NightShares ETFs.

The vault can't pay $110 if the losing holder owes nothing. Caps, early termination or extra capital could help, but the supplied paper doesn't specify a rule.

Promising concept. It needs clear loss rules, reliable price feeds and affordable liquidity before the historical overnight anomaly becomes a new primitive.
