text:
Larping fundamentally changed my life. If you're early career and maybe below average IQ you need to LARP oh and definitely find some smart people to listen to

At the start of 2025 while I was thinking about applying to business school a friend told me to go work at a startup like Kalshi instead. 

At the time it was a much much much smaller company than it is today ... and also trailing far behind in volume and awareness to the larger prediction market at the time: Polymarket. 

I had no clue why my friend was telling me he would drop everything to work for these 2 MIT founders.

I'm usually super skeptical person but this friend was claude before claude. He had the reading every wikipedia article type of autism, 4.0 GPA while taking all the hardest math courses in university. If there's one thing I have learned in life is you just gotta listen to folks who know ball.

So I read everything Kalshi had ever put out. Every interview, article, youtube video. 

And my conclusion was I had to work here. Tarek and Luana have always been obssessed about building a fundementally sound business. Something you read about in business school case studies. 

Why learn the theory when you can go experience it first hand.

So I wrote a 4-page Notion doc on every gap I could find, and how I’d fix each one and emailed their chief of staff.

@beckhardt  was impressed enough by the homework and reluctantly took a call.

And when he was slow to respond to my emails… I just started doing the job.

Nobody hired me. I showed up anyway. For a month I did the work like I had the job, until they realized the hadn't actually hired me. 

Today Kalshi is worth $40B. I was just smart enough to join before the hyper growth.

I didn’t build that. I’m just a barnacle on the whale.

But here’s the biggest takeaway if you're early in your career:

1. You don’t need to be the smartest person in the room.
2. But you need to get in the room with the smartest people.
3. Then refuse to leave.

Find your shamu and hold on for dear life
author: salmanso_
quoted_text:
Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

text:
raising Fund II has never been harder. only 12% of first-time VC funds from the 2022 vintage have raised a second fund so far. here are 7 reasons i think so many struggle

1. they're better at fundraising than investing

some managers are great at telling LPs what they want to hear. they have a compelling story, a convincing deck, and a thesis that sounds amazing. but can they actually pick companies that will generate returns? that's a very different skill. 50 out of 99 VC funds failed to return invested capital after fees, while 62 out of 100 failed to outperform public markets after fees and carry.

the problem is that you won't know the final results for years. by the time Fund II fundraising comes around, LPs are already judging you on early portfolio performance, the quality of your decisions, and whether your original thesis is playing out. you need to show progress before the exits happen.

2. they have no real edge in deal flow

venture returns are driven by a tiny number of exceptional companies. less than 4% of invested capital in its dataset of venture-backed exits generated returns of 10x or more. everyone wants those winners. but how are you actually going to find them and get onto their cap tables? if your strategy is just going to events, asking for intros, and competing for the same deals as everyone else, you're going to have a hard time.

you need a real reason why the best founders would come to you, ideally before everyone else knows about them. otherwise, you're often left competing for deals that stronger investors have already passed on.

3. they don't have a plan for their winners

finding a great company is only half the job. you also need enough ownership for that company to make a meaningful difference to your fund. i think this is where follow-on strategy becomes really important. as an existing investor, you get to see how founders execute, how the team works, and whether the business is actually delivering on its promises. that information can give you a real advantage when deciding where to put more capital.

of course, doubling down doesn't always make sense. valuation, dilution, and concentration risk still matter. but if you've found an exceptional company, you should have a plan for how to benefit from being right.

4. they can't explain why LPs should choose them

this one is pretty funny. VCs constantly ask founders what makes their startup different, why they'll win, and why anyone should invest. then some of those same investors go out to raise their own funds and struggle to answer exactly those questions.

what's your investor-market fit? what's your edge? why should an LP trust you instead of giving that money to an established manager? especially when you're starting out, you need a convincing answer. and the fundraising environment isn't making things easier. only 81 first-time US VC funds closed through Q3 2026.

5. they're competing in a market where capital keeps concentrating

this is probably the toughest part because even good managers can't control it. through Q3 2026, US funds of $500M+ captured 78.1% of all VC capital raised, despite representing just 6% of funds closed. firms raising their fourth fund or later took 88.2% of the capital, while the median fund size fell to $10M.

think about that. huge amounts of money are flowing into venture, but most of it is going to a relatively small group of established firms. a new manager can have a strong thesis, good founders, and a promising portfolio and still struggle to raise the next fund.

6. they underestimate how much LP relationships matter

i've seen how important this is. some managers only start building LP relationships when they're ready to raise, but by that point, they're already behind. LPs want to know how you think, how you make decisions, how you handle problems, and whether they can trust you over the long term. regular updates, honest reporting, and actually understanding what matters to each LP can make a huge difference.

ideally, by the time you start raising Fund II, your existing LPs already know exactly why they want to invest again. and if they don't, you should understand why long before fundraising starts.

7. they don't think enough about liquidity

this one is becoming increasingly important. a fund can have impressive paper returns, but LPs can't reinvest unrealized gains. TVPI matters, especially early on, but DPI tells a different story. at some point, investors want to see actual distributions. and when exits slow down, even funds with strong portfolios can struggle to return capital.

that doesn't mean every Fund I needs substantial DPI before raising Fund II. but managers should understand their portfolio's path to liquidity and be able to explain it clearly to LPs.

here are a few investors who recently raised their second funds and are worth following: @JedBreed, @jakobdiepen, @brettcalhounn, @yoheinakajima, @jamoses92, @kola_aina

Sharing an update on SVRN’s 20-F and the Nasdaq process.

We know the lack of answers over the past couple of weeks has been frustrating for SVRN investors. Given the ongoing matters before Nasdaq and the SEC, the Company must communicate developments through its public disclosures, as we have done today.

We did not file our 2025 Annual Report by the October 27 deadline, and Nasdaq issued the anticipated delisting determination. We intend to request a hearing on or before November 6, 2026, which will stay the suspension of trading for 15 days from the date of the request, and seek an extended stay pending completion of the hearings process. We expect our shares to continue trading on Nasdaq during the initial stay period and, if the Nasdaq Hearings Panel grants our request, through the extended stay period. However, there can be no assurance that the Panel will grant an extended stay or that the Company will ultimately maintain its Nasdaq listing.

On October 29, under the oversight of our Audit Committee, we submitted a pre-filing consultation to the SEC’s Office of the Chief Accountant regarding the classification of certain instruments, including our preferred stock and certain outstanding warrants. We intend to file our 2025 Annual Report as promptly as practicable following the conclusion of the consultation and within any period granted by the Nasdaq Hearings Panel. The timing and outcome of the SEC staff’s review are not within our control.

We also expect to miss the December 31 deadline for furnishing our interim financial information for the first half of 2026, as completion of that report depends on resolution of the same accounting matters.

The filing delays do not affect our operations, which continue across our validator and staking operations and our FastNEAR infrastructure business.

We will continue to update shareholders on material developments through the Company’s disclosures. Full release is below:

text:
I grew from 400 to 3,500+ followers on X. My sales from X were almost nothing.

Then I found the step nobody talks about.

3 prompts below, one per step. Paste them into Claude or your Grok Bot (easy to copy).

Followers don't pay. Buyers do.

What finally worked was a path in 3 steps. Followers → subscribers → buyers. One prompt per step.

Step 1: Get the followers

Most small accounts post "value" and wait. I did that for 9 months, stuck at 400.

What took me to 2,000 in 17 days: replying to fresh "let's connect" posts within minutes, with the person's name, one specific thing about them, "followed you" and a question.

The prompt:

"Here are 5 fresh posts from people I want to connect with, with a line from each person's bio: [paste]. For each one, write a reply: their name + one specific thing from their post or bio + 'followed you' + one real question. If a reply could be pasted under another post, rewrite it."

Write them yourself afterwards if you can. The prompt is the training wheels.

Step 2: Turn followers into email subscribers

A post lives about 48 hours. An email list is yours, and it keeps selling for years. One of my buyers was on my list for 7 years before she bought.

So give your followers one free thing worth an email, and put it in your bio and in the first reply under your best posts.

The prompt:

"I'm building [product] for [customer]. The questions people ask me most: [paste from DMs and replies]. Suggest 5 lead magnets that are useful in 10 minutes and lead to my paid product. Pick the best one, outline it, and write the signup page headline: [Result] in [time], without [the annoying part]."

Step 3: Turn subscribers into buyers

Don't sell in the first email. Give first: a welcome, a story, a check-in. Then one clear offer.

That's how 91% of my sales come in.

The prompt:

"Write my 5-email welcome sequence. I sell [product] for [price] to [customer]. They signed up for [lead magnet]. My story: [why I built it + one thing that went wrong].

Email 1 (right away): deliver [lead magnet], say who I am and why I care.
Email 2 (day 2): one question to learn what they need.
Email 3 (day 4): a confession, something that went wrong and what

text:
We entered Bunker Mode in early October at Nonce Capital. 

The recent security incidents across crypto and the broader tech industry over the last several months, led us to enter into "Bunker Mode" at Nonce Capital. Bunker mode is a more conservative, risk-off approach across all https://t.co/pimiDk5MVs Liquid vault positions we curate.

Prioritizing security kept us free from impact of the Binance hack yesterday. We started moving positions before the Binance hack and is a main reason why we were not impacted.

With Bunker Mode we are prioritizing:

- Reduced collateral exposure: Favoring isolated, single-collateral markets.
-Fewer layers: Minimizing smart contracts and protocols between vaults and underlying assets.
-Stronger asset protection: Favoring off-chain or allowlisted assets with controlled minting and redemption.
-Full transparency: Only holding positions with independently verifiable returns.

This policy applies across the entire Nonce Capital portfolio, including longstanding, well-performing positions. We believe this is the right tradeoff to protect capital and will resume more active strategies when the risk/reward becomes attractive again. 

Thank you for your continued trust in Nonce Capital

text:
What a week. 

So much appreciation and gratitude for the @ZcashFoundation and what they’ve built. This was my first #ZCon, and it’s been the best conference I’ve ever attended. Sure, it was 100% focused on #Zcash, which is naturally a reason for me to love it, but it was also intimate with strong small-group discussions. Great speakers, great conversations, great vibes.

But a lot of this week was overshadowed by subversive activity happening on X, with people saying deeply ugly things, revealing their overt and covert bigotry, and attacking and ganging up on individuals who are laser-focused on helping Zcash succeed, something everyone benefits from. Debating governance is one thing. Attacking and calling into question people’s hard work and their missions is something else. It’s embarrassing and reflects poorly on the Community that’s worked so hard to get Zcash to where it is. 

Candidly, I’m physically and emotionally exhausted. It’s hard watching good, decent people—friends, new and old—get attacked in a virtual “town square.” In a real town square, if someone’s harassing you and in your face, you can walk away, get assistance from public safety officials and others, or (I don’t endorse violence) physically fight them off. How do you do that on a social media platform where the people attacking you are cowards hiding behind screens and blocking someone is your only real option? How do you discuss things meaningfully when you’re limited to 280 characters in a response? How do you even know if the responses you’re receiving are from real people? 

It’s great that there’s consensus building around how to move forward with Zcash governance. Was it necessary to burn so many bridges and leave so many scars in the process?

If anything, Zcon showed me how strong and resilient this Community is, how beautifully diverse it is, and it exponentially strengthened my own sense of purpose and mission-driven advocacy. Many people’s lives and safety legitimately depend on Zcash succeeding. And that’s why we need to keep fighting. Just maybe not with each other.

Vamos.

text: how to do evals in 2026 101
author: chiefofautism
quoted_text:
No pressure, Ryan 😅

"Pipeline" can mean three different eval problems:

1) Multi-step LLM app: evaluate the end-to-end outcome and every nondeterministic step. Instrument arbitrary functions with W&B Weave Ops/Calls and run versioned evals over the same cases and scorers.

2) Agent: also evaluate trajectories, tool use, handoffs, and final state. Agent Lens for agent tracing, captures production sessions, clusters failures, turns them into test cases, lets humans calibrate custom judges, and compares candidate fixes.

3) Training/inference system: evaluate quality plus throughput, latency, reliability, and cost under realistic load. CoreWeave ARENA is built for that production-readiness test.

Across all three: start with real tasks, edge cases, and production failures; use code graders for objective checks, model judges for fuzzy behavior, and human review to calibrate them; run multiple trials; compare candidate vs incumbent; gate releases; and turn every new failure into a regression test.

That's the vendor-neutral answer. The concrete CoreWeave implementation is Forge: W&B Models for experiment tracking and versioned datasets; Notebooks for slicing results; Registry for lineage and rollback; Sandboxes for isolated eval execution; Serverless/Dedicated Inference for running candidates; Serverless SFT, Serverless RL, and Model Distillation (preview) when the model itself needs improvement; ARIA for analyzing deltas and proposing the next experiment; Skills/MCP + Automations to keep iteration moving.

Caveat: no platform can rescue weak eval design. Representative cases, explicit success criteria, and trustworthy graders still decide whether the score means anything.

text:
Lately I've been building a lot more with "infrastructure agents". When I joined AWS as a mobile dev, I was excited to learn how to build scalable cloud services. After a few years I was able to do a lot, but there was so much more to learn, and it becomes very complex and tedious.

Frontier models are great at designing and provisioning what I'd consider complex infrastructure and tying it together with frontends. I started by creating test accounts with limited spend/scoped creds on AWS, and prompting creative things that I thought were challenging to get right. Agents are good at creating these interconnected multi-service cloud stacks. I've used the CLI and MCP, even signed in to AWS on a cloud agent browser and let the agent provision through the UI via computer use. And it's simple to spin them down (which used to be a challenge on it's own!). Because of this, not much tech debt because it's easy to fix and migrate as things evolve.

Taking this beyond AWS of course this applies to other services like @convex, really anything.. You don't really need to even set up the API keys, just sign in to accounts via a cloud agent browser like @DevinAI, send a prompt, then close your computer. When the session is done everything is shipped, your environment variables are stored securly, you have a packaged up production ready app ready to go. 

And when you're ready to tear it all down it's also just a prompt away.

It's such a new way of thinking for me. Most of my career this was so out of reach (or too time consuming) so my mind today still lives with these assumptions, I keep having to remind myself that "no, it really is this simple" (many such cases).

Today I'm building three @EpicGames Unreal Engine games on an AWS fleet my agent provisioned, including Blender assets and GPU playtests 🤯. Devin created this diagram showing how it works:

today we are announcing openrouter for commerce: https://t.co/qLbYqziMtG

a single endpoint that integrates 5k stores, including Doordash, Amazon and most shopify stores, with payments using Agentcard (Stripe Link and Shop coming soon).

we built opencommerce to solve 3 problems:
* coverage: one endpoint to integrate 5k stores. agentic purchasing is a core feature for most personal assistants, but not their main business. searching for products and buying on behalf of users shouldn’t be as painful as it is today (e.g. it shouldn’t involve browser automations or dealing with PSPs). opencommerce solves that: 1 tool, every online store.

* reliability: 100% uptime. the challenge with browser automations is that they fail (e.g. captchas, bot-detection, etc). we run thousands of tests every couple of hours on every one of the stores to guarantee that the integration works when your user tries to buy something.

* speed: responses in under 10s. consumers are used to Amazon speed, and agentic purchases have so far felt like a downgrade. most agents spend minutes finding products before they come back with results. we monitor speed and improve it constantly.

text:
Capital doesn't create a market. Neither does demand. You can have willing buyers, willing sellers and an obvious economic reason to trade, yet no financial instrument that makes the transaction possible. This is one of the central problems we're working on at @formation_mkts 

Our latest SLAM paper, From Exposure to Claim: The Formation of Frontier Financial Markets and ISDA, examines why. 

A missing financial market isn't necessarily evidence of missing demand. Sometimes nobody has worked out a contractual arrangement the relevant institutions can actually use. 

Compute is a good example. @ComputeDesk and @OrnnExchange are developing price references for GPU capacity. In my earlier piece on @CoreWeave's financing, I discussed how a rental-price hedge could perform exactly as intended while leaving the borrower exposed to an early debt repayment.

This is where Coase becomes super salient. Working out what a usable financial claim should look like is expensive, and much of that expense comes before anyone knows whether the transaction can happen. 

The paper looks at this through ISDA's contractual architecture and three case studies, and explores how SI agents negotiating across institutions could change those economics. 

What interests us is the possibility of making new financial claims much easier to create, so that financial institutions can originate and trade risks that aren't economically practical to structure today.

- Equity buffer increased to c. $8bn, but mainly thanks to M2M, esp. BTC going up after the market bottomed in Q2. Additionally, $1.5bn moved back to the parent, offsetting last quarter's movement and confirming the fungibility of capital within the group. Quite important given group equity is likely closer to $30bn: beyond letting USDT benefit from that balance sheet, it also gives Tether the ability to act as crypto's lender of last resort, if that were ever required (in events like yesterday's)

- First time gold reserves dropped: -3.4t. Tether could have either sold gold or dividended out to the parent but worth noting. More BTC got bought, +1.1k, but accumulating more corn quite slowly. Both combined imply they stopped adding to the risk bucket this quarter. That being said, not much movement towards GENIUS on the reserve side, e.g. secured loans up a bit as demand for leverage came back in Q3 (probably reduced since due to Uptover). So no change in strategy here

- Funny enough, opening equity was restated +$0.5bn to match the KPMG audit. This means BDO attested quite conservative numbers & KPMG's audit resulted in a restatement translating into bigger historical profits

- Burried normally in the footnotes but mentions of the redemption fee disappeared. In Q2, it implied it was closer to 9bps on average (vs 10bps stated fee), which meant specific counterparties may have gotten a better schedule. Obviously doesn't prove anything, but more flexibility there would improve USDT integration in existing institutional financial rails, facilitate DeFi growth and reduce the USDT/USDC discount during bear markets. I may be extrapolating a bit but thought it was a noteworthy ommission

又是一篇很棒的文章，《You're probably overprompting Claude》Addy 太高产了，我觉得对于现在最强大的模型来说，已经不需要要那么多提示词了，太多提示词完全是限制大模型的发挥。

所以作者说不要 overprompting，给定一个清晰的目标，给定一个明确的验证条件（我喜欢用 E2E 通过和录屏通过），不确定需求的时候，可以 grill-me 一下，把需求界定清楚即可。

系统的提示可以大幅精简，大多数都没啥用了，文中说，Opus 5 / Fable 5 去掉了超过 80% 的系统提示，评测几乎没下降。

所以说之前大部分的 skills 都完全可以删除了，过度约束就是让新的模型戴着镣铐跳舞，完全没必要，可以放手看看它的创造力怎么样。

I'm really wondering why I see so many people complain about the Gemini 4 Argon quota. Testing it, obviously, it seems that, in a Pro account, the discrepancy in quota between Pro and the two Ultra account subscriptions seems to be huge.

I'm a long-lasting Gemini user. I was, until a few months ago, on the $200 plan because I was using Opus 4.6 back then until the quota was extremely limited, and Gemini 2.5 was not a very good model for coding. 

That's why I reduced my plan, but I'm using many other Google applications that are in the Gemini bundle, so I stayed with them on the Ultra subscription for $99. The Ultra plan is a pretty nice package, specifically if you like to have a bit more cloud storage, but also YouTube Pro and things like that.

Now, after testing Argon for3 days, I worked intensively with it. It's the third day in full, with several sessions, and my weekly quota was down to 16%. Now, a few hours ago, I upgraded to the $200 subscription, and looking at how slowly the weekly quota and the 5-hour quota are draining, I would say this is definitely more quota on the $200 plan than you would get for an Anthropic Max plan.

I'm absolutely positive that this is a much better deal because it's also a much more reliable model, specifically when you have projects where you don't want to break something while you implement something new (like it will happen with the other so-called frontier models). 

I didn't have time until now to go into creative discussions with it to see how strong it is as a thinking partner, but as a coding agent and senior software engineer, it's really stunning.

text:
I joined Kalshi a little over four years ago.

The exchange was live. There were almost no users. No one cared about us.

But I believed deeply in the vision: give anyone the ability to express a view, hedge a risk, or use markets to understand what’s likely to happen. On anything.

I couldn’t believe it didn’t already exist. I knew it had to.

There were about 20 people. Tarek and Luana were extremely smart, with huge ambitions. Meeting the rest of the team convinced me this was where I wanted to be.

Before I accepted, Tarek asked me to go for a walk on a Saturday. He pulled out a list and rattled off all the grueling things I’d be signing up for.

I told him I was ready. We agreed on a number on the spot, shook hands, and started the journey of a lifetime.

Since then, I’ve touched about every part of the company. These days, I focus on growth. It’s a lot more fun when the line goes up. For a long time, ours went sideways.

Market-maker partnerships fell through. We went through painful layoffs. Election markets were blocked, and we fought in court to get them live.

Believing something should exist and bringing it to life are very different things.

Even when we could barely get anyone to trade, Tarek and Luana were talking about building one of the most important financial exchanges in the world.

We just announced another $1B in funding at a $40B valuation.

$40B is a nice number on a piece of paper. What means more to me is the millions of people using prediction markets. The infrastructure we’ve built. The team we’ve assembled. How much closer we are to the vision that made me want to join.

I’m grateful to Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara for bringing me in, to everyone I’ve built alongside, and to the users who’ve made this possible.

Four years later, I believe in this more than ever. There’s still so much left to build.
author: salmanso_
quoted_text:
Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

‼️ A COUP IS HAPPENING IN POLAND 🇵🇱

Poland's Constitutional Tribunal is being subjected to an extraordinary takeover operation by pro-EU Prime Minister Donald Tusk. 

Its official website has been taken over, an announcement has appeared removing its president and vice-president from their duties, and police have been deployed around the institution.

The Tribunal's existing leadership has declared the operation illegal and accused those responsible of committing a coup d'état.

The Constitutional Tribunal is the institution responsible for reviewing whether laws comply with the Constitution. It is broadly comparable to the constitutional-review function of the United States Supreme Court.

Today, its website announced that President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański had been suspended for one month. 

The person now claiming authority over Poland's Constitutional Tribunal is Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, elected to the Tribunal by Donald Tusk's parliamentary majority in March 2026.

But there is a fundamental legal problem: she has never taken her judicial oath before the President of Poland, Karol Nawrocki.

Under Article 4 of the Act on the Status of Constitutional Tribunal Judges, newly elected judges must take their oath before the President of the Republic.

Nawrocki refused to receive her oath. Instead, on April 9, Korwin-Piotrowska participated in an alternative swearing-in ceremony organised inside the Polish Parliament, without the President's presence or participation.

The Presidential Chancellery explicitly declared that this procedure had no legal basis and could not confer judicial authority. The existing leadership of the Constitutional Tribunal maintains that she is therefore not legally a judge of the institution.

And now, a woman whose authority to serve as a constitutional judge is rejected by the President and the Tribunal's existing leadership is being presented as the person entitled to take control of the entire court.

Poland's Constitution does not give the prime minister or his government the power to dismiss the Constitutional Tribunal's leadership.

Article 194 establishes the Tribunal's composition and the procedure for appointing its president. Article 195 guarantees the independence of its judges. 

The announcement of a suspension relies on Article 130 of the law governing ORDINARY COURTS. Invoking this article to suspend the leadership of the Constitutional Tribunal is a legally indefensible distortion of the law, revealing a staggering disregard for elementary constitutional principles.

HOW DID POLAND GET HERE?

Donald Tusk returned to power in December 2023, promising to reverse the judicial reforms introduced under the conservative Law and Justice government.

Those reforms had been fiercely opposed by the European Commission, which initiated rule-of-law proceedings against Poland and linked access to European funding to judicial conditions.

Tusk's government subsequently presented Brussels with a programme for restructuring the judiciary, including the Constitutional Tribunal. The European Commission welcomed that programme and ended its Article 7 proceedings against Poland in 2024.

The methods used by the EU and its supporters undermine the very constitutional principles they claim to restore.

President Karol Nawrocki has reportedly interrupted his journey to Senegal to return to Poland.

《美光崛起》

1980年,爱达荷州博伊西。
一个70多岁的老人走进了一家牙科诊所的地下室。
里面坐着四个年轻人。
没有办公室,没有工厂,没有产品。
老人种了一辈子土豆,是麦当劳最大的冷冻薯条供应商。
他看了看,掏出100万美元,拿走了40%的股权。
没有尽调,没有投委会。
46年后,这家公司市值一度突破万亿美元。
美光。

先说这地方有多不像硅谷。
爱达荷州,全州人口200万,美国最没存在感的州之一。
最有名的东西是:土豆、土豆,和土豆。
1978年,美光在博伊西一家牙科诊所的地下室成立。
没有制造业务,全部收入来自一项:给一家叫Mostek的公司做设计咨询。
他们没拿VC的钱,拿的是几个本地乡绅的钱。
一年后,当头一棒。
1979年,Mostek被收购。合同没了。
唯一的客户,没了。

一家刚失去唯一客户的四人公司,怎么办?
他们的答案是:那我们自己造芯片。
于是有了那位土豆大亨。
为什么他要投一家地下室里的四人存储公司?
也许只是因为——薯条和芯片,英文都叫chips。

100万当然不够建厂。
但它是一张信用通行证。
有了背书,他们从当地银行拿到贷款,又从其他爱达荷商人那里筹到钱。
然后用一种极度"土"的办法省钱:
当时一座DRAM工厂要花上亿美元。
他们拿了一家超市的建筑方案来改厂房。
把肉类冷藏空间,扩建成洁净室。
设备全买别人淘汰的二手货。
1981年建成,总成本约700万美元。
别人花一亿,他们花700万。
在一个肉类冷藏室改的洁净室里,开始生产64K DRAM。
同一年,IBM PC进入市场。
个人电脑爆发,DRAM需求飙升。
三年后,1984年,美光上市。
从地下室到纳斯达克,六年。

然后是残酷的部分。
今天我们觉得存储是韩国人的天下。
但早期的存储,是美国公司的天下。
英特尔的第一款量产产品就是存储芯片。
IBM、德州仪器、AMD、摩托罗拉,全都做过。
然后,游戏规则变了。
国家意志进场了。
定向扶持,极高强度的资本支出,行业下行也要逆势投资。
目的只有一个:熬死对手。
打法大差不差——
我挣不挣钱无所谓,我要的是你不能活。
在这样的碾压下,美国几乎所有半导体公司都退出了存储。
只剩美光一棵独苗。

为什么只有它活下来?
它没有国家控制的银行输血。
美国资本市场也不允许一家公司长期一边亏损一边砸钱。
答案是:美光身上同时长出了"美国性"和"东亚性"。

先说美国性。
第一层:它会玩资本。
1998年,周期底部,德州仪器急着甩掉亏损的存储业务。
美光接了,表面价值8亿多美元。
但它一毛钱现金没出——付的是定增股票和公司债券。
更离谱的是:德仪不仅没拿到现金,还反向给美光提供了7.5亿美元融资,用来改造工厂。
不花一分现金,拿下德仪全部存储业务。
第二层,更狠:它会玩法律。
1985年日本厂商把美国同行逼入绝境,美光提起反倾销申诉,促成了《美日半导体协议》。
90年代韩国崛起,它再次发起反倾销调查。
2002年收购海力士失败,它转头推动针对韩国补贴的调查。
但最经典的是这一次:
2002年,美国司法部调查多家DRAM厂商串通涨价。
美光率先举报,申请宽大处理,成为首家主动配合的涉案企业。
最终三星、海力士、英飞凌、尔必达,全部被处以巨额罚款。
而美光作为"吹哨人"——
既没被起诉,也没交一分罚款。

为什么只有美光这么拼?
因为英特尔、德仪、IBM都有利润更高的主业。
存储只是分支,下行期剥离掉就行。
但美光没有退路。
它只有存储。

再说东亚性。
2008年金融危机,德国奇梦达崩了。
美光约4亿美元收购其持有的华亚科技35%股权。
但这4亿里,华亚借给它8500万,南亚母公司借给它2亿。
实际自掏现金约1.13亿。
2012年,日本存储国家队尔必达破产。
美光用2000亿日元拿下100%股权。
但交易时只先付600亿现金,剩下的分6年、用尔必达自己的代工现金流以日元偿付。
然后日元在还款期间大幅贬值。
美光实付的美元成本,远低于最初协议。
它还顺手收了尔必达与力晶合资的瑞晶电子。
一夜之间,拿到广岛、秋田和台中的产能。
总产能跃居全球第二,仅次于三星。

于是今天出现了一个有意思的局面。
美光在政治上是地道的美国公司。
但制造上高度"东亚化"。
美国本土只剩弗吉尼亚一座传统工厂。
先进DRAM和HBM产能在台湾、日本、新加坡。
它用美国的资本市场和法律体系作战。
用东亚的工程师红利和制造生态生产。

然后AI来了。
这一轮出现了一个戏剧性的反转。
SK海力士极早重仓HBM,占了全球约六成市场。
代价是:它把大量DRAM产能倾斜给了HBM。
结果通用DRAM全行业短缺,合约价暴涨90%以上。
而HBM多是提前锁价的长协,短期利润弹性反被压制。
美光在HBM上本来是落后的。
但更均衡的传统DRAM敞口,让它吃尽了通用内存涨价的红利。
落后的那一手,意外成了护城河。
长期看,HBM仍是胜负手。
美光早年押注HMC失误,前两代落后。
2017年转向后,它直接跳过HBM3,全部资源压在HBM3E上,切进了英伟达H200供应链。
2026年提前量产12层堆叠的HBM4,通过英伟达下一代平台认证。
重新站回同代起跑线。

今天,美光已经是美国必须保住的战略资产。
《芯片法案》给了巨额补贴。
它宣布到2035年在美国本土投资超过2500亿美元。

The Ordo Iuris Institute for Legal Culture expresses its gravest concern at, and firm opposition to, the forcible takeover of the seat of the Constitutional Tribunal.

On 30 October 2026, police officers took control of the empty building of the Tribunal and have since been denying the Tribunal’s security staff, the Vice-President of the Tribunal and its Director entry to the premises.

We recall that under Article 128 § 1 of the Polish Penal Code (Kodeks karny), anyone who, with the intent of removing a constitutional organ of the Republic of Poland by force, engages in activity directly aimed at achieving that objective is liable to a penalty of up to 20 years’ imprisonment.

The Ordo Iuris Institute demands:
1. The immediate withdrawal of police officers from the seat of the Constitutional Tribunal and the restoration of full access to the building for the Tribunal’s organs and staff;
2. The disclosure of the legal basis for the actions taken and of the identity of those who ordered them, together with the political accountability of the members of the Council of Ministers concerned;
3. The immediate initiation of proceedings by the public prosecutor’s office in respect of the attack on a constitutional organ of the State (Article 128 of the Penal Code) and the abuse of powers by public officials (Article 231 of the Penal Code).

We call upon all fellow Poles, at the moment of the gravest constitutional crisis in the history of the Third Republic of Poland, to stand in defence of the constitutional order and to repel the coup d’état. In this hour of trial, the eyes of citizens are turned towards the President of the Republic of Poland, who, upon receiving news from the capital, turned back his flight to Senegal and is now returning to his Homeland. It is in his hands that the Constitution places the task of guaranteeing the continuity of State authority (Article 126(1) of the Constitution) and of ensuring observance of the Constitution (Article 126(2) of the Constitution).

With no great hope, the Institute calls upon the Venice Commission, the institutions of the European Union, the Council of Europe and the OSCE/ODIHR to respond urgently to the forcible assault on the constitutional court of a Member State. text:
小路读了 Marc Andreessen 昨天发的这篇短文，推荐给您。全文只讲一个词：混乱。

主线可以压成一条链：
混乱入场->有人认领->建栖息地->自动驾驶的公司（chaos->claim->habitat->self-driving company）

起因是 Replit 推出了 Replit for Business。CEO Amjad Masad 说，现在大多数 agent 活在混乱的地方：聊天窗口、个人账号、一次性脚本里，手里拿着别人随手给的权限和数据。没人决定它们能碰什么，也没人看得见它们做了什么。

Andreessen 由此给了一个判断：一项技术会不会真的改变世界，有个信号，就是它进公司的方式乱不乱。接着他引了 Andy Grove 的问题：谁来让混乱发生，然后再把混乱收拢？

他举了三个历史例子。

电脑。PC 当年是员工自己带进办公室的。有人在采购单上撒谎，说买的是示波器、打字机，甚至一张桌子。1983年华盛顿邮报的一篇文章就担心，公司里会冒出管理层看不见的"影子数据处理部门"。

电子表格。外行也能自己建模、做预测，有的表格很值钱，有的就是"幻觉"：没文档，难审计，公式出错，只有做表的人看得懂。Mitch Kapor 1984年说过，您看到最终结果，却不知道规则是什么。后来的解法是数据权限、锁单元格、版本历史和审计。

邮件。以前公司有收发室，信息怎么流动由它控制。邮件让任何人都能联系任何人，有一阵子，发邮件要经理批准听起来也合理。后来才有了带权限的公司通信。

作者的结论有两条。一，总得有人把混乱收拢一点，建一个让这种行为长得最好的栖息地。二，混乱本身是信号，说明员工认领了某个对自己和公司都有价值的东西。他的用词是 free-range：不关笼子，也不完全放养。

到了 agent 这一步，他认为代码是最强的"对齐产物"，因为代码就是公司的业务逻辑。他提到 Replit 的一个例子：Sumitomo Mitsui Finance and Leasing 的一名员工，把原本六个人六个月的开发流程，一个人一周做完。他自己写的是"I believe"，所以细节小路没法核实。他还预言，以后可以用 agent 栖息地的丰富程度，来衡量一家公司的对齐程度。

简单总结一下就是：新技术先乱着进来，是因为有人认领了它。公司要做的是建栖息地，而不是掐灭它。agent 和前几次不同的地方，是它会自己动手，栖息地能不能建好，还要看验证做不做得成。

quoted_text:
It looks like Figure AI founder Brett Adcock was onto something last year when he predicted that Agility Robotics would be out of business within 12 months.   

Though Oregon-based Agility hasn't gone under, its 2026 SEC filing shows that its management believed the robotics firm did not have enough cash to fund operations for the following year without raising more.   

The filing is unusually serious for a company preparing to go public. Agility reported never having a positive cash flow and said that losses could become greater as it expands operations. Agility reported losing $138.1 million in 2025 and warned that losses could become greater. 

"Without consideration of the proposed business combination transaction, Agility has concluded there is substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern, which could materially adversely affect the Post-Closing Company’s business, financial condition, and the value of your investment," the filing says.   

Agility's auditor cited the company's ability to continue as a going-concern based on financial statements for 2024 and 2025. The startup later raised another $100 million in July 2026 by selling SAFEs, which are agreements that give investors the right to receive company shares in the future.    

Agility, spun out of Oregon State University in 2015, is pursuing an SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI that would take the company public and give it access to additional capital. The planned deal values Agility at around $2.5 billion and includes a separate $201 million PIPE investment.   

If it closes, the SPAC could extend Agility's runway considerably, but the startup is still burning cash. Describing itself as an early-state company, Agility burned $99.8 million in operating cash in 2025, up from $70.7 million the prior year, and it has since added more overhead by expanding into Silicon Valley. The company opened a new facility in Fremont in July 2026 to serve as a software and AI development hub.   

According to the filing, Agility's Digit v4 humanoid robots are deployed or committed for deployment across nine customer facilities. Named customers include Amazon, GXO Logistics, Schaeffler, Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada, and Mercado Libre. Most of the work they're doing is simple material-handling jobs like moving bins and totes.   

Agility says it's also secured $300 million in multi-year orders for 1,000 Digit v5 robots under 3-year Robots-as-a-Service (RaaS) agreements. However, those orders hinge on Agility meeting certain product and contract milestones.   

Though the deals offer a reason for optimism, Agility says the RaaS model still has not proven it can make money at scale. The economics depend on still-unproven assumptions about Digit's useful life, repair costs, customer renewals, and servicing expenses. Since Agility owns the hardware, it spends the money from the RaaS deals to build them upfront and receives money gradually afterward.   

Agility names Boston Dynamics, Tesla, Figure AI, Apptronik, 1X Technologies, Sanctuary AI, Hexagon, and NEURA Robotics as its main competitors in the filing. The company says many of them have more resources for technical development, mass manufacturing, and marketing as well as stronger brand recognition and more existing customer relationships.

text:
David Lieb, socio de Y Combinator y cofundador de Google Photos, dice que es la demo más loca que ha visto. Lo entiendo.

Subvocal es una startup de San Francisco de tres personas, de la tanda de otoño de 2026 de Y Combinator. Acaba de levantar 1,3 millones de dólares con YC y Afore Capital. Hacen unas gafas que leen los movimientos casi invisibles de los músculos con los que hablas por dentro. Mueves la boca sin emitir sonido y el texto aparece a más de 200 palabras por minuto. Sin cámaras y sin leer los labios.

La idea tiene historia. En 2018 Arnav Kapur, investigador del MIT Media Lab, presentó AlterEgo, unos electrodos pegados a la mandíbula que reconocían palabras dichas en silencio con un 92% de acierto. Funcionaba con vocabularios limitados, como números y comandos. Lo que ha cambiado es la IA, que ya sabe convertir señales del cuerpo en frases abiertas. Según Lieb, Subvocal lo ha construido en cuatro meses.

Primero fue el teclado, luego la pantalla táctil, luego la voz. La voz tiene un problema que todos conocemos: nadie quiere dictarle un correo al móvil en un tren lleno o en una oficina. Si hablar en silencio funciona, la conversación con la IA puede ser continua y privada.

Me quedan dos preguntas. ¿Funcionará en cualquier persona? La propia empresa dice que hará falta una calibración corta. ¿Y quién guarda esas señales? Son palabras que decidiste no decir en voz alta.

La reserva cuesta 199 dólares y los primeros envíos están previstos para el primer trimestre de 2027.

Pronto lo raro será teclear.

text:
Every time you make your library more flexible, somebody has to pay for it. Not always you.

If you hide a dependency behind an interface, your code becomes simpler, but now all clients must implement this interface.

If you add hooks so clients can plug in their own code, you're running code you don't control. It can throw or block your thread for a second. You can wrap it in a try-catch, move it to a thread pool, and still wait for the slowest one.

The complexity doesn't disappear. The only thing to decide is where it goes.

Free this week on @EngPolymathic

quoted_text:
DoubleZero Edge for Builders is now on testnet.

Edge for Builders is a permissionless way for third parties to publish their own real-time data feeds on DoubleZero Edge, reach their subscribers, and charge their own customers. It gives them the send-once delivery model traditional exchanges use for market data, on the DoubleZero network, without operating distribution infrastructure of their own.

How it works:
The publisher sends each update once, and DoubleZero's dedicated network links deliver it to every subscriber. Served over WebSockets and cloud APIs, every new subscriber is another copy for the publisher to send. Builders create their own feeds and publishers through the builder API, and sign every action with their own key.

Existing Edge subscribers can add builder feeds on the connection they already have.

Edge for Builders was announced at TOKEN2049. This is the earliest access, open now to ambitious teams distributing real-time data to many subscribers: exchanges and venues, data aggregators, pricing providers, and any project serving real-time data over WebSockets or cloud APIs.

Docs: https://t.co/RLgd0aEeiv

今年做的 trading stack 基本上是一个 3-5 年内业内竞争都难以饱和的业务，因为充满了脏活累活，以及纯粹的腿脚业务，低效定价遍地。但也正是脏活累活的密度，使得有一些固定的时间壁垒没有办法被一个聪明人 + agent 组合轻易逾越（这个事在当代比较关键）。

从业务复利角度当然是我比较喜欢的，因为把握了一些确定性赢面，在旅途中是比较舒心的。但其实更大的还是在于实践复利，还是在 agent workflow 的熟练定义上面。

这是这个时代真正的金铲子，以及真正的经营平权，代表了你控制和组织顶尖算力智力（同时最大程度压缩成本）的经营和管理水平——而不需要透过一个粗糙的金融信贷体系和草台人力班子白手起家 or 乘风破浪。

老实说为了掌握这一点，经营什么也并不是最重要的，只是说你必须通过一个正向的业务不断去佐证经验。

为了认知正确，保持不脱产、不和市场脱节是很重要的。

工程出身的人喜欢 general & consistent model，喜欢可以到处铺开和无限复用的东西，如今把自己和业务 24/7 扔进新兴的算力组织架构里，就是这么个东西。

太多的 alpha 可以捡取，太多的实践范式可以复利终身。

author: claudhadd
quoted_text:
Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

lnd v0.20.7 and v0.21.6 have been released, which contain a Go-specific mitigation (MPTCP flag off) for CVE-2026-98432 (use-after-free in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP).

https://t.co/teYiy9R44U
https://t.co/ygHT5u4d3H

We recommend that all users update to this new version.

Existing binaries can be protected by running them with the GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 env variable: https://t.co/ptTwUv5U6j.

Note that as this is a Linux kernel level vulnerability, the only way to fully mitigate the vuln is to patch your kernel, as any network facing service may be affected (known PoCs use MPTCP, but other exploit vectors may be possible).

quoted_text:
🚨 0.77€ de taxe pour regarder un film Netflix ! 

Ce vendredi, les députés viennent d'adopter un amendement socialiste visant à taxer les données qui circulent sur Internet à hauteur de 5,5 centimes par gigaoctet reçu en France.

Ils ont complètement pété les plombs. 

Voici quelques exemples de ce que ça va désormais vous coûter :
🔴 Vous regardez un film Netflix de 2 heures en 4K ? Jusqu'à 0,77 € de taxe brute sur les données transmises.
🔴 Vous téléchargez un jeu vidéo de 150 Go ? 8,25 €.
🔴 Vous récupérez 200 Go de photos personnelles stockées chez Google ? 11 €.
🔴 Vous rapatriez 1 To de vos propres fichiers depuis Google Drive ? 55 €.
🔴 Vous restaurez 2 To de sauvegardes après une panne informatique ? 110 €.

Ces taxes seront facturées aux plateformes américaines, qui vous vous en doutez bien, vous redescendront la facture ! 

Ils sont en train de construire une fiscalité qui pénalise le simple fait de transmettre de la donnée. 

Et ceci alors que nous sommes à l'aube d'une révolution technologique majeure avec l'IA ! 

Pour rester compétitifs, tous les pays doivent accélérer leur transformation numérique.

Et nous en France, que trouve-t-on comme idée de génie ?

UNE PUTAIN DE TAXE SUR LA DATA ! 

Et en plus ils ont le culot de nous la présenter comme une mesure écologique qui encouragerait à réduire les volumes de données échangées.

Quelle bande de guignols. 

Il faut être totalement déconnecté des réalités économiques pour considérer qu'un pays peut retrouver sa prospérité en multipliant indéfiniment les prélèvements sur les activités productives.

Cet amendement n'est pas encore une loi définitive, mais le simple fait qu'une telle proposition ait été adoptée à l'Assemblée nationale en dit long sur la manière dont nous sommes gouvernés.

Ces fous du bus vont vraiment nous mettre au fond du ravin.

Guillermo Rauch (@rauchg), Founder & CEO @Vercel

在整个加密商业史里，OKX 拿到的原本是一张胜算最低的“地狱级开局牌”。

当年友商靠着巧舌如簧的全球公关、挥金如土的超级碗广告、甚至买下 NBA 球馆冠名权把声量推向神坛的时候，他们却深陷提币风波的至暗时刻，被全网唱衰、判定死刑。

但如果你复盘过去这五年，谁完成了整个行业最不可思议的战略大逆转，答案只能是 OKX。

商业世界最残酷但也最公平的底层法则是：
风口上的喧嚣和造神运动，终究敌不过地心引力的算力清算；
而那些在所有人都在浮躁捞金时，反常识死磕硬核产品力的人，时间终究会把整座江山还给他们。

他们干成了三件几乎逆着全行业共识走的“重体力活”：
第一，当大家都在抢着造假数据、发空气币拉盘时，他们把几百名顶级工程师关在小黑屋里，死磕业内第一套“统一交易账户（Portfolio Margin）”。

把跨币种保证金、现货衍生品对冲的底层数学模型全部打通，硬生生把一家交易所的底层风控，做成了连极端黑天鹅行情都击不穿的金融级装甲车。

第二，当所有 CEX（中心化平台）都在拼命筑高围墙、想把用户的私钥和资产死死锁在自己服务器里时，他们却带头砸重金去革自己的命：
做自托管的 OKX Web3 钱包。

不仅开源、不仅把资产控制权双手奉还给用户，甚至把几百条公链的复杂操作、铭文索引、DEX 聚合，打磨成了全行业体验最丝滑的“链上瑞士军刀”。

别人以为他们在自掘坟墓，结果他们直接靠产品力把 Web3 钱包做成了全网十数倍于传统交易所的超级流量总闸门。

第三，在 FTX 轰然崩塌、全行业遭遇信任雪崩的那一年，他们没有找公关发通稿，而是第一个把 100%+ 默克尔树储备证明（PoR）常态化。

每月按时向全世界公开所有链上资产储备，哪怕被显微镜逐行审查也不退缩，硬生生用最笨拙但也最硬核的代码透明度，把破碎的行业信任一寸一寸拼接了回来。

很多人做商业喜欢走捷径，迷信资本运作和流量奇迹。
但 OKX 用十年逆袭证明了一件极度朴素的事：
在充满投机和欺骗的沼泽里，最锋利的武器从来不是舌灿莲花的叙事，
而是顶住所有冷眼与周期阵痛，把一行行代码、一套套风控、一张张底牌，彻底焊进用户心智里的纯粹硬实力。

Here’s my 40,000-foot view of the coup in Poland and how it connects to the Russia-Ukraine war and our midterms.

Poland is the main land bridge. It shares a long border with Ukraine and Belarus and has been the primary corridor for Western weapons, ammunition, fuel, and aid since 2022. It hosts refugees, NATO troops, and forward bases. Whoever controls the Polish government controls how easily that pipeline stays open or gets restricted.

The previous PiS governments were strongly pro-Ukraine and anti-Russia but clashed with the EU over sovereignty and the courts. Tusk’s government is locked into the Brussels position and is more likely to keep maximum pressure on Russia and less likely to support any deal that involves territorial compromise, reduced arms flows, or energy arrangements with Moscow.

President Trump wants to end the war. Any negotiation will involve territory, security guarantees, sanctions, and energy. European governments that want the war to continue until Russia is permanently weakened have leverage if they control the main supply route and the political narrative in a key frontline state. Keeping Poland inside a hard-line EU consensus makes it harder for Washington to cut a deal that parts of Europe will immediately reject or try to sabotage.

Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal just called what is happening a coup. Police on the court. The president turning his plane around mid-flight. The same forces that spent years using institutions against President Trump are moving openly in Europe, and the timing is not a coincidence.

We are days from our midterms. What happens in Congress determines whether the next two years are justice and momentum or nonstop investigations and blocks. You voted for President Trump for four years, not two. 

A hostile House weakens his hand abroad while he is trying to end the war.

Yesterday the head of the European Central Bank appeared on video with bandages on her face to announce she is stepping down. She later said it was minor skin-cancer surgery. The optics still landed in a week when Europe’s institutions are under visible strain and the war is still open.

President Trump is trying to end the war. The people seizing courts in Europe are working to make that harder. Capture the courts. Use the police. Call it rule of law. Marginalize anyone who resists. Then use the result to shape the larger map.

Vote MAGA. The people in the foxhole next to you are not the enemy.

BREAKING: France just voted to tax the internet.

French lawmakers approved a tax of €0.055 (5.5 cents) for every gigabyte of data that companies like Netflix and YouTube send to French users. It’s a tax on the companies, not users directly, but the cost could get passed on to subscribers.

quoted_text:
Very few podcasts will actually make you smarter AND make you laugh.

No politics, no egos, just tech.

The biggest news this week:

- Anthropic Files S1 Ahead of $2TRN IPO
- Instinct's Rumoured $30BN Fundraise
- Microsoft Lays off 27,000 While Meta Taps Equity Markets for $95BN Capex Spending Spree

My notes with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. Analysis of Anthropic S1

Anthropic's S1 beat expectations on margins and operating income, even after stock-based compensation, leaving the burden of proof on the naysayers. It also looked strong on customer concentration, compute efficiency and cash. Some questions remain, including the undisclosed Q3 revenue number.

2. Is the Value Extraction Requirement From the Latest Models a Benefit or a Curse of Anthropic?

Eighty percent of Anthropic's revenue comes from models less than six months old, and 70 to 80% of compute costs go to training. Models are expensive to build and highly profitable to serve, but only for six to twelve months. Few companies can write a $10 to 12BN compute check, so this short shelf life can favour Anthropic if it stays aggressive.

3. Brutal Reality Is Microsoft Have Just Admitted They Don't Want 27% of Their Workforce

Whatever gets said on LinkedIn, Microsoft's move says it does not want 27% of its people. That is a worse scarlet letter than a pure layoff, because the company has told these employees they do not meet its minimum bar.

4. Chinese Open-Source Models Have Peaked and Will Decline From Here

Chinese open-weight models are close to finished in the US, and this is the beginning of the end for them. Despite DeepSeek's latest raise, it is starting to be banned across all federal agencies.

5. Why No CIO Will Take a Chance on a Chinese Model

Even if confidential data reaches Alibaba servers in Asia only one time in 100,000, without consent, no CIO or CISO will approve the model. If it keeps happening and Alibaba stays silent, anyone using these models will lose their job.

6. Why OpenAI Is an Underappreciated Asset to Invest in Today

OpenAI is mispriced at the $1.25 TN round. Brief market panic has created a dislocation like Anthropic's round at around $183BN, even though OpenAI has closed all its competitive gaps.

7. What Is the Upside of OpenAI at $1.25 Trillion?

OpenAI and Anthropic are both expected to become $10 to 20TN companies. Anthropic takes only 0.1% of Fortune 500 budgets today, and even conservative estimates put that at 2 to 3%. Because OpenAI is not priced to perfection, the worst case is doubling the money.

LINK:NYC was one of the most institutional rooms I've ever been in. Almost every conversation came back to moving trillions onchain.

For years the line was that the institutions are coming. After this week I'd put it more simply, they're here, and they're building.

What struck me most is how quiet the end state sounds.

Someone buying Apple on Schwab may never know it's tokenized, and honestly, they may not care. Securities that sit idle in brokerage accounts start earning for the people who own them.

Collateral moves just in time instead of just in case. Markets stop closing.

Capital wants to be free and liquid, and the plumbing is finally being built to let it.

I've also come around to the idea that the word crypto may fade. Its exports won't.

Stablecoins, smart contracts and tokenized assets carry far less baggage, and they're quietly becoming part of finance itself.

There will be more tokenized assets tomorrow than there were today, and that trend isn't reversing.

If this is what winning looks like, it won't feel like a revolution. It'll just feel like finance working better.

text:
This line was buried in @AnthropicAI 's October 27 announcement:
“We’ve also begun drug discovery efforts of our own.”

My working hypothesis: Frontier AI labs are becoming the next gen of biotech platforms, not merely AI vendors to the pharma industry.

@AnthropicAI appears to be the most aggressive lab in AIDD today. Two biotech acquisitions, an in-house wet lab, infrastructure for AI-controlled experiments, and the recruitment of Nobel Prize-winning talent.

Why build internal drug pipelines?

Train better models. Owning research programs creates a closed loop between model reasoning, hypothesis generation, wet-lab validation, and model improvement.

Owning discovery doesn’t mean owning the entire drug development process. Anthropic could advance candidates through preclinical, then partner with, license to, or sell programs to pharma co. There is already a mature market for early-stage drug assets.

Biotech platform in the making. Biotech has historically been a hit-or-miss business. If AIDD is real (still a very big if), then model co. are becoming true biotech platforms - a repeatable discovery engine - the value creation could be enormous.

---
Implications for Biotech and Big Pharma

Pretending I have a crystal ball for a moment (and again, IF AIDD actually works):

>> Biotech: Potentially the biggest disruption

I expect significantly more biotech to collaborate with frontier AI labs. Labs get data and domain expertise, and offers attractive partnerships, at least initially. Each direction within drug discovery gets more competitive, bc AI now makes it easier. The 1.7T biotech industry is potentially at risk.

>> Big Pharma: Better positioned than many might think; frontier lab’s biggest competitors

Big Pharma has a data advantage, but a model disadvantage, at least for now. Its ability to compete on the model side depend partly on how quickly open-source models catch up.

The relative value of routine scientific work may decline, but proprietary data, experimental infrastructure, scientific judgment, and clinical development capabilities could become even more important.

I actually think some pharmaceutical companies are very well positioned:

$LLY: My leading candidate to build a pharmaceutical-owned AI discovery platform that could eventually serve the broader biotech ecosystem. @EliLillyandCo  TuneLab is (still) way underappreciated. 
A powerful data flywheel: Lilly’s historical data + proprietary models → biotech adoption → real experiments → new training data through federated learning → better models → more biotech adoption. @DaveARicks 

@Roche  / Genentech: Potentially the strongest competitor in the combination of foundation models, biological data, and automated wet-lab infrastructure.

$REGN: Particularly well positioned around scarce human disease biology, genetics, and target validation.

https://t.co/Z14rTahSan

author: FredaDuan
quoted_text:
AI Drug Discovery Is Becoming a Bottleneck Trade

I get excited when an industry starts going through a real regime change. AI drug discovery (“AIDD”) increasingly looks like one of those moments.

Two things are happening:
1/ Upstream: the frontier AI labs are piling in.
2/ Downstream: The supply chain is clearly moving.

Supply-chain checks suggest the upstream picks-and-shovels of discovery and early preclinical R&D are starting to feel the increase in experimental volume.

DNA → protein → assays → sequencing → automation → preclinical testing

Names across that stack include $TWST , @GenScript , $ILMN , $TXG , lab-automation vendors and CROs.

$TWST expects triple-digit percentage growth in AI-enabled drug-discovery orders in FY26, and another year of triple-digit order growth in FY27.

@GenScript's AIDD business doubled YoY in 1H26. Its current platform advertises industrial-scale validation of 4,000+ designs/day, with integrated sequence-to-data workflows. Our channel checks suggest the ramp is moving even faster: roughly 8,000 designs/day currently, with a path toward ~16,000/day by YE26.

---
Why does AI drive more wet-lab demand?

1/ AI makes hypothesis generation almost free → way more shots on goal.
The bottleneck is moving from expert-driven design to biological validation.

2/ AI models need continuous experimental feedback — and both good and bad data are useful.
Traditionally, only the highest-conviction A+ candidates might get pushed into expensive validation. With AI, even the B/C candidates can be valuable because failed experiments generate training data.

@GenScript has said its sequence-to-binding workflow can return data in 4–7 days, and that faster cycle times matter because AI models depend on continuous experimental feedback.

@Anthropic is a clean example. @claudeai  designed 1,320 protein binders. @adaptyvbio  converted those digital sequences into DNA, expressed the proteins and tested binding. Only 354 actually bound. And the 966 failures are not wasted. They are useful negative labels: what does not express, what does not bind, what has poor affinity. Those results help train the next model iteration.

3/ Wet labs are no longer just making drugs. They are making training data.
$TWST  / @GenScript  increasingly look like biological data foundries.

$TWST explicitly talks about generating model-ready data from AI-designed sequences. In some workflows, the customer may care less about receiving the physical protein than about getting structured experimental results back into the model.

Traditional drug discovery asks: “Does candidate X work?”

AI drug discovery also asks: “What can this experiment teach the model?”

---
TAM of AIDD

If AI is simply a better R&D tool, the relevant spending pool is the $300–400B of annual global pharma R&D. If AI meaningfully increases the number of viable drug programs, the opportunity is larger because it expands downstream demand for DNA synthesis, protein production, assays, and preclinical work.

Near term, we can also size demand from AI-company spending. If Anthropic reaches $80B of ARR in 2026 and spends just 1% on AIDD, that alone would imply ~$800M of annual investment.

---
Trade setup

This is a trade that could have long legs. It’s hard to really stop working until PhaseI/II results (2028+)

It smells a lot like the bottleneck trade we just saw in semis: GPUs → HBM → networking → power/cooling. In biology, It basically follows the drug discovery process downstream: AI models → designs → DNA/protein → assays → preclinical capacity.

After the upstream picks-and-shovels, animal testing could become the next bottleneck. Monkey prices are already near prior highs and CRO capacity is tight. AIDD pushing more candidates into preclinical development would only add demand.

?? But clinical trials are still the bottleneck?
This is the biggest pushback I keep coming back to. No matter how fast discovery becomes, drugs still need to go through preclinical → Phase I → Phase II → Phase III → approval. You still need patients, time and capital.

But that doesn’t mean the bottleneck trade won’t work. More viable candidates — especially with higher success rates — still means more demand throughout the development process.

And who knows: clinical trials themselves may eventually be optimized by AI.

?? What breaks the trade?
Near term, the picks-and-shovels trade breaks if experimental budgets stop growing, AI-generated designs don’t translate into useful wet-lab hits, or capacity catches up too quickly.

Longer term, the thesis breaks if AI drugs look great in discovery / Phase I but fail at normal rates in Phase II/III. That is why Phase II matters so much.

?? Milestones
Late 2026–2027: first Isomorphic-designed drugs enter human trials; more AI-native programs move into IND-enabling work / tox.

2028–2030: clinical trial results start telling us whether AI-designed drugs actually perform better than conventional drugs.

Calling all the "bottleneck bros". :) @jukan05 @zephyr_z9 @aleabitoreddit @ParadisLabs 

+++

author: shenpengwdh
quoted_text:
王兴和李想私下里经常推荐的一本书。

《高效能人士的七个习惯》这本书的价值，仍然是被低估的。

我印象中，美团的王兴、理想汽车的李想，还有水滴的沈鹏，都曾在不同场合推荐过这本书。

李想曾经说过，这是他在过去创业和生活的二十多年里，遇到的一本最好的系统和教程。

今天飞深圳，在路上打开微信读书，偶然翻到了之前收藏的一篇文章，是李想早年在理想汽车内部讲《高效能人士的七个习惯》的培训稿。

又从头到尾认真读了一遍，虽然已经工作了十年多，但收获仍然还是非常大。

这本书讲的道理看起来都很简单，但真正理解，并且在工作和生活中用起来，其实挺难的。

整理了一些笔记，分享给大家。

1、我们每天都会关注很多问题，比如今天天气如何，上班路上是否堵车，老板会不会给我涨薪，某个工作该怎么做，房价会不会跌，董宇辉的直播怎么看的人少了。

这些问题中，有些自己可以掌控，有些则无能为力。

如果一个人总把焦点放在那些无能为力的事情上，那久而久之，他会变得消极，凡事喜欢上纲上线，争论一些自己根本没有办法改变的事情。

2、积极主动的人心里清楚，应该把精力放在那些自己能够改变或者影响的事情上。总盯着无能为力的事，比如别人的缺点，或者大环境的问题，那只能让自己越来越消极。

永远把 80% 的精力着眼于自己能够控制和影响的事情上。这样，随着能量的增强，你的影响圈也会越来越大，能够改变的事情也会越来越多。

3、如果我们长期关注那些我们影响不了的事情，那自身的气场、能量会不断缩小；反之，改变自己，积极主动，那做事的能量便会不断增强。

这个思维方式对我的影响是决定性的。我觉得强者和弱者的区别也在这里。

4、《高效能人士的七个习惯》其实是一套完整的个人成长系统。前三个习惯，主动积极、以终为始、要事第一，帮助一个人从依赖走向独立。

接下来三个习惯，双赢思维、知彼解己、统合综效，帮助一个独立的人学会与他人合作。

最后一个习惯，不断更新，让自己能够持续成长。这七个习惯是有先后关系的，一个人只有先做好自己，才有能力与别人建立真正良好的合作关系。

5、一个人是否成年，和年龄没有太大关系。真正的成年人，能够主动做选择，愿意为自己的选择承担责任，而且能够不断地问自己，眼下最重要的事情是什么。

很多人虽然已经工作多年，但依然习惯于等别人安排任务，遇到问题就找外部原因，也不愿意为结果负责。这样的人即使年龄再大，也很难真正独立。

6、主动积极，首先意味着我们有选择如何回应一件事情的权利。

比如看到马云很成功，有人会觉得，他家里一定有背景，所以才能成功。也有人会主动研究他的产品、经营方式，以及他为什么能够把企业做得这么成功。

同样一件事情，前一种反应只会让自己更加消极，后一种反应却可能带来新的知识和经验。

7、人与人之间的差距，很多时候就是这样慢慢拉开的。

在汽车之家，曾经有不少刚毕业的大学生，起点差不多，但工作三年之后，主动积极的人和消极被动的人，在个人能力和产能上可能相差十倍。

因为遇到困难时，积极的人会想办法解决，每解决一个问题，就积累一次经验。

而消极的人习惯于回避问题，认为这件事跟自己没关系。三年下来，两个人积累的经验和能力自然完全不同。

8、主动积极还有一个重要的表现，就是能够控制自己对外界的反应。

2019 年，有媒体批评理想汽车工厂没有建好，杂草丛生，无法按时投产。

面对这样的报道，理想汽车没有选择反击，而是解释工厂的实际情况，承诺及时清理杂草，并向对方提供建设进展，最后还邀请这位媒体朋友参加试驾。

很多时候，别人的行为我们无法控制，但可以选择如何回应。不同的回应方式，往往会让事情走向完全不同的结果。

9、以终为始，就是一个人需要有自己的长期使命和愿景。使命是你为什么而活，愿景是你希望这一辈子成为怎样的人。

它们就像一部人生的宪法，能够帮助你做出重要决定。否则，一个人很容易被外界的评价、要求和各种短期利益牵着走，忙忙碌碌很多年，最后却发现自己根本不知道想要什么。

10、怎么找到自己的使命？有一个很实用的方法，就是先把自己在人生中扮演的不同角色列出来。

比如在公司是管理者，在家里是父亲、丈夫、儿子。然后分别思考，未来五到十年，希望自己成为怎样的管理者，怎么样的父亲和丈夫。

只有把这些问题想清楚，才能知道今天应该把时间花在哪里。

11、很多人觉得工作太忙，没办法照顾家庭。但高质量的陪伴，本身就是需要主动安排的事情。

比如每周只有一天能够陪伴家人，那就应该提前想好带孩子去哪里玩，和妻子去哪里吃饭，每年什么时候安排一次家庭旅行。

如果每次都等家人问起来，才用一句随便应付过去，那家庭生活的质量自然很难提高。真正重要的事情，应该提前进入自己的日程。

12、要事第一，核心是找到真正重要的事情，然后把时间和精力集中在上面。

比如一个 CEO，每天可能有十五件事情需要处理，但真正安排的只有三件，而且这三件事必须和周计划、月计划、年计划有关。

因为在实际工作中，头部 10%的重要事情，往往决定了大部分结果。

一个人每天做了多少事情，并不能说明他有多高效，更重要的是，他有没有把最重要的事情做好。

13、什么事情最重要，取决于你当前的角色和所处的阶段。

比如一家公司即将完成产品研发，准备进入下一个发展阶段，此时 CEO 最重要的职责可能就是组织建设。

如果每天忙着做销售、参加各种会议，看起来非常勤奋，但公司的组织能力始终没有建立起来，那就是没有抓住要事。

所以，做好时间管理，还有一个非常重要的能力，就是知道哪些事情可以不做。

14、双赢思维的基础，是尊重别人和自己不一样，也尊重自己和别人不一样。

不断在所有人际关系中寻求互惠互利的一种思维和情感模式。

没有格局和胸怀是根本不可能达成合作的，你要敢于接受别人的不一样。

人与人之间的差异，本身就可能创造价值。

如果一个人永远要求别人和自己保持一致，就很难找到真正能够互补的合作伙伴。

15、我觉得吧，《高效能人士的七个习惯》很大程度上说的就是一个人的思维方式。什么是思维方式，其实就是我们遇到事情时的应激反应机制。

而思维方式，是可以刻意练习和调整的。

A pattern can be perfectly ordered without ever repeating itself. Penrose tiling demonstrates this using just two kinds of rhombus, arranged according to precise matching rules. The resulting geometry has no repeating unit cell, yet it contains remarkable mathematical order.

The golden ratio appears naturally in its structure, while fivefold symmetry emerges without ordinary periodic repetition. This reveals something deeper about geometry: order does not necessarily require periodicity, a principle also found in the atomic arrangements of quasicrystals.
